nlp-classical-q1.testing: whether you place a preprocessing step by who consumes its output, instead of reciting two definitions.
nlp-classical-q1.trap: recommending either one as default preprocessing in front of a transformer.
nlp-classical-q1.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "Both collapse inflected forms so that run, runs and running match. Stemming chops suffixes by rule. Lemmatization looks the word up, with its part of speech, and returns the dictionary form."
2 · Where stemming wins "Stemming belongs in a search index. It is fast, needs no dictionary, and nobody ever reads the stems, so an ugly stem like 'studi' costs nothing and buys recall."
3 · Where lemmatization wins "Lemmatization belongs where a person or a downstream rule sees the output: keyword lists, aspect extraction, linguistic features. There 'better' has to become 'good', not stay a fragment."
4 · The deciding question "So I ask one thing: does anyone read the normalised form, or is it only a matching key?"
5 · What I'd pick in 2026 "In the neural path I use neither. Subword tokenizers and context already handle morphology, and chopping words removes signal the model was trained on."
Close "So: stemming for the sparse index, lemmatization for visible output, raw text for transformers."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
"Same goal, two mechanisms: one cuts by rule, one maps through a vocabulary."

Stemming Lemmatization
How suffix-stripping rules (Porter, Snowball) dictionary plus morphology, needs the part of speech
Output may not be a word (studi) always a dictionary form (study)
Speed very fast, no model slower: a tagger runs first
Typical error merges unrelated words, or misses irregular ones wrong lemma when the tag is wrong
Pick when matching key nobody reads output is read or reasoned over

stages.name: Where stemming wins
stages.html:
"A stem is a matching key. If it matches, it has done its job."

Prove it — rule against dictionary:

def stem(w):                                   # toy rules in the spirit of Porter
    for suf, rep in (("ies", "i"), ("ing", ""), ("es", ""), ("s", "")):
        if w.endswith(suf): return w[: -len(suf)] + rep
    return w
lemma = {"studies": "study", "running": "run", "better": "good", "was": "be"}   # dictionary + POS
for w in ("studies", "running", "better", "was"):
    print(w, "→", stem(w), "|", lemma.get(w, w))
# → studies → studi | study
# → running → runn | run
# → better → better | good
# → was → wa | be
In an index:document texttokenisestempostings list
At query time:query texttokenisesame stemmerlookup
  • The rule never learns that better belongs with good, and it leaves wa for was. In an index that only costs a little precision.
  • The index and the query must run the same analyzer, or nothing matches.

stages.name: Where lemmatization wins
stages.html:
"When the normalised form is shown or counted, it has to be a real word with the right sense."

Input Part of speech Lemma Why a stemmer can't do it
saw verb see irregular form, no suffix to strip
saw noun saw same string, different lemma
better adjective good suppletive form
meeting noun meeting a stemmer cuts it to meet

Example: an aspect-based sentiment report that lists "batteri" and "deliveri" as top complaint topics is unreadable. Lemmas give "battery" and "delivery".

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html:
Who consumes the normalised text Use Because
an inverted index (BM25) stemming recall matters, throughput is high, stems are hidden
a person, a report, a rule engine lemmatization the form must be a correct word
a TF-IDF or linear classifier on little data either, test both smaller vocabulary helps sparse features
a transformer neither its tokenizer expects raw text

stages.name: What I'd pick in 2026
stages.html:
"Over-normalising is now the bigger risk than under-normalising."

Sparse arm of hybrid search:raw textanalyzer with stemmingBM25
Dense arm:raw textmodel's subword tokenizerembedding
  • A stemmed string was rarely seen in pre-training, so it splits into odd subword pieces.
  • Both techniques survive as index-time analyzers and in cheap, low-resource pipelines.

Why this matters: the same document can be stemmed for one arm and left raw for the other. The choice is per consumer, not per corpus.

followUps.question: What are over-stemming and under-stemming?
followUps.html:
Two opposite errors of a rule-based stemmer.

Error Example (Porter) Effect on search
Over-stemming universe, university both become univers unrelated documents match: precision drops
Under-stemming alumnus and alumni keep different stems related documents miss: recall drops

followUps.question: "Stemming is cheap, so do it before BERT anyway."
followUps.html:
No. It moves the input away from what the model was trained on.

runningmodel's tokenizerknown pieces
runnmodel's tokenizerrare, odd pieces

The embedding of a rare fragment is worse than the embedding of the original word.

followUps.question: Why does a lemmatizer need a part-of-speech tag?
followUps.html:
Because the same string has different lemmas in different roles.

Token Tag Lemma
leaves noun leaf
leaves verb leave

A wrong tag gives a wrong lemma, so tagger accuracy caps lemmatizer accuracy.

followUps.question: Does this hold for Turkish, Finnish or Hindi?
followUps.html:
Less well: suffix rules written for English break on rich morphology.

  • Agglutinative languages: one word carries many suffixes, so a light stemmer under-stems badly.
  • What works: a language-specific analyzer, a morphological lemmatizer, or character n-grams in the index.
  • Neural path: a multilingual subword tokenizer, unchanged.

followUps.question: You want to change the stemmer on a live index. What does it cost?
followUps.html:
A full reindex, because old postings were written with the old stems.

Safe rollout:build a second indexreplay queries on bothcompare recall and NDCGswitch the aliasdrop the old index

Changing only the query-side analyzer silently breaks matching for every stemmed term.

dontSay: "Lemmatization is just better stemming" — they serve different consumers; in an index the extra cost buys little.
"Always lowercase, remove stopwords and stem first" — that is a sparse-feature habit and it damages transformer input.
"Stemming gives the root word" — it gives a stem, which is often not a word at all.

nlp-classical-q2.testing: whether you can state the training rule of each algorithm in one line, and then turn it into a consequence for cost and retrieval.
nlp-classical-q2.trap: describing all three as "they split words into pieces" with no difference in how the vocabulary is chosen.
nlp-classical-q2.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "Subwords won because they sit between two failures. Word vocabularies can't cover new words, so information is lost to an unknown token. Characters cover everything but make sequences long and each unit weak."
2 · How each one builds "The three differ in how they pick the vocabulary. BPE starts from characters and merges the most frequent adjacent pair, again and again. WordPiece also merges, but scores a pair by how much more often it occurs than its parts would predict. Unigram goes the other way: it starts with a large vocabulary and prunes the pieces whose removal hurts corpus likelihood least."
3 · Prove it "On a four-word toy corpus, BPE's first merges are 'es', then 'est', then 'lo' and 'low': frequent endings become single tokens."
4 · What it costs or breaks "The cost is that token counts depend on the corpus the tokenizer was trained on. Rare words, numbers, IDs and under-represented languages split into many pieces."
5 · So what for the system "So I count tokens with the target model's tokenizer, never swap a tokenizer without the model, and keep keyword search next to embeddings for IDs."
Close "Frequency, likelihood gain, or likelihood pruning: three ways to learn the same compromise."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
"Common words stay whole, rare words break into pieces, nothing is unknown."

Unit Vocabulary Sequence length Fails on
Words unbounded, grows with morphology short new words become UNK
Characters tiny very long each unit carries little meaning
Subwords fixed, chosen (tens of thousands) moderate rare strings split into many pieces

stages.name: How each one builds
stages.claim: merge by count, merge by gain, prune
stages.html:
BPE WordPiece Unigram
Starts from characters or bytes characters a large candidate vocabulary
Each step merge the most frequent pair merge the pair with the best score drop the pieces that cost least likelihood
Segmenting new text replay the merges in order longest match first best-scoring split (Viterbi)
Seen in GPT family, RoBERTa (byte-level) BERT family T5, XLNet, ALBERT via SentencePiece 
BPE        pick the pair (a, b) with the highest count(ab)
WordPiece  pick the pair with the highest count(ab) / (count(a) × count(b))   ← frequent together, not just frequent
Unigram    P(split) = Π p(piece) ; keep the vocabulary that maximises corpus likelihood

SentencePiece is the packaging: it trains BPE or Unigram on raw text and treats the space as a symbol, so it needs no whitespace pre-tokenisation. That matters for Japanese, Chinese and Thai.

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: four BPE merges on a toy corpus
stages.html:
Prove it:

import re
from collections import Counter
words = {"l o w": 5, "l o w e r": 2, "n e w e s t": 6, "w i d e s t": 3}   # word → count
for step in range(1, 5):
    pairs = Counter()
    for w, f in words.items():
        s = w.split()
        for a, b in zip(s, s[1:]): pairs[a, b] += f
    (a, b), n = pairs.most_common(1)[0]
    pat = re.compile(rf"(?<!\S){re.escape(a)} {re.escape(b)}(?!\S)")
    words = {pat.sub(a + b, w): f for w, f in words.items()}
    print(step, f"{a}+{b}", n)
print(list(words))
# → 1 e+s 9
# → 2 es+t 9
# → 3 l+o 7
# → 4 lo+w 7
# → ['low', 'low e r', 'n e w est', 'w i d est']
Merge Pair Count What it shows
1 e + s 9 the pair shared by newest and widest wins
2 es + t 9 a suffix became one token after two merges
3–4 l+o, lo+w 7 a whole frequent word is built next

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.claim: the corpus decides what is cheap
stages.html:
Where Symptom Why
Cost and context the same sentence is more tokens in some languages their strings were rarer in the tokenizer's training corpus
Numbers 12345678 becomes several digit chunks merges follow frequency, not place value
IDs and SKUs fragments with weak embeddings no merge ever covered that string
Whitespace a leading space changes the token the space is part of the piece

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.claim: the tokenizer is part of the model
stages.html:
Budgeting:sample real traffic per languagecount with the model's tokenizerset limits in tokens
  • Never swap a tokenizer under a trained model: the ID-to-embedding mapping is learned.
  • Retrieval: keep a BM25 arm for codes and rare names (layer: retrieval).
  • Unigram sampling of alternative splits is a training-time augmentation, not an inference setting.

followUps.question: Why does byte-level BPE never produce an unknown token?
followUps.html:
Because the base vocabulary is all 256 byte values.

any stringUTF-8 bytesapply learned mergesworst case: one token per byte

An unseen script or emoji is expensive, never unrepresentable.

followUps.question: "A bigger vocabulary is always better."
followUps.html:
No. It trades sequence length against table size and data per token.

Vocabulary Sequences Embedding and output table Rare tokens
Small longer small few, each well trained
Large shorter large many, each seen rarely

followUps.question: 🧪 After the four merges above, how is "lowest" segmented?
followUps.html:
low + est: two tokens, though "lowest" was never in the corpus.

l o w e s t
→ l o w es t      ← merge 1 (e+s)
→ l o w est       ← merge 2 (es+t)
→ lo w est        ← merge 3 (l+o)
→ low est         ← merge 4 (lo+w)

That generalisation to unseen words is the reason subwords won.

followUps.question: How does Unigram's subword regularisation work?
followUps.html:
It samples a segmentation instead of always taking the best one.

  • Training: the same word appears under several splits, which acts as augmentation.
  • Inference: use the single best split, for determinism.
  • Helps most: low-resource translation and noisy text.

followUps.question: You're migrating to a model with a different tokenizer. What changes operationally?
followUps.html:
Every number measured in tokens is void until re-measured.

Re-measure Why
Cost and rate limits tokens per request change, unevenly per language
Chunk sizes a chunk sized for the old tokenizer may overflow
Truncation and stop sequences boundaries fall in different places

dontSay: "They all just split words into pieces" — the selection rule is the whole question.
"WordPiece is BPE with a different name" — the scoring differs, and so does segmentation at inference.
"Tokens are roughly words" — the ratio moves with language, domain and tokenizer.

nlp-classical-q3.testing: whether you know which preprocessing belongs to sparse features and which to pre-trained models, and can prove the damage instead of asserting it.
nlp-classical-q3.trap: saying "remove it all" without a measurement, or defending the pipeline because "clean text is good".
nlp-classical-q3.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name it "This is a bag-of-words pipeline placed in front of a model that was pre-trained on natural text. Each step was designed to shrink a sparse vocabulary. A transformer has no such problem."
2 · What each step destroys "Lowercasing removes case, which a cased model uses for names. Stopword removal deletes 'not' and the function words that carry syntax. Stemming produces strings the tokenizer has rarely seen, so they split into odd pieces."
3 · Confirm with evidence "I'd show it: after the pipeline, 'this is not working' and 'this is working' become the same input."
4 · Fix by experiment "Then I'd run one change at a time on the same evaluation set: raw text first, then keep only safe cleaning such as Unicode normalisation and stripping markup."
5 · Validate "I'd compare on slices, not only the aggregate: negation, named entities and short texts are where the difference shows."
6 · Productionise "Whatever wins becomes one shared function used in training and in serving, with the tokenizer version pinned."
Close "Clean the noise, keep the language: the model's own tokenizer does the rest."

stages.name: Name it
stages.claim: a sparse-feature habit on a neural model
stages.html:
"These steps solve a problem this model does not have."

TF-IDF or linear model Pre-trained transformer
Vocabulary problem every surface form is a separate feature subwords share pieces across forms
Word order and function words ignored anyway used by attention
What normalisation buys fewer, denser features nothing: it moves input off the training distribution

stages.name: What each step destroys
stages.html:
Step What is lost Who is hurt
Lowercase Apple the company against apple the fruit, US against us NER and any cased model (an uncased model lowercases by itself)
Stopword removal not, no, but, prepositions sentiment, intent, entailment, relation extraction
Stemming real word forms every task: stems fragment into rare subwords
What the model sees:workingknown subwordsgood embedding
After stemming:work from working, hir from hiringrare piecesworse embedding

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.html:
Prove it — the pipeline on three inputs:

stop = {"the", "is", "not", "a", "this", "was"}
def old_pipeline(t):
    return [w[:-3] if w.endswith("ing") else w for w in t.lower().split() if w not in stop]
for t in ("This is not working", "This is working", "Apple is hiring"):
    print(t, "→", old_pipeline(t))
# → This is not working → ['work']
# → This is working → ['work']
# → Apple is hiring → ['apple', 'hir']
Observation Likely cause Next action
opposite sentences give identical input not is on the stopword list drop stopword removal first
Apple and apple are identical lowercasing in front of a cased model remove it, or switch to the uncased checkpoint on purpose
hir appears in the input stemming remove it
errors cluster on negated examples the above, visible in a slice build a negation slice in the evaluation set

stages.name: Fix by experiment
stages.html:
Experiment 1

Raw text

I'd feed the unprocessed text straight into the model's tokenizer and retrain or re-evaluate.

Why? It is the input distribution the model was pre-trained on, so it is the baseline every other variant must beat.

Best suited when the text is already reasonably clean.

Experiment 2

Minimal cleaning only

I'd add Unicode normalisation (NFC), strip HTML and boilerplate, and collapse repeated whitespace.

Why? These remove noise without removing language.

Best suited when the source is scraped pages, emails or chat logs.

Keep Drop
Unicode normalisation, markup stripping, PII masking where required stopword removal, stemming, lemmatization
a truncation policy that keeps the informative part blanket lowercasing for a cased model

stages.name: Validate
stages.html:
Slice Why it is sensitive Metric
Negation ("not", "never", "no longer") stopword removal flips the meaning measure
Named entities case carries the signal measure
Short texts each deleted word is a large share of the input measure
Aggregate can hide all three measure

I'd also check that the gain is larger than run-to-run noise: several seeds, or a bootstrap interval on the difference.

stages.name: Productionise
stages.claim: one function for train and serve
stages.html:
One path:raw textclean() from a shared packagepinned tokenizermodel
  • A preprocessing step that exists in the training notebook but not in the service is training-serving skew.
  • The sparse arm of a hybrid retriever keeps its own analyzer: stemming is still right there.

followUps.question: Is any normalisation still worth doing before a transformer?
followUps.html:
Yes: the kind that removes noise, not words.

  • Unicode normalisation: one code-point sequence per visible string.
  • Markup and boilerplate removal: navigation text, signatures, tracking parameters.
  • PII masking: when policy requires it, applied the same way in training and serving.

followUps.question: "Stopwords are noise, removing them speeds things up."
followUps.html:
True for a bag of words, wrong for a model that reads order.

Sentence After stopword removal
"to be or not to be" empty
"flights from Delhi to Pune" direction is lost

The saving in tokens is small and the meaning lost is not.

followUps.question: The old pipeline scores higher on your test set. Now what?
followUps.html:
Suspect the comparison before the conclusion.

Check What it would reveal
was the model fine-tuned on stemmed text? it has adapted: compare after retraining on raw text
is the test set tiny or one seed? the gap may be noise
is the data so small that sparsity dominates? then a TF-IDF baseline may be the honest winner

followUps.question: Cased or uncased checkpoint?
followUps.html:
Cased when capitalisation is signal, uncased when it is noise.

Text Choice
news, contracts, NER cased
social posts, search queries, ASR output uncased

Either way the tokenizer handles it. Lowercasing by hand in front of a cased model is the mistake.

followUps.question: How do you stop this class of bug returning?
followUps.html:
Make preprocessing a versioned artefact with a test.

Guard:shared clean()unit test with negation and case examplesversion stored with the modelserving loads the same version

A golden-input test that asserts "not working" and "working" stay different would have caught this in review.

dontSay: "Clean text is always better" — clean of noise, yes; clean of language, no.
"Stopwords carry no information" — negation and prepositions are stopwords.
"Just remove everything" without proposing the measurement that proves it.

nlp-classical-q4.testing: whether you can derive the two terms from first principles, and name where a 1970s weighting scheme still earns its place.
nlp-classical-q4.trap: calling it obsolete because embeddings exist.
nlp-classical-q4.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "TF-IDF scores a word in a document by how often it appears there, discounted by how many documents contain it. A word matters when it is frequent here and rare elsewhere."
2 · How it works "Term frequency says what this document is about. Inverse document frequency is the log of total documents over documents containing the term, so a word in every document gets zero and a rare word gets a high weight. The log keeps a word that is a thousand times rarer from being a thousand times more important."
3 · Prove it "On three toy documents, 'the' scores zero everywhere, 'sat' scores a little in two, and 'invoice' scores highest in the one document that has it."
4 · What it costs or breaks "It has no notion of meaning: 'car' and 'automobile' are unrelated columns. And raw term frequency keeps growing with repetition and document length, which is what BM25 fixes."
5 · So what for the system "It is still everywhere because it needs no GPU, no training data and is fully explainable. It is the baseline for text classification, the idea inside BM25, and the keyword arm of hybrid retrieval."
Close "I start with it, measure, and only add a model where it beats that baseline."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
"A word is a good descriptor of a document when it is common in that document and uncommon in the collection."

Word in a support-ticket corpus In this ticket In the corpus Weight
the many times every ticket near zero
refund twice many tickets moderate
chargeback twice few tickets high

stages.name: How it works
stages.claim: a count times a rarity score
stages.html:
tf(t, d)   = count of t in d / length of d          ← what this document talks about
idf(t)     = log( N / df(t) )                       ← N documents, df(t) of them contain t
tfidf(t,d) = tf(t, d) × idf(t)

df = N        →  idf = log 1 = 0                    ← a word in every document carries no information
df = N / 1000 →  idf = log 1000 ≈ 6.9               ← the log damps rarity
  • Why a log: IDF is the information content of "this document contains t", which is −log P(t).
  • Variants: sublinear TF (1 + log tf), smoothed IDF (log((1+N)/(1+df)) + 1, the scikit-learn default), then L2-normalised rows so cosine similarity works.
Pipeline:documentstokenisecountweight by IDFsparse vector per document

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: three documents, three kinds of word
stages.html:
Prove it — plain TF × log(N/df):

import math
docs = ["the cat sat on the mat", "the dog sat on the log", "the invoice total is overdue"]
N = len(docs); toks = [d.split() for d in docs]
def tfidf(term, i):
    tf = toks[i].count(term) / len(toks[i])
    df = sum(term in t for t in toks)
    return round(tf * math.log(N / df), 3)
for term in ("the", "sat", "invoice"):
    print(term, [tfidf(term, i) for i in range(N)])
# → the [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
# → sat [0.068, 0.068, 0.0]
# → invoice [0.0, 0.0, 0.22]
Term Document frequency Result
the 3 of 3 zero everywhere: no stopword list needed
sat 2 of 3 small weight in both
invoice 1 of 3 the highest weight, only in its document

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.html:
Limit Symptom Fix, and its layer
No semantics "car" misses "automobile" dense retrieval or query expansion (retrieval)
Linear TF repeating a word keeps raising the score BM25 saturation
Length bias long documents collect more matches BM25 length normalisation
Vocabulary is fitted new terms at serving time are dropped refit on a schedule; fit on training data only

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.claim: the baseline and the keyword arm
stages.html:
Use in 2026 Why TF-IDF
Text-classification baseline TF-IDF plus logistic regression trains in seconds and is hard to beat on topical tasks
Keyword arm of hybrid search exact terms, IDs and rare names that embeddings blur
Keyword extraction, deduplication, feature for a ranker cheap and interpretable
Explaining a result the top-weighted terms are the explanation

Evaluation hook: any proposed model is reported as a delta over this baseline on the same split.

followUps.question: Where is the leak if I fit TF-IDF before splitting the data?
followUps.html:
IDF and the vocabulary are learned statistics, so fitting on all data leaks the test set.

Wrong:fit on all textsplittrainscore
Right:splitfit on train onlytransform validation and testscore

In scikit-learn the vectoriser goes inside the Pipeline so cross-validation refits it per fold.

followUps.question: How is BM25 different?
followUps.html:
Same idea, with two corrections to term frequency.

TF-IDF BM25
Repeated terms score grows linearly saturates (parameter k1)
Document length long documents favoured normalised (parameter b)

followUps.question: 🧪 A term appears in 10 of 1,000 documents and 5 times in a 100-word document. Its score?
followUps.html:
About 0.23 with natural log.

tf    = 5 / 100          = 0.05
idf   = ln(1000 / 10)    = ln 100 ≈ 4.605
tfidf = 0.05 × 4.605     ≈ 0.23

followUps.question: When does TF-IDF beat an embedding model?
followUps.html:
When the signal is in specific words, not in paraphrase.

  • Exact identifiers: error codes, SKUs, legal citations.
  • Topical classification with plenty of text per document.
  • Tight latency or no GPU: a sparse dot product is microseconds.

followUps.question: How would you justify shipping TF-IDF plus a linear model instead of an LLM call?
followUps.html:
By the measured gap against the cost and latency of closing it.

Dimension TF-IDF + linear LLM call
Latency sub-millisecond, in process network round trip
Cost per request negligible per token
Explainability weights per term needs extra work
Quality measure measure

If the quality gap is small on the eval set, the cheap model handles the bulk and the LLM takes only low-confidence cases.

dontSay: "TF-IDF is dead" — it is the baseline, the BM25 ancestor and half of hybrid search.
"IDF is just a heuristic" — it is the information content of a term's presence.
"I'd fit the vectoriser on the full dataset" — that leaks.

nlp-classical-q5.testing: whether you know what each measure ignores, and when two of them rank identically.
nlp-classical-q5.trap: "cosine is for text" with no reason, or not knowing that on unit vectors cosine and Euclidean give the same ranking.
nlp-classical-q5.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "The three differ in what they ignore. Cosine ignores vector length and compares direction. Jaccard ignores counts and compares sets. Euclidean ignores nothing, so length differences dominate."
2 · Where cosine wins "Cosine is the default for weighted vectors, TF-IDF or embeddings, because a long document and a short one on the same topic point the same way."
3 · Where Jaccard wins "Jaccard is right when the objects are sets: shingles for near-duplicate detection, tag sets, token overlap. It also has MinHash, which estimates it at billion-document scale."
4 · Where Euclidean fits "Euclidean only makes sense when magnitude means something, or when vectors are already normalised. On unit vectors, squared Euclidean distance is two minus two times cosine, so the ranking is identical."
5 · The deciding question "So the choice changes the answer in two cases: when lengths differ a lot, and when counts matter. For embeddings I use whatever the model was trained with."
Close "I pick the measure by what should be ignored: length, counts, or nothing."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
cosine(a, b)    = a·b / (‖a‖ ‖b‖)            ← direction only; length cancels
jaccard(A, B)   = |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|          ← set overlap; counts and weights ignored
euclidean(a, b) = ‖a − b‖                    ← absolute position; length differences count
Cosine Jaccard Euclidean
Input weighted vectors sets vectors
Ignores magnitude frequency and weights nothing
Range −1 to 1 (0 to 1 for non-negative text vectors) 0 to 1 0 upward (a distance)

stages.name: Where cosine wins
stages.html:
Prove it — one document against a 10× copy of itself, and against a partial match:

import math
a = {"refund": 1, "order": 1}; b = {"refund": 10, "order": 10}; c = {"refund": 1, "delay": 1}
def cos(x, y):
    dot = sum(x[k] * y.get(k, 0) for k in x)
    return round(dot / (math.hypot(*x.values()) * math.hypot(*y.values())), 2)
def euc(x, y): return round(math.sqrt(sum((x.get(k, 0) - y.get(k, 0)) ** 2 for k in set(x) | set(y))), 2)
def jac(x, y): return round(len(set(x) & set(y)) / len(set(x) | set(y)), 2)
for name, y in (("b = a repeated 10x", b), ("c = one shared word", c)):
    print(name, "| cosine", cos(a, y), "| euclidean", euc(a, y), "| jaccard", jac(a, y))
# → b = a repeated 10x | cosine 1.0 | euclidean 12.73 | jaccard 1.0
# → c = one shared word | cosine 0.5 | euclidean 1.41 | jaccard 0.33
Pair Cosine Euclidean Reading
a against a repeated 10× 1.0 12.73 cosine says identical; Euclidean says far apart
a against one shared word 0.5 1.41 Euclidean ranks the partial match closer than the copy

Why this matters: on raw counts, Euclidean distance mostly measures document length.

stages.name: Where Jaccard wins
stages.html:
Near-duplicate detection:documentword shinglessetMinHash signatureLSH bucketscandidate pairs
Use Why Jaccard
Near-duplicate pages overlap of shingle sets is exactly the question
Tag or category sets there are no counts to weight
Quick lexical overlap of two short strings no vectors or IDF needed

Where it fails: it treats the and chargeback as equal members, and a document that repeats a term 50 times looks the same as one that mentions it once.

stages.name: Where Euclidean fits
stages.html:
for unit vectors (‖a‖ = ‖b‖ = 1):
‖a − b‖²  =  ‖a‖² + ‖b‖² − 2 a·b  =  2 − 2·cos(a, b)      ← same ranking, opposite direction
Situation Verdict
L2-normalised embeddings cosine, dot product and Euclidean rank identically: pick the one the index is fastest with
Raw count vectors Euclidean is dominated by length: avoid
k-means on embeddings uses Euclidean, so normalise first (spherical k-means)

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html:
If the data is And you want to ignore Use
TF-IDF or embedding vectors document length cosine
embeddings from a model trained with dot product nothing the model learned dot product, as trained
sets of shingles or tags counts Jaccard
normalised vectors in an ANN index — any of the three: same order

Example: for a deduplication job I'd use Jaccard over shingles for copy-paste duplicates, and cosine over embeddings for paraphrased ones. They catch different things.

followUps.question: Dot product or cosine for embeddings?
followUps.html:
The one the embedding model was trained with.

Model trained with Use Note
cosine or normalised output either: they are equal on unit vectors most sentence-embedding models
dot product, unnormalised dot product magnitude carries learned signal, often popularity

followUps.question: "Cosine similarity of 0.8 means they are 80% similar."
followUps.html:
No. The number has no absolute meaning across models.

  • Anisotropy: some embedding spaces put every pair above 0.6.
  • Use it to rank, and set thresholds per model from labelled pairs.
  • Changing the model invalidates every stored threshold.

followUps.question: 🧪 Two unit vectors have cosine 0.5. Their Euclidean distance?
followUps.html:
Exactly 1.

‖a − b‖² = 2 − 2 × 0.5 = 1
‖a − b‖  = 1

followUps.question: Is there a weighted version of Jaccard?
followUps.html:
Yes: sum of minimums over sum of maximums.

weighted_jaccard(a, b) = Σ min(aᵢ, bᵢ) / Σ max(aᵢ, bᵢ)      ← equals plain Jaccard on 0/1 vectors

It keeps counts or IDF weights while staying a set-style overlap.

followUps.question: How does the metric constrain your vector index?
followUps.html:
It is fixed at index build time, so a mismatch is a silent quality bug.

Check before launch:model card states the metricindex created with the same metricvectors normalised if requiredrecall@k measured against exact search

An index built for Euclidean distance over unnormalised dot-product embeddings still returns results, just the wrong ones.

dontSay: "Cosine is always best for text" — not for sets, and not for a model trained with dot product.
"Euclidean and cosine are completely different" — on unit vectors they rank identically.
"0.8 is a good similarity" — thresholds are per model and need labelled pairs.
