nlp-classical-q6.testing: whether you can state the training objective, explain why negative sampling exists, and connect it to how embeddings are trained today.
nlp-classical-q6.trap: stopping at "king minus man plus woman equals queen".
nlp-classical-q6.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "Word2Vec learns a vector per word by training a tiny classifier on a fake task: given a word, predict the words around it. The vectors are the by-product we keep."
2 · How it works "Skip-gram slides a window over text and makes centre-context pairs. A full softmax over the vocabulary would be too expensive per pair, so negative sampling turns it into binary classification: the real pair scores high, a handful of randomly drawn words score low."
3 · Prove it "Negatives are drawn from the unigram distribution raised to the three-quarters power. On a toy vocabulary that moves a rare word from under one percent to about two and a half percent of the draws."
4 · What it costs or breaks "The limit is one vector per word: 'bank' the river and 'bank' the lender share it. Unseen words have no vector at all."
5 · So what for the system "It still matters because the recipe survived. Sentence-embedding models, two-tower recommenders and item2vec all train by pulling true pairs together against sampled negatives."
Close "The vectors were replaced; the contrastive training idea was not."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
"You shall know a word by the company it keeps, turned into a training objective."

The idea:raw text(centre, context) pairstrain a shallow classifierkeep the input weights as word vectors
Variant Predicts Better for
Skip-gram context words from the centre word rare words, smaller corpora
CBOW centre word from averaged context speed, frequent words

stages.name: How it works
stages.claim: real pairs up, sampled pairs down
stages.html:
full softmax        P(c | w) = exp(u_c · v_w) / Σ over all V words exp(u_j · v_w)     ← V dot products per pair
negative sampling   maximise  log σ(u_c · v_w)  +  Σ over k negatives  log σ(−u_n · v_w)
                              └ real pair → 1 ┘     └ k random words → 0 ┘
Trick What it does
Negative sampling updates k + 1 output vectors per pair instead of the whole vocabulary
Sampling ∝ count^0.75 rare words are drawn as negatives more often than raw frequency would give
Subsampling frequent words drops many the, of tokens, which widens the effective window

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
Prove it — share of negative draws, raw frequency → frequency^0.75:

counts = {"the": 1000, "model": 100, "tokenizer": 10}
total = sum(counts.values())
p75 = {w: c ** 0.75 for w, c in counts.items()}; z = sum(p75.values())
for w, c in counts.items():
    print(w, round(c / total, 3), "→", round(p75[w] / z, 3))
# → the 0.901 → 0.827
# → model 0.09 → 0.147
# → tokenizer 0.009 → 0.026

vocabulary V = 100,000, k = 5 negatives      (illustrative)
full softmax        100,000 output vectors touched per pair
negative sampling   5 + 1 = 6 output vectors touched per pair

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.html:
Limit Symptom What replaced it
Polysemy bank, apple, python get one blended vector contextual embeddings (ELMo, then BERT)
Out-of-vocabulary a new word or typo has no vector fastText character n-grams, then subwords
No word order beyond the window "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" average the same sequence models
Bias corpus stereotypes show up in the geometry measurement and mitigation at the application layer

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html:
Today's system The Word2Vec idea inside it
Sentence-embedding models contrastive loss with in-batch negatives
Two-tower retrieval and recommenders sampled negatives, dot-product scoring
item2vec, node2vec sessions or graph walks treated as sentences
Cheap on-device or CPU features static vectors, averaged, into a linear model

Why this matters: knowing how negatives are chosen is the lever for embedding quality today, in the form of hard-negative mining.

followUps.question: Why 0.75 and not raw frequency?
followUps.html:
It was chosen empirically (Mikolov et al., 2013) to flatten the distribution.

Sampling Effect
raw frequency negatives are almost always the, of: easy, uninformative
uniform too many very rare words: noisy
frequency^0.75 in between: rare words get useful updates

followUps.question: "The king − man + woman = queen result shows the model understands gender."
followUps.html:
It shows that co-occurrence statistics are roughly linear in this space, nothing more.

  • The usual evaluation excludes the three input words from the candidates, which flatters the result.
  • Analogies are an intrinsic test and correlate weakly with downstream task quality.
  • The same geometry encodes corpus bias.

followUps.question: 🧪 "the cat sat on mats", window 2. How many skip-gram pairs?
followUps.html:
Fourteen.

context sizes per position:  2 + 3 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 14 (centre, context) pairs
with k = 5 negatives:        14 × (1 + 5) = 84 binary examples

followUps.question: How do GloVe and fastText differ?
followUps.html:
Same goal, different statistic or unit.

Model Trains on Adds
Word2Vec local windows, one pair at a time —
GloVe the global co-occurrence matrix uses corpus-wide counts directly
fastText windows, with words as bags of character n-grams vectors for unseen and misspelled words

followUps.question: When would you still train static embeddings in 2026?
followUps.html:
When the "words" are not language, or the budget rules out a transformer.

  • Non-text sequences: product IDs in sessions, merchant codes, log event types.
  • Tight latency or on-device: a lookup table and an average.
  • A feature for a ranker: cheap similarity signals alongside heavier ones.

dontSay: "Word2Vec is a deep neural network" — it is one hidden layer with no non-linearity.
"It understands meaning" — it compresses co-occurrence counts.
"Nobody uses this any more" — the training recipe is in every embedding model.

nlp-classical-q7.testing: whether you know that a model produces good similarity only if it was trained for similarity, and can place bi-encoders and cross-encoders correctly.
nlp-classical-q7.trap: "BERT understands sentences, so its average must be a good sentence vector."
nlp-classical-q7.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "BERT was trained to predict masked tokens. Nothing in that objective asks two similar sentences to end up close under cosine similarity, so the averaged vectors don't."
2 · Why averaging fails "The raw token vectors sit in a narrow cone: they share a large common direction driven by frequency. Average them and every sentence looks similar to every other one."
3 · Prove it "A toy shows it. With a big shared component, a refund sentence scores about one against a paraphrase and about one against a weather sentence. Remove the mean and they separate."
4 · What fixed it "The fix was training for the task. Sentence-BERT put two copies of the encoder side by side and fine-tuned on sentence pairs. Later models use a contrastive loss with in-batch and hard negatives."
5 · So what for the system "In a system that gives me a bi-encoder for fast retrieval over millions of vectors, and I add a cross-encoder to rerank the top few, because scoring every pair jointly doesn't scale."
Close "Similarity is a trained behaviour, so I use a model trained for it and pool the way its card says."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: the objective never asked for similarity
stages.html:
Model Trained to Is cosine between sentences meaningful?
BERT, pre-trained only fill in masked tokens no
BERT as a cross-encoder score a pair fed together yes, but one forward pass per pair
Sentence-embedding model place similar sentences close yes: that is the loss

stages.name: Why averaging fails
stages.html:
"The vectors occupy a narrow cone, so cosine is high for everything."

What happens:token vectorslarge frequency-driven common componentmean poolall sentence vectors point nearly the same way
  • This is called anisotropy.
  • The [CLS] vector has the same problem before fine-tuning: it was trained for next-sentence prediction, not similarity.
  • On semantic-similarity benchmarks, averaged BERT vectors did worse than averaged GloVe vectors (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019).

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: remove the common part and pairs separate
stages.html:
Prove it — three toy sentence vectors, each a shared component plus a small own part:

import math
def cos(x, y): return round(sum(a * b for a, b in zip(x, y)) / (math.hypot(*x) * math.hypot(*y)), 2)
common = [5, 5, 5]                                   # the direction every sentence shares (toy)
own = {"refund": [1, 0, 0], "money back": [0.9, 0.1, 0], "weather": [0, 0, 1]}
raw = {k: [c + v for c, v in zip(common, s)] for k, s in own.items()}
mean = [sum(col) / 3 for col in zip(*raw.values())]
cen = {k: [a - m for a, m in zip(v, mean)] for k, v in raw.items()}
for name, e in (("raw", raw), ("centred", cen)):
    print(name, cos(e["refund"], e["money back"]), cos(e["refund"], e["weather"]))
# → raw 1.0 0.99
# → centred 0.96 -0.99
Space refund vs "money back" refund vs weather Usable?
raw 1.0 0.99 no: paraphrase and unrelated are indistinguishable
centred 0.96 −0.99 yes

Illustrative geometry. Centring or whitening helps a little in practice; training for similarity helps far more.

stages.name: What fixed it
stages.html:
contrastive (InfoNCE) loss for a pair (q, p⁺) in a batch of B:
L = − log  exp(sim(q, p⁺) / τ)  /  Σ over B candidates exp(sim(q, pⱼ) / τ)
          └ pull the true pair together ┘   └ push the other B−1 in the batch away ┘
Step in the lineage What it added
Sentence-BERT (2019) siamese fine-tuning on NLI and similarity pairs, then cosine
SimCSE (Gao et al., 2021) contrastive loss; dropout alone as the positive pair in the unsupervised form
Retrieval-trained models query–passage pairs, hard negatives mined with BM25 or an earlier model

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.claim: bi-encoder to retrieve, cross-encoder to rerank
stages.html:
Serving path:querybi-encoder vectorANN search, top 100cross-encoder scores 100 pairstop 10
Bi-encoder Cross-encoder
Documents encoded once, offline with every query
Cost per query one encode plus ANN lookup one forward pass per candidate
Quality good better: tokens of both texts attend to each other
Pick when first-stage recall over millions precision over the top tens

followUps.question: [CLS] or mean pooling?
followUps.html:
Whichever the embedding model was trained with.

  • Read the model card: pooling is part of the model, like the tokenizer.
  • Mean pooling must ignore padding via the attention mask.
  • Mixing them up runs without error and quietly loses recall.

followUps.question: "Just use the last hidden state of a bigger LLM."
followUps.html:
Size doesn't fix the objective.

Source of vectors Similarity quality
generative LLM hidden states, untrained for retrieval unreliable
the same backbone, contrastively fine-tuned strong: this is how many current embedding models are built

followUps.question: 🧪 Why can't a cross-encoder find the most similar pair among 10,000 sentences?
followUps.html:
Because it needs one forward pass per pair.

pairs = 10,000 × 9,999 / 2 = 49,995,000 forward passes
bi-encoder: 10,000 encodes, then cheap cosine

The Sentence-BERT paper reports about 65 hours against about 5 seconds for this task (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019).

followUps.question: What is a hard negative and why does it matter?
followUps.html:
A wrong passage that looks right, so the model has to learn the fine distinction.

Mining:run BM25 or the current modeltake high-ranked passages that are not labelled relevantfilter likely false negativestrain on them

Random negatives are too easy after the first epochs.

followUps.question: Retrieval quality is poor on your domain. Fine-tune the embedder or add a reranker?
followUps.html:
Reranker first: it is the cheaper change to ship and undo.

Option Cost Changes
Add a reranker latency on the top-k only no re-embedding
Fine-tune the embedder labelled or synthetic pairs, then re-embed the whole corpus recall of the first stage

If the right document isn't in the top 100 at all, only the embedder or a hybrid arm can fix it.

dontSay: "BERT embeddings are great for similarity" — only after similarity training.
"Cosine 0.9 means near-identical" — in an anisotropic space everything is 0.9.
"Cross-encoders are just slower bi-encoders" — they see both texts at once, which is why they rerank better.

nlp-classical-q8.testing: whether you see smoothing as moving probability mass to unseen events, and can name Kneser-Ney's continuation idea.
nlp-classical-q8.trap: answering "add one to every count" and stopping.
nlp-classical-q8.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "An n-gram model estimates the next word from the previous n minus one words by counting. Smoothing exists because most valid word sequences never appear in the training data, and a count of zero makes the whole sentence impossible."
2 · How it works "Every smoothing method takes a little probability from seen n-grams and gives it to unseen ones. The methods differ in how they share it out: add a constant, back off to a shorter context, or interpolate the two."
3 · Prove it "On a toy corpus, 'like milk' has probability zero under raw counts. With add-one it gets about eleven percent, but 'like tea' falls from sixty-seven to thirty-three: far too much mass moved."
4 · What it costs or breaks "The one idea worth remembering is Kneser-Ney. When backing off, don't ask how frequent a word is; ask how many different contexts it follows. 'Francisco' is frequent but only follows 'San'."
5 · So what for the system "N-gram models still run where latency and memory are tight: keyboards, speech first-pass decoding, filtering training data by perplexity."
Close "Smoothing is reserving mass for the unseen; Kneser-Ney reserves it for words that are versatile, not merely common."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
chain rule         P(w₁ … wₙ) = Π P(wᵢ | w₁ … wᵢ₋₁)
Markov assumption  P(wᵢ | all history) ≈ P(wᵢ | wᵢ₋₁)                 ← bigram
estimate           P(wᵢ | wᵢ₋₁) = count(wᵢ₋₁ wᵢ) / count(wᵢ₋₁)        ← maximum likelihood
one unseen bigram  →  one factor is 0  →  the sentence has probability 0, perplexity is infinite

stages.name: How it works
stages.claim: take from the seen, give to the unseen
stages.html:
Method How mass is moved Verdict
Add-k (Laplace) add a constant to every count simple, moves far too much with a large vocabulary
Backoff unseen trigram → use the bigram, then the unigram uses lower orders only when needed
Interpolation always mix trigram, bigram and unigram estimates more stable
Absolute discounting subtract a fixed d from each seen count the base of Kneser-Ney
Kneser-Ney discounting plus a continuation probability for the lower order the standard for count-based models

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: add-one fixes the zero and overpays
stages.html:
Prove it — bigram probabilities after "like", vocabulary of 6:

from collections import Counter
toks = "i like tea . i like coffee . you like tea .".split()
uni, bi = Counter(toks), Counter(zip(toks, toks[1:])); V = len(uni)
def p(w, prev, k=0): return round((bi[prev, w] + k) / (uni[prev] + k * V), 3)
print("MLE   ", p("tea", "like"), p("coffee", "like"), p("milk", "like"))
print("add-1 ", p("tea", "like", 1), p("coffee", "like", 1), p("milk", "like", 1))
# → MLE    0.667 0.333 0.0
# → add-1  0.333 0.222 0.111
Next word Raw counts Add-one Reading
tea (seen twice) 0.667 0.333 halved
coffee (seen once) 0.333 0.222 reduced
milk (unseen) 0.0 0.111 no longer impossible, but too generous

With a real vocabulary of tens of thousands, the unseen events together take most of the mass.

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.claim: frequency is the wrong backoff signal
stages.html:
"Ask how many different words it follows, not how often it occurs."

P_continuation(w) = number of distinct words that precede w  /  number of distinct bigram types

"Francisco"   high unigram count, follows almost only "San"   → low continuation probability
"tea"         follows many different words                    → high continuation probability
Remaining limits of any n-gram model Why
Sparsity grows with n the table has up to V^n entries
No sharing between similar words cat and dog are unrelated symbols
Fixed short context nothing beyond n−1 words

Those three limits are what neural language models removed.

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html:
Use in 2026 Why an n-gram model
On-device keyboard prediction a lookup, tiny memory, no GPU
Speech recognition, first-pass decoding or rescoring fast scoring of many hypotheses
Filtering web text for training data perplexity under a KenLM model flags gibberish
Spelling correction the language-model term of the noisy channel

The idea that carried over: label smoothing in neural training is the same move, taking a little mass from the observed class.

followUps.question: Backoff or interpolation?
followUps.html:
Interpolation is usually better: it uses all orders even when the high order was seen.

Uses lower orders Risk
Backoff only when the higher-order count is zero a single noisy count is trusted fully
Interpolation always, with weights tuned on held-out data slightly more to tune

followUps.question: "Add-one is fine, it removes the zeros."
followUps.html:
It removes them by giving unseen events most of the probability.

count("like") = 3, vocabulary V = 50,000
P(seen word | like) = (2 + 1) / (3 + 50,000) ≈ 0.00006      ← a word seen twice out of three now looks impossible

followUps.question: 🧪 A model assigns uniform probability over 1,000 words. Its perplexity?
followUps.html:
1,000.

PPL = exp( −(1/N) Σ ln p ) = exp( −ln(1/1000) ) = 1000      ← the effective number of equally likely choices

followUps.question: How do you compare two language models with perplexity?
followUps.html:
Only on the same test text with the same vocabulary and tokenisation.

  • Different tokenizers give different numbers of predictions, so per-token perplexity isn't comparable.
  • Lower is better, and it measures fit to that text, not usefulness for a task.
  • Out-of-vocabulary handling must match.

followUps.question: Would you ever choose an n-gram model over a small neural one today?
followUps.html:
Yes, when the budget is microseconds or kilobytes.

Constraint Choice
decoding thousands of hypotheses per second on CPU n-gram (KenLM)
phone keyboard, offline n-gram or a very small neural model
quality is the only goal neural

dontSay: "Smoothing means adding one" — that is the weakest method.
"N-gram models are extinct" — they are still in keyboards and speech pipelines.
"Perplexity of model A beats model B" across different tokenizers.

nlp-classical-q9.testing: whether you can state the fixed-vector bottleneck precisely and trace the line from additive attention to self-attention.
nlp-classical-q9.trap: explaining transformer self-attention and calling it Bahdanau attention.
nlp-classical-q9.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "The original encoder-decoder squeezed the whole source sentence into one fixed-size vector, and the decoder had to generate everything from that. Quality fell as sentences got longer."
2 · How it works "Bahdanau's fix was to keep every encoder state. At each output step the decoder scores each source position against its own state, turns the scores into weights with a softmax, and takes the weighted sum as a fresh context vector."
3 · Prove it "In a toy example, while emitting 'cat', the weights go mostly to 'chat' and 'noir' and almost none to 'le'. The context is rebuilt for every word."
4 · What it costs or breaks "It costs a score for every source-target pair, and the model is still recurrent, so training can't be parallel across time steps."
5 · So what for the system "The transformer kept the attention and dropped the recurrence: every position attends to every other in one step. Retrieval-augmented generation is the same move one level up: don't compress everything, look up what you need."
Close "Attention replaced 'remember everything' with 'look back at the right place', and everything since builds on that."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: one vector can't hold a sentence
stages.html:
Before attention:source wordsencoder RNNone final hidden statedecoder RNNtarget words
Symptom Cause
quality drops on long sentences a fixed-size vector, whatever the input length
early source words are forgotten they are many recurrent steps away from the final state
reversing the source helped (Sutskever et al., 2014) a hint that distance to the bottleneck was the problem

stages.name: How it works
stages.html:
for output step i, over every source position j:
eᵢⱼ = vᵀ · tanh(W·sᵢ₋₁ + U·hⱼ)       ← additive (Bahdanau) score: decoder state against encoder state
αᵢⱼ = softmax over j of eᵢⱼ           ← attention weights, sum to 1
cᵢ  = Σⱼ αᵢⱼ · hⱼ                     ← context vector, rebuilt at every step
sᵢ  = RNN(sᵢ₋₁, yᵢ₋₁, cᵢ)             ← decoder uses it to emit the next word
Bahdanau (2015) Luong (2015)
Score additive: a small feed-forward net multiplicative: dot product or bilinear
Uses decoder state previous step current step

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
Prove it — dot-product scoring for brevity, toy states:

import math
enc = {"le": [1, 0], "chat": [0, 1], "noir": [1, 1]}    # encoder states (toy)
dec = [0.2, 2.0]                                       # decoder state while emitting "cat"
score = {w: sum(a * b for a, b in zip(h, dec)) for w, h in enc.items()}
z = sum(math.exp(s) for s in score.values())
w = {k: round(math.exp(s) / z, 2) for k, s in score.items()}
ctx = [round(sum(w[k] * enc[k][i] for k in enc), 2) for i in range(2)]
print(w, ctx)
# → {'le': 0.07, 'chat': 0.42, 'noir': 0.51} [0.58, 0.93]
Source word Weight while emitting "cat"
le 0.07
chat 0.42
noir 0.51

The weights are a soft alignment: the model learned word alignment as a by-product, which statistical MT needed a separate model for.

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.html:
Cost Detail
Scoring source length × target length scores per sentence
Sequential training each decoder step waits for the previous one, so no parallelism over time
Long-range links inside one sequence still pass through many recurrent steps

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html:
The lineage:fixed vector (2014)attention over encoder states (2015)self-attention, no RNN (2017)pre-trained transformers
Later idea What it took from Bahdanau
Self-attention the same score-softmax-sum, applied within one sequence
Cross-attention in encoder-decoder transformers the same mechanism, between decoder and encoder
Retrieval-augmented generation by analogy: look up external text instead of compressing it into weights

Engineering consequence: removing recurrence is what made training parallel across positions, and that is what made large-scale pre-training practical.

followUps.question: How is self-attention different from this?
followUps.html:
Same operation, different pair of sequences.

Bahdanau attention Self-attention
Query comes from the decoder state every position of the same sequence
Attends over encoder states the same sequence
Recurrence yes none: positions come from positional encodings

followUps.question: "Attention weights explain the model's decision."
followUps.html:
They show where information was read from, not why the output was chosen.

  • Different weight patterns can give the same prediction (Jain & Wallace, 2019).
  • Useful as a debugging hint and an alignment view.
  • Not valid as a faithful explanation for audit.

followUps.question: Does attention help on a three-word source sentence?
followUps.html:
Barely: a fixed vector holds three words fine.

Source length Bottleneck Gain from attention
short not binding small
long binding large

The original paper shows the gap opening as sentence length grows.

followUps.question: Why the softmax over scores?
followUps.html:
To turn scores into a differentiable weighting that sums to one.

raw scoressoftmaxweights in 0–1convex combination of encoder states

A hard pick of one position isn't differentiable, so it can't be trained with plain backpropagation.

followUps.question: What did this change for how teams build systems?
followUps.html:
It replaced a pipeline of separately trained parts with one model trained end to end.

Statistical MT Neural MT with attention
alignment model, phrase table, language model, tuned separately one network, one loss
errors compound across components components are learned jointly

The same shift is why most task-specific NLP pipelines later collapsed into one pre-trained model.

dontSay: "Attention was invented in the transformer paper" — that paper removed recurrence; attention was two years older.
"The encoder output is a summary vector" — with attention, the decoder reads all encoder states.
"Attention weights are explanations."

nlp-classical-q10.testing: whether you understand that tags depend on each other, and can say when a strong encoder makes the extra layer unnecessary.
nlp-classical-q10.trap: "always add a CRF" or "transformers made CRFs obsolete": both skip the conditions.
nlp-classical-q10.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "A per-token softmax picks each tag independently. A CRF scores the whole tag sequence: it adds a learned score for every tag-to-tag transition and picks the best path with Viterbi."
2 · Where the CRF wins "That matters because BIO tags have grammar. An inside tag can't follow an outside tag. Softmax can output that; a CRF learns it is impossible. The gain is largest with small data, weaker encoders and long entities."
3 · Where softmax is enough "With a strong pre-trained transformer and plenty of labels, the encoder already sees the whole sentence, so the gain shrinks to a fraction of a point, and the CRF makes training slower."
4 · The deciding question "So I ask: how much data, how strict must the output be, and how long are the entities?"
5 · What I'd pick in 2026 "My default is a transformer with softmax, plus constrained decoding that masks illegal transitions. That gets valid spans without training a CRF. I add the CRF for low-resource or long-span domains like clinical or legal text, after measuring."
Close "The CRF buys consistency of the sequence; I pay for it only where the encoder doesn't already provide it."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: independent tags against a scored sequence
stages.html:
softmax   P(y | x) = Π over tokens  P(yᵢ | x)                       ← each tag decided alone
CRF       score(x, y) = Σᵢ emit(yᵢ, x, i) + Σᵢ trans(yᵢ₋₁, yᵢ)        ← transitions are learned
          P(y | x) = exp(score(x, y)) / Z(x)                         ← normalised over all tag sequences
decode    best path with Viterbi
Softmax head CRF head
Models tag-to-tag dependence no yes
Can emit O then I-PER yes learns it is invalid
Training cost cross-entropy per token forward algorithm, O(n·K²)

stages.name: Where the CRF wins
stages.claim: small data and strict tag grammar
stages.html:
Prove it — two tokens, three tags, toy scores:

tags = ["O", "B", "I"]
emit = [{"O": .5, "B": .4, "I": .1}, {"O": .2, "B": .1, "I": .7}]     # per-token scores, 2 tokens (toy)
trans = {("O", "O"): .8, ("O", "B"): .2, ("O", "I"): 0, ("B", "O"): .3, ("B", "B"): .1, ("B", "I"): .6,
         ("I", "O"): .4, ("I", "B"): .1, ("I", "I"): .5}
print("per-token argmax:", [max(e, key=e.get) for e in emit])
score = lambda ab: emit[0][ab[0]] * trans[ab] * emit[1][ab[1]]
best = max(((a, b) for a in tags for b in tags), key=score)
print("best sequence:  ", list(best), round(score(best), 3))
# → per-token argmax: ['O', 'I']
# → best sequence:   ['B', 'I'] 0.168
Decoder Output Valid BIO?
per-token argmax O, I no: an entity can't start with I
best sequence with transitions B, I yes
Point What it means
Small training sets the transition matrix is a strong prior.
BiLSTM or CNN encoders less context per token, so the CRF adds more.
Long entities one wrong tag in the middle splits the span; sequence scoring resists that.

stages.name: Where softmax is enough
stages.html:
Condition Why the CRF adds little
pre-trained transformer encoder each token's representation already depends on the whole sentence
thousands of labelled sentences invalid transitions become rare without help
latency-sensitive training or serving Viterbi and the forward pass add cost

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html:
Ask If yes
fewer than a few thousand labelled sentences? CRF likely helps
must every output be a valid span, with no exceptions? CRF or constrained decoding
are entities long (drug regimens, legal clauses)? CRF likely helps
are entities nested or overlapping? neither: use a span-based model

stages.name: What I'd pick in 2026
stages.html:
Default:transformerper-token logitsmask illegal transitionsViterbi over the masked scoresvalid spans
  • Constrained decoding needs no retraining and removes the invalid-sequence class of errors.
  • I'd add a trained CRF only if entity-level F1 on the eval set moves by more than seed noise.
  • Evaluation is at entity level (exact span and type), not token accuracy.

followUps.question: HMM, MEMM, CRF: what is the difference?
followUps.html:
Generative, locally normalised, globally normalised.

Model Normalises Weakness
HMM joint probability of words and tags features limited to the current word
MEMM per step label bias: states with few exits win unfairly
CRF over the whole sequence slower training

followUps.question: "BERT made the CRF layer obsolete."
followUps.html:
It made the gain small on high-resource English news, not everywhere.

  • Low-resource and domain text: reported gains are still positive.
  • Invalid spans still occur with a softmax head unless decoding is constrained.
  • Measure on your data instead of quoting a benchmark.

followUps.question: What about nested entities?
followUps.html:
A linear-chain CRF can't express them: one tag per token.

Entity structure Model
flat BIO tagging, softmax or CRF
nested or overlapping span classification, or one tagger per entity layer

followUps.question: How is the normaliser Z computed?
followUps.html:
With the forward algorithm: Viterbi with a sum where the max was.

Viterbi   δₜ(k) = max over j  [ δₜ₋₁(j) + trans(j, k) ] + emit(k, t)       ← best path
Forward   αₜ(k) = logsumexp over j [ αₜ₋₁(j) + trans(j, k) ] + emit(k, t)  ← total over all paths = log Z

followUps.question: Would you replace the tagger with an LLM extraction prompt?
followUps.html:
For prototyping and rare entity types, yes; for volume, usually no.

Fine-tuned tagger LLM extraction
Labels needed hundreds to thousands a few examples
Cost and latency at volume low high
Character offsets exact must be recovered and validated

A common pattern: the LLM labels data, the small tagger serves traffic.

dontSay: "CRF is always better" — with a strong encoder and data, the gain can be within noise.
"Token accuracy is 98%" — NER is scored on entities, and O dominates tokens.
"The CRF learns context" — the encoder does; the CRF learns tag transitions.

nlp-classical-q11.testing: whether you can state the dynamic-programming argument in one sentence and fill a small trellis.
nlp-classical-q11.trap: describing it as "trying all paths efficiently" without saying why paths can be discarded.
nlp-classical-q11.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "Viterbi finds the single most likely sequence of hidden states for an observed sequence, for example the best tag sequence for a sentence."
2 · How it works "The trick is that the best path ending in a given tag at position t must extend the best path ending in some tag at t minus one. So for each position and tag I keep only one score and one back-pointer, then trace back from the best final tag."
3 · Prove it "For 'fish swim fast' with two tags, the table fills in three columns and the back-pointers give noun, verb, noun."
4 · What it costs or breaks "The cost is sentence length times tags squared, instead of tags to the power of the length. It relies on the first-order assumption: a score may depend only on adjacent tags."
5 · So what for the system "I meet it today in CRF decoding, in constrained decoding for taggers, and in Unigram tokenization."
Close "Exponential search made linear by keeping one best path per state."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: the best path, not the best tags
stages.html:
Question Algorithm
most likely tag sequence as a whole Viterbi
most likely tag at each position separately forward-backward (posterior decoding)
total probability of the observation forward algorithm

The best whole sequence and the sequence of individually best tags can differ.

stages.name: How it works
stages.claim: one best path per state per step
stages.html:
δ₁(k) = start(k) × emit(k, x₁)
δₜ(k) = max over j [ δₜ₋₁(j) × trans(j → k) ] × emit(k, xₜ)      ← keep the max
ψₜ(k) = the j that gave that max                                 ← back-pointer
answer: start at argmax over k of δ_T(k), follow ψ backwards

Why discarding is safe: any path through tag k at step t has a future that depends only on k. So among all paths reaching k, only the best can be part of the overall best.

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
Prove it — two tags (N, V), toy HMM:

states = ["N", "V"]; start = {"N": .6, "V": .4}
trans = {"N": {"N": .3, "V": .7}, "V": {"N": .8, "V": .2}}
emit = {"N": {"fish": .5, "swim": .1, "fast": .4}, "V": {"fish": .3, "swim": .6, "fast": .1}}
obs = ["fish", "swim", "fast"]
v = [{s: start[s] * emit[s][obs[0]] for s in states}]; back = []
for o in obs[1:]:
    ptr = {s: max(states, key=lambda p: v[-1][p] * trans[p][s]) for s in states}
    v.append({s: v[-1][ptr[s]] * trans[ptr[s]][s] * emit[s][o] for s in states}); back.append(ptr)
path = [max(states, key=v[-1].get)]
for ptr in reversed(back): path.insert(0, ptr[path[0]])
for o, col in zip(obs, v): print(o, {s: round(x, 4) for s, x in col.items()})
print(path)
# → fish {'N': 0.3, 'V': 0.12}
# → swim {'N': 0.0096, 'V': 0.126}
# → fast {'N': 0.0403, 'V': 0.0025}
# → ['N', 'V', 'N']
Word δ(N) δ(V) Best predecessor
fish 0.3 0.12 start
swim 0.0096 0.126 V came from N (0.3 × 0.7 × 0.6)
fast 0.0403 0.0025 N came from V (0.126 × 0.8 × 0.4)

Trace back from the largest final value: N ← V ← N.

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.html:
brute force   K^n tag sequences        n = 20 words, K = 45 tags  →  45²⁰ ≈ 10³³
Viterbi       n × K² operations        20 × 45² = 40,500
Limit Consequence Usual fix
First-order only a second-order model costs n·K³ accept it, or use beam search
Products of small numbers underflow on long sequences add log-probabilities instead
Very large state spaces (speech) K² is too many beam pruning: approximate

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html:
Place What the "states" are
CRF and constrained tagger decoding BIO tags, with illegal transitions masked
Unigram tokenizer possible subword pieces ending at each character
Speech alignment and HMM decoding phone or word states
Spelling and word segmentation candidate words

followUps.question: How does it differ from the forward algorithm?
followUps.html:
One operator: max instead of sum.

Combines predecessors with Returns
Viterbi max the best single path
Forward sum the probability over all paths

followUps.question: "Greedy decoding gives the same result."
followUps.html:
No. Greedy commits to each tag before seeing what follows.

Greedy:pick best tag at tnever revisit
Viterbi:keep the best path for every tag at tdecide at the end

A locally worse tag can sit on the globally best path because of the transition that follows it.

followUps.question: 🧪 30 tokens, 9 BIO tags. How many operations?
followUps.html:
2,430, against 9³⁰ sequences.

n × K² = 30 × 81 = 2,430
K^n    = 9³⁰ ≈ 4 × 10²⁸

followUps.question: Why work in log space?
followUps.html:
Because multiplying many probabilities underflows to zero.

  • Products become sums, which stay in floating-point range.
  • The argmax is unchanged, since log is monotonic.
  • Neural taggers already emit log-scores, so this is the natural form.

followUps.question: Is Viterbi the same as beam search?
followUps.html:
No. Viterbi is exact under a Markov assumption; beam search is approximate without one.

Viterbi Beam search
Needs scores that depend only on adjacent states nothing
Guarantee the optimal path none
Used for taggers, CRFs, HMMs autoregressive generation, where each step depends on the full prefix

dontSay: "It tries every path quickly" — it never enumerates paths; it prunes all but one per state.
"It gives the most likely tag for each word" — it gives the most likely sequence.
"It works for any model" — it needs the Markov property.

nlp-classical-q12.testing: whether you separate "which real-world thing is this" from "how are two things related", and design for the fact that errors multiply down a pipeline.
nlp-classical-q12.trap: "send every document to an LLM and ask for triples" with no linking step, no confidence gate and no provenance.
nlp-classical-q12.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "Entity linking maps a mention in text to an identifier in the knowledge base: which 'Jordan' is this. Relation extraction decides how two mentions are related: 'acquired', 'works for'. Population needs both, because a triple is only useful when its ends are resolved IDs."
2 · Constraints and numbers "I'd fix three things first: is the relation schema closed or open, what precision the knowledge base must hold, and how fresh it has to be. A knowledge base usually wants precision over recall, because a wrong fact gets reused everywhere."
3 · Baseline design "The pipeline is: find mentions with NER and coreference, link each mention, classify relations between linked pairs, then gate on confidence. High-confidence triples are written with their source sentence; the rest go to review."
4 · Deep-dive the hard part "Linking is the hard part. It is two stages: generate candidates from an alias table and an embedding index, then disambiguate with the surrounding context. It also has to say 'none of these' for entities the knowledge base doesn't have yet."
5 · Failure modes "Errors compound: three stages at ninety percent give about seventy-three percent correct triples, so I measure each stage and the end-to-end result separately."
6 · Evolve "Today an LLM with schema-constrained output does the relation step well with few labels. I keep the linker, the gate and provenance around it."
Close "Resolve the entities, type the relation, and write only what you can trace back to a sentence."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.claim: which thing, and how are two things related
stages.html:
Entity linking Relation extraction
Input one mention plus context two mentions plus context
Output a knowledge-base ID, or NIL a relation type, or none
Example "Jordan" → the basketball player's ID (Jordan, played_for, Chicago Bulls)
Hard because names are ambiguous and have many aliases the same relation is phrased in many ways

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
Decision Options Effect
Schema closed list of relation types / open extraction closed is cleaner to store and evaluate
Precision target set by the downstream use sets the confidence threshold and the review load
Freshness batch nightly / streaming decides whether the linker index must update online
Volume documents per day (illustrative: 1 million) rules out an LLM call per sentence without a filter

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html: Every stored triple carries its source document, sentence and extractor version, so it can be audited and re-derived.

stages.name: Deep-dive the hard part
stages.html:
Linking one mention:mentioncandidates from alias table and ANNscore each against the contextbest above threshold, else NIL

Trace — "Jordan signed with the Bulls in 1984":

Candidate Prior (how often the alias means this) Context match Decision
Jordan, the country high low rejected
Michael Jordan, basketball player medium high: "Bulls", "signed" linked
Michael B. Jordan, actor low low rejected
  • The prior alone would pick the country. Context is what fixes it.
  • NIL handling decides whether new entities are created, queued or dropped.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
end-to-end accuracy ≈ NER × linking × relation
                    = 0.90 × 0.90 × 0.90 = 0.729        (illustrative stage accuracies)
Failure Symptom Control
Compounding good stages, poor triples evaluate per stage and end to end
Wrong link, right relation a fact attached to the wrong entity linking threshold, NIL option
Duplicate entities the same company under two IDs entity resolution pass before writing
Stale facts "CEO of" from a 2019 article store the document date; time-scope relations

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
Stage Classical 2026 default
Mentions NER tagger NER tagger: cheap, exact offsets
Linking alias table plus bi-encoder the same: it is a retrieval problem
Relations supervised classifier per schema LLM with schema-constrained JSON, few examples
Verification rules second pass that checks the triple against the source sentence

The extracted triples are model output, so they are untrusted until they pass the gate. The same store later serves graph-based retrieval.

followUps.question: How do you get training data for relation extraction without labelling?
followUps.html:
Distant supervision: align an existing knowledge base with text.

known triple (A, r, B)find sentences mentioning A and Blabel them rtrain

It is noisy: many sentences mention both without stating the relation, so it needs denoising or a review sample.

followUps.question: "An LLM returns triples directly, so linking is unnecessary."
followUps.html:
It returns strings, not identifiers.

LLM output Problem
("Jordan", "played_for", "Bulls") which Jordan, which Bulls
("M. Jordan", …) and ("Michael Jordan", …) two nodes for one person

Without linking the graph fragments into duplicates.

followUps.question: The entity isn't in the knowledge base at all. What happens?
followUps.html:
The linker must return NIL, and policy decides what follows.

  • Cluster NIL mentions across documents to find the same new entity.
  • Create it automatically only above a support threshold.
  • Otherwise queue it for review.

followUps.question: How do you evaluate the pipeline?
followUps.html:
Per stage and end to end, on a hand-labelled sample.

Level Metric
NER entity-level F1
Linking accuracy on linkable mentions, plus NIL precision
Relations precision and recall per relation type
Knowledge base precision of a random sample of written triples

followUps.question: What does a wrong triple cost, and who owns it?
followUps.html:
More than a wrong search result, because it is reused by every consumer.

  • Provenance on every triple makes correction and retraction possible.
  • A deletion path: when a source is retracted, its triples go too.
  • An owner for the schema: new relation types are a governed change.

dontSay: "Entity linking is the same as NER" — NER finds the span; linking resolves its identity.
"The LLM extracts the graph" — without IDs, a gate and provenance it is a pile of strings.
"Each stage is 90% accurate, so the pipeline is 90%" — they multiply.

nlp-classical-q13.testing: whether you choose by the cost of an unfaithful sentence, and know that each approach fails in a different way.
nlp-classical-q13.trap: "abstractive, because LLMs write better summaries": fluency is not the requirement in a legal setting.
nlp-classical-q13.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "Extractive summarization selects sentences from the source. Abstractive summarization generates new sentences. So the axis is faithfulness by construction against fluency and compression."
2 · Where extractive wins "Extractive can't invent a fact: every sentence is a quote. It fails by omission, by picking redundant sentences, and by reading choppily."
3 · Where abstractive wins "Abstractive merges and rephrases, so it is shorter and reads well. It fails by stating things the source doesn't say: a changed number, a swapped party, a dropped 'not'."
4 · The deciding question "I ask what one wrong sentence costs. In a news digest, little. In a contract, a changed obligation is a liability."
5 · What I'd ship for legal "For legal documents I ship an extractive core: key clauses quoted with their location. If the product needs prose, I add an abstractive layer where every sentence must cite a source span and pass a faithfulness check, with amounts, dates and parties copied, never rephrased."
Close "Quote where errors are expensive, paraphrase where they are cheap, and always keep the link to the source."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: select sentences or write new ones
stages.html:
Extractive Abstractive
Mechanism score sentences, pick the top ones generate text conditioned on the source
Classic method TextRank, centroid or TF-IDF scoring encoder-decoder, now LLMs
Faithfulness guaranteed at sentence level must be checked
Typical failure omission, redundancy, dangling pronouns fabricated or altered facts
Pick when wrong statements are costly readability and compression matter most

stages.name: Where extractive wins
stages.html:
Prove it — frequency-scored extraction, top 2 of 4 sentences:

from collections import Counter
sents = ["The tenant shall pay rent monthly.", "Rent is due on the first day.",
         "The landlord may terminate if rent is unpaid for 30 days.", "Notices must be in writing."]
words = lambda s: [w.strip(".").lower() for w in s.split()]
tf = Counter(w for s in sents for w in words(s))
score = lambda s: sum(tf[w] for w in words(s)) / len(words(s))
for s in sorted(sents, key=score, reverse=True)[:2]: print(round(score(s), 2), s)
# → 1.71 Rent is due on the first day.
# → 1.67 The tenant shall pay rent monthly.
What it shows Reading
both picks are verbatim nothing can be invented
the termination clause was not picked frequency rewards the common topic, not the important sentence
TextRank instead of raw frequency:sentencessimilarity graphPageRanktop-ranked, with redundancy removed

So an extractive system for contracts needs a signal for importance: clause type, defined terms, or a classifier.

stages.name: Where abstractive wins
stages.claim: fluent, compressed, and able to drift
stages.html:
Source Abstractive output Error type
"terminate if rent is unpaid for 30 days" "terminate if rent is late" condition weakened
"the Tenant shall indemnify the Landlord" "the Landlord shall indemnify the Tenant" parties swapped
"liability not exceeding the annual fee" "liability equal to the annual fee" a cap turned into an amount

Each reads perfectly well. That is why abstractive errors are harder to notice than extractive ones.

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: what does one wrong sentence cost
stages.html:
Domain Cost of an unfaithful sentence Default
news digest, meeting notes low abstractive
support-ticket history medium abstractive with citations
legal, medical, financial filings high extractive core, constrained abstraction on top

stages.name: What I'd ship for legal
stages.html:
Pipeline:contractsegment into clausesclassify and rank clausesquote key clauses with locationoptional cited prosefaithfulness checkreviewer
  • Copy, don't paraphrase: amounts, dates, party names and durations are carried over verbatim.
  • Every generated sentence cites a span. A sentence with no supporting span is dropped.
  • Evaluation hook: lawyers grade a sample for missed obligations and wrong statements; ROUGE alone doesn't see either.

followUps.question: How do you check faithfulness automatically?
followUps.html:
Test each summary sentence against the source as an entailment problem.

summary sentenceretrieve supporting spansNLI model or LLM judge: entailed?keep, or flag

It catches contradictions and unsupported claims better than overlap metrics, and it still needs a human-labelled sample to calibrate.

followUps.question: "ROUGE went up, so the summaries are better."
followUps.html:
ROUGE measures word overlap with a reference, not truth.

Summary ROUGE Correct?
copies the reference but drops "not" high no
correct paraphrase with different words low yes

followUps.question: The contract is 300 pages. Does that change the design?
followUps.html:
Yes: summarise by structure, not by truncation.

Hierarchical:split by sectionextract per sectionmerge section summariesfinal view grouped by clause type

Even when it fits in a context window, per-section processing keeps citations precise and makes omissions visible.

followUps.question: What makes extractive summaries read badly, and how do you reduce it?
followUps.html:
Sentences lifted out of context.

  • Dangling references: "it", "the aforementioned party": resolve coreference or pull the previous sentence too.
  • Redundancy: apply maximal marginal relevance when selecting.
  • Order: keep source order, not score order.

followUps.question: Who is accountable when the summary misses a clause?
followUps.html:
The product has to be framed as an aid, with the source one click away.

  • Coverage report: which clause types were found and which were not.
  • Reviewer sign-off for anything that leaves the firm.
  • Logged versions of model, prompt and document, so an error can be traced.

dontSay: "Abstractive is strictly better now" — it is more fluent, not more faithful.
"Extractive can't be wrong" — it can omit the one clause that matters.
"We'll evaluate with ROUGE" as the only gate for legal text.

nlp-classical-q14.testing: whether you match the tool to volume, latency and how subtle the language is, and know that document-level polarity is often the wrong output.
nlp-classical-q14.trap: "just call an LLM for every review" at millions of rows a day.
nlp-classical-q14.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "There are three rungs: a lexicon with rules, a small trained classifier, and an LLM call. They trade cost and latency per item against how much nuance they handle."
2 · Where a lexicon wins "A lexicon like VADER wins when there are no labels, the text is short and informal, and I need a signal today at almost no cost, for example a trend line over social posts."
3 · Where a small classifier wins "A fine-tuned small model wins once I have a few thousand labels and high volume. It learns the domain: in device reviews 'thin' is good, in soup reviews it is bad."
4 · Where the LLM earns it "The LLM earns its cost on the hard tail: sarcasm, mixed opinions, new product names. I send it only what the cheap model is unsure about, and use it to label training data."
5 · What aspect-based adds "Aspect-based sentiment changes the output from one score to pairs: battery positive, screen negative. That is what a product team can act on."
Close "Cheap model for the bulk, LLM for the uncertain tail, and aspects instead of a single number."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: three rungs of cost and nuance
stages.html:
Lexicon + rules Small classifier LLM call
Labels needed none hundreds to thousands a few examples
Latency per item microseconds milliseconds network round trip
Cost at high volume negligible low high
Handles domain meaning no yes, after training mostly
Handles sarcasm, mixed opinion no partly best of the three
Pick when no labels, need a signal now steady high volume hard tail, or bootstrapping labels

stages.name: Where a lexicon wins
stages.claim: no labels, and where it breaks
stages.html:
Prove it — a bare lexicon, summing word scores:

lex = {"good": 1, "great": 2, "bad": -1, "terrible": -2, "sick": -1}
score = lambda t: sum(lex.get(w, 0) for w in t.lower().split())
for t in ("great phone", "not good at all", "this drop is sick", "battery great but screen terrible"):
    print(t, "→", score(t))
# → great phone → 2
# → not good at all → 1
# → this drop is sick → -1
# → battery great but screen terrible → 0
Input Score Verdict
"great phone" 2 correct
"not good at all" 1 wrong: negation ignored
"this drop is sick" −1 wrong: slang
"battery great but screen terrible" 0 two opinions cancel into "neutral"

VADER adds rules on top of the lexicon for negation, intensifiers, capitals, punctuation and emoji, which fixes the second row. It can't fix the third or fourth.

stages.name: Where a small classifier wins
stages.html:
Word Domain where it is positive Domain where it is negative
thin laptops soups, towels
unpredictable film plots car steering
cheap prices build quality
Build:sample ticketslabel, or LLM-label and spot-checkfine-tune a small encodercalibrateserve on CPU

A general lexicon can't know these; a model trained on in-domain labels does.

stages.name: Where the LLM earns it
stages.html:
Cascade:all itemssmall classifierconfident?done
Low confidence:uncertain itemsLLManswer, and a new training label
Sent to the LLM Why
sarcasm ("great, another outage") surface words are positive
comparisons ("better than the last one, still bad") needs the reference point
new product or feature names not in the training data yet

Evaluation hook: track the share escalated and the agreement between the two models on a sample.

stages.name: What aspect-based adds
stages.claim: a table instead of a number
stages.html:
"Battery is great but the screen is terrible, and delivery was late."

Aspect Opinion term Polarity
battery great positive
screen terrible negative
delivery late negative
Pipeline:reviewextract aspect termsmap to an aspect categoryclassify polarity per aspectaggregate per product
  • Document-level sentiment would call this review "mixed" and lose all three facts.
  • Aspect categories need a governed list, or the dashboard fills with near-duplicates.

followUps.question: How do you evaluate a sentiment system fairly?
followUps.html:
With macro-F1 on a labelled sample that matches production, plus slices.

  • Class balance: neutral often dominates, so accuracy flatters.
  • Slices: negation, sarcasm, short texts, each product line.
  • Label agreement: annotators disagree on sentiment; measure it before blaming the model.

followUps.question: "VADER is outdated, nobody should use it."
followUps.html:
It is still a sensible zero-label baseline for short social text.

Good fit Poor fit
trend lines, coarse monitoring, day one of a project domain reviews, long documents, anything a decision depends on

followUps.question: Reviews arrive in Hinglish with emoji. Which rung still works?
followUps.html:
The English lexicon doesn't; a multilingual model or the LLM does.

Rung On code-mixed text
English lexicon most words are unknown
Multilingual small encoder, fine-tuned workable with in-domain labels
LLM usually the strongest zero-shot option

followUps.question: Why calibrate the classifier?
followUps.html:
Because the cascade routes on its confidence.

raw scorestemperature scaling on held-out dataconfidence that matches accuracythreshold for escalation

An over-confident model never escalates the cases it gets wrong.

followUps.question: How do you justify the cascade to finance?
followUps.html:
By cost per item at the measured escalation rate.

cost per item = cost_small + escalation_rate × cost_LLM
escalation_rate = 8%  (illustrative)  →  the LLM is paid for on 8 of every 100 items

The escalation rate is a dial: raising the confidence threshold buys quality with a known cost.

dontSay: "Sentiment is a solved problem" — sarcasm, domain shift and mixed opinions are not.
"One score per review is enough" — it hides exactly what the product team needs.
"LLM for everything" without a volume and latency number.

nlp-classical-q15.testing: whether you know that the two methods define "topic" differently, and can pick by document length and by what the output is used for.
nlp-classical-q15.trap: treating discovered topics as ground-truth categories without checking coherence or stability.
nlp-classical-q15.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "They define a topic differently. In LDA a topic is a distribution over words, and each document is a mixture of topics. In a BERTopic-style pipeline a topic is a cluster of documents in embedding space, described afterwards by its distinctive words."
2 · Where LDA wins "LDA works from word co-occurrence, so it needs long documents. It wins when I want mixtures, say a report that is sixty percent finance and forty percent legal, and when I need a small, explainable model on CPU."
3 · Where embedding clustering wins "Embedding clustering wins on short text such as tickets and reviews, where there is too little co-occurrence for LDA, and on multilingual data, because the embedding carries the meaning."
4 · The deciding question "So I ask: how long are the documents, and do I need mixtures or one label per document?"
5 · What I'd reach for now "For most product work today I start with embeddings, dimensionality reduction, density clustering and class-based TF-IDF for the keywords, then check coherence and stability across seeds and have a person name the topics."
Close "LDA explains documents as mixtures of word distributions; embedding clustering groups documents and labels the groups."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
LDA BERTopic-style
A topic is a probability distribution over words a cluster of documents
A document gets a mixture over all topics one cluster, or "outlier"
Signal used word co-occurrence within documents a pre-trained embedding
Number of topics chosen up front (K) found by the clustering, tuned by its parameters
Pick when long documents, mixtures matter short or multilingual text

stages.name: Where LDA wins
stages.html:
The generative story:draw a topic mixture for the documentfor each word, draw a topicdraw the word from that topic
θ_d ~ Dirichlet(α)     ← topic mixture of document d;  small α → few topics per document
φ_k ~ Dirichlet(β)     ← word distribution of topic k; small β → few words per topic
inference reverses the story: given the words, estimate θ and φ
Strength Why
Mixed membership one document can belong to several topics with weights
Interpretable knobs α and β have a direct meaning
Cheap bag-of-words, CPU, no pre-trained model

stages.name: Where embedding clustering wins
stages.html:
The pipeline:documentssentence embeddingsUMAP to a few dimensionsHDBSCAN clustersc-TF-IDF keywords per cluster
c-TF-IDF: treat all documents of a cluster as one document
W(t, c) = tf(t, c) × log(1 + A / f(t))      ← A: average words per cluster; f(t): frequency of t across clusters

Trace — three support tickets:

Ticket Shared words LDA Embedding clustering
"card declined at checkout" none with the next row sees no link same cluster
"payment failed, bank says ok" none with the previous row sees no link same cluster
"where is my parcel" — — different cluster

A ticket has a dozen words; LDA has almost no co-occurrence to learn from.

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html:
If Then
documents are long (articles, filings) and mix themes LDA, or NMF on TF-IDF
documents are short (tickets, reviews, posts) embedding clustering
several languages in one corpus embedding clustering with a multilingual model
the result feeds a classifier taxonomy either, then a person merges and names topics

stages.name: What I'd reach for now
stages.html:
Check How Why
Coherence NPMI or c_v on the top words do the keywords belong together
Stability rerun with different seeds, compare clusters UMAP and HDBSCAN are sensitive to seed and parameters
Outlier share fraction HDBSCAN leaves unassigned a large share means the parameters or the embedding don't fit
Human naming a person reads 20 documents per topic keywords alone mislead

Why this matters: topics are an exploration tool. Before they drive a dashboard or a routing rule, they become a fixed taxonomy with a classifier.

followUps.question: How do you choose the number of topics in LDA?
followUps.html:
Sweep K, plot coherence, then let a person decide among the top few.

fit K = 5, 10, 20, 40coherence per Kshortlist the plateauread the topicspick

Held-out perplexity can keep improving while topics become less interpretable (Chang et al., 2009).

followUps.question: "The model found 12 topics, so we have 12 categories."
followUps.html:
It found 12 for this seed and these parameters.

  • Rerun and count how many topics survive.
  • Merge near-duplicates and split catch-alls by hand.
  • Freeze the taxonomy before anything depends on it.

followUps.question: HDBSCAN marks 40% of documents as outliers. Now what?
followUps.html:
Decide whether they are noise or an untuned cluster setting.

Cause Action
min_cluster_size too large lower it
embeddings don't separate the domain try a domain-tuned embedding model
truly miscellaneous text assign each outlier to its nearest topic, or keep an "other" bucket

followUps.question: What do α and β do in practice?
followUps.html:
They set how sparse the mixtures are.

Parameter Small value Large value
α (document–topic) each document uses few topics each document spreads over many
β (topic–word) each topic uses few words topics share many words

followUps.question: Where does an LLM fit in topic discovery now?
followUps.html:
At the two ends: naming clusters and, for small corpora, proposing the taxonomy.

Step Classical With an LLM
Group clustering, at any volume not per document at scale: too costly
Name top keywords a short label and description from sampled documents
Assign new documents nearest cluster or a trained classifier only the low-confidence ones

dontSay: "LDA and BERTopic do the same thing" — one gives mixtures over words, the other hard clusters of documents.
"Lower perplexity means better topics" — it doesn't track interpretability.
"The topics are the truth" — they are one run of an unsupervised method.

nlp-classical-q16.testing: whether you can name saturation and length normalisation, say what k1 and b do, and explain why a formula from the 1990s still anchors retrieval evaluation.
nlp-classical-q16.trap: "BM25 is keyword search, embeddings replaced it."
nlp-classical-q16.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "BM25 is TF-IDF with two corrections to term frequency: saturation and document-length normalisation."
2 · How it works "Saturation means the tenth occurrence of a word adds much less than the first; the parameter k1 sets how fast the curve flattens. Length normalisation means a term in a short document counts more than the same count in a long one; b sets how strongly. The score is the sum over query terms of IDF times that adjusted frequency."
3 · Prove it "With the usual settings, going from one occurrence to a hundred only takes the term's contribution from one to about two point two. And three occurrences score one point eight in a short document, under one in a long one."
4 · What it costs or breaks "It only matches words. A synonym or a paraphrase with no shared term scores zero."
5 · So what for the system "It is still the baseline because it needs no training, no GPU, and it transfers to any domain. Dense retrievers trained on one domain have often lost to it on another. So I report every retriever against BM25, and I keep it as the keyword arm of hybrid search."
Close "Two knobs, no training, hard to beat out of domain: that is why it stays."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
Problem with raw TF-IDF BM25's answer Knob
repeating a term keeps raising the score term frequency saturates k1 (typically 1.2–2.0)
long documents match more terms by chance frequency is scaled by relative length b (typically 0.75)

stages.name: How it works
stages.html:
score(q, d) = Σ over query terms t   IDF(t) × tf × (k1 + 1) / ( tf + k1 × (1 − b + b × |d| / avgdl) )

IDF(t) = ln( (N − df + 0.5) / (df + 0.5) + 1 )      ← rare terms weigh more
tf                                                  ← count of t in d
k1                                                  ← how quickly repeats stop counting; limit is k1 + 1
b × |d| / avgdl                                     ← longer than average → the same tf counts less
b = 0  → no length normalisation     b = 1  → full normalisation

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
Prove it — the term-frequency part (k1 = 1.2, b = 0.75, average length 100), then IDF:

import math
def tf_part(tf, dl, avgdl=100, k1=1.2, b=0.75):
    return round(tf * (k1 + 1) / (tf + k1 * (1 - b + b * dl / avgdl)), 2)
print([tf_part(tf, 100) for tf in (1, 2, 5, 20, 100)])          # saturation
print(tf_part(3, 50), tf_part(3, 100), tf_part(3, 400))         # same tf, short / average / long doc
idf = lambda df, N=1_000_000: round(math.log((N - df + 0.5) / (df + 0.5) + 1), 2)
print(idf(50), idf(500_000))                                    # rare term, common term
# → [1.0, 1.38, 1.77, 2.08, 2.17]
# → 1.76 1.57 0.96
# → 9.89 0.69
Same term, 3 occurrences Document length Contribution
short 50 1.76
average 100 1.57
long 400 0.96

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.html:
Limit Symptom Fix, and its layer
Vocabulary mismatch "laptop won't boot" misses "notebook fails to start" dense arm, or query expansion (retrieval)
No word order or meaning "dog bites man" equals "man bites dog" reranker (retrieval)
Analyzer choices matter stemming and tokenisation change results tune the analyzer per language (index)
Fields are not equal a title match should outweigh a body match BM25F: per-field weights

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html:
Why it stays Detail
Zero training works on a new corpus the day it is indexed
Robust out of domain on the BEIR benchmark, BM25 beat many dense retrievers in zero-shot transfer (Thakur et al., 2021)
Cheap inverted index on CPU, millisecond latency
Exact terms IDs, codes, rare names

Rule I apply: no retriever ships without a row for BM25 in the same eval table, and hybrid search keeps BM25 as one arm.

followUps.question: How do you tune k1 and b?
followUps.html:
Grid search on a labelled query set, per field type.

Content Tendency
long, verbose documents higher b: normalise length more
short fields (titles, product names) lower b, lower k1: one match is enough

The defaults are a good start; the gain from tuning is usually modest.

followUps.question: "Dense retrieval made BM25 obsolete."
followUps.html:
In-domain with training data, dense often wins; out of domain and on exact terms, it often doesn't.

  • Hybrid beats either arm alone on most mixed query sets.
  • BM25 remains the reference row in any evaluation.

followUps.question: 🧪 k1 = 1.2. What is the most a single term can contribute before IDF?
followUps.html:
Just under 2.2.

as tf → ∞:   tf × (k1 + 1) / (tf + k1 × …)  →  k1 + 1  =  2.2
tf = 100 already gives 2.17

followUps.question: What is learned sparse retrieval?
followUps.html:
A model that outputs term weights for an inverted index, including terms not in the text.

BM25 Learned sparse (for example SPLADE)
Weights from counts predicted by a transformer
Expansion none adds related terms
Index inverted inverted

It narrows the vocabulary gap while keeping the sparse infrastructure.

followUps.question: Would you run BM25 in the vector database or in a search engine?
followUps.html:
Wherever the analyzers, filters and operations are mature enough for the corpus.

Option Strength Watch
search engine (Lucene family) analyzers per language, field weights, mature ops a second system to run
vector store with a sparse index one system, simpler fusion check tokenisation and BM25 parameters are configurable

dontSay: "BM25 is just TF-IDF" — saturation and length normalisation are the point.
"Keyword search is legacy" — it is half of hybrid retrieval.
"Our dense retriever is good" with no BM25 number next to it.

nlp-classical-q17.testing: whether you can explain the failure at the tokenizer and embedding level, and design a hybrid path instead of swapping the model.
nlp-classical-q17.trap: "use a bigger embedding model" or "fine-tune it on SKUs".
nlp-classical-q17.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name it "This is the lexical gap of dense retrieval. An embedding model places text by meaning, and a SKU like XJ9-4471B has none. The tokenizer splits it into rare fragments, and the vector lands near other codes, not on this one."
2 · Rule out the fakes "First I'd rule out plumbing: is the SKU in the indexed text at all, is a filter excluding it, and is approximate search dropping it."
3 · Confirm with evidence "Then I'd confirm: run exact nearest-neighbour search for a sample of SKU queries. If the right product still isn't near the top, it is the embedding, not the index."
4 · Fix by experiment "The fix is hybrid retrieval. Add a BM25 arm and fuse the two rankings with reciprocal rank fusion. For queries that look like an identifier, route to an exact lookup on the SKU field first."
5 · Validate "I'd validate on a sliced query set: identifier queries, natural-language queries and mixed ones, each with its own recall number."
6 · Productionise "In production the SKU is a keyword field, the router is a tested rule, and the identifier slice is a release gate."
Close "Exact things need exact matching; meaning needs embeddings; the system needs both."

stages.name: Name it
stages.claim: identifiers have no meaning to embed
stages.html:
What happens to the query:XJ9-4471Bsubword pieces such as X, J, 9, -, 44, 71, Bpooled vectornear other alphanumeric strings
Keyword (BM25) Dense
Matches on the exact token closeness in meaning
XJ9-4471B against XJ9-4471C different tokens: no match nearly identical vectors
"charger for my laptop" against "notebook power adapter" no shared word: miss close: hit

The split shown is illustrative; the exact pieces depend on the tokenizer.

stages.name: Rule out the fakes
stages.html:
Check What it would reveal
is the SKU in the text that was embedded? chunking or templating dropped the field
does a metadata filter exclude the product? wrong tenant, locale or stock filter
does exact (brute-force) search find it when ANN doesn't? ANN recall or parameters
was the query or document truncated? the code sat beyond the token limit

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.html:
Observation Likely cause Next action
exact vector search ranks the product low the embedding can't separate codes add a lexical arm
exact search finds it, ANN doesn't index parameters raise ef_search or probes; re-measure recall
SKU absent from the embedded text ingestion fix the document template
only some SKU formats fail tokenisation of hyphens or case normalise the field and the query the same way

stages.name: Fix by experiment
stages.claim: add a sparse arm, then a router
stages.html:
Prove it — RRF over the two rankings for "XJ9 charger":

sparse = ["sku-XJ9", "d7", "d2", "d5"]      # BM25 order for the query "XJ9 charger"
dense = ["d2", "d5", "d9", "sku-XJ9"]       # embedding order
k = 60; score = {}
for ranking in (sparse, dense):
    for rank, d in enumerate(ranking, 1):
        score[d] = score.get(d, 0) + 1 / (k + rank)
print([(d, round(s, 4)) for d, s in sorted(score.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1])])
# → [('d2', 0.0323), ('sku-XJ9', 0.032), ('d5', 0.0318), ('d7', 0.0161), ('d9', 0.0159)]
Experiment 1

Hybrid with RRF

I'd add BM25 and fuse with score = Σ 1 / (60 + rank).

Why? The SKU document moves from rank 4 in the dense list to rank 2 after fusion.

Best suited when queries mix words and codes.

Experiment 2

Identifier router

I'd detect identifier-shaped queries with a pattern and answer them from an exact match on the SKU field.

Why? Fusion alone left the SKU at rank 2. For a pure code query, exact match should be rank 1 every time.

Best suited when identifiers follow a known format.

stages.name: Validate
stages.claim: one recall number per query type
stages.html:
Slice Before After hybrid After router
identifier queries measure measure measure
natural-language queries measure measure measure
mixed ("XJ9 charger") measure measure measure

The natural-language slice is there to prove the fix didn't cost anything.

stages.name: Productionise
stages.html:
Point What it means
Index SKU stored as an un-analysed keyword field, normalised for case and hyphens on both sides.
Router the pattern lives in config with unit tests, and falls through to hybrid when the lookup returns nothing.
Gate recall on the identifier slice must not drop in any release.
Monitor zero-result rate and click position, split by query type.

followUps.question: Why RRF instead of adding the two scores?
followUps.html:
Because BM25 and cosine scores are on different, unbounded scales.

Fusion Needs Risk
weighted score sum normalised scores, a tuned weight one arm's scale dominates
RRF ranks only ignores how large the score gap was

followUps.question: "Fine-tune the embedding model on SKUs."
followUps.html:
It asks a similarity model to memorise an exact-match table.

  • New SKUs arrive daily and would need retraining.
  • Near-identical codes must be far apart, the opposite of what embeddings learn.
  • A keyword field solves it exactly, today.

followUps.question: The user types the SKU with a typo. Now what?
followUps.html:
Exact match fails, so fall through to fuzzy matching on the field.

exact lookupedit-distance or character n-gram match on SKUshow "did you mean"hybrid as last resort

followUps.question: What does k = 60 do in RRF?
followUps.html:
It flattens the difference between top ranks.

1 / (60 + 1) = 0.0164      1 / (60 + 4) = 0.0156      ← rank 1 and rank 4 are close
smaller k → the top rank of either arm dominates

followUps.question: What else in the catalogue has this problem?
followUps.html:
Anything where the exact string is the meaning.

  • Identifiers: order numbers, part numbers, error codes, legal citations.
  • Rare proper nouns: new brand or drug names.
  • Numbers with units: "65W" against "45W".

I'd list these fields with the catalogue owners and make each a keyword or structured field.

dontSay: "Use a better embedding model" — the failure is structural, not a quality gap.
"Semantic search replaces keyword search" — this question is the counter-example.
"Hybrid fixed it" without a number for the identifier slice.
