nlp-classical-q18.testing: whether you choose a metric from how the results are consumed, and know what each one is blind to.
nlp-classical-q18.trap: reporting one metric for every stage of the stack, or trusting any of them on incomplete relevance labels.
nlp-classical-q18.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "I pick the metric by two questions: how many relevant results does the user need, and does the order inside the top k matter to whoever consumes it?"
2 · Where MRR fits "MRR is for one right answer: navigational search, question answering, autocomplete. It is one over the rank of the first relevant result. Its blind spot is everything after that first hit."
3 · Where MAP and NDCG fit "MAP is for several relevant results with yes-or-no labels; it rewards putting all of them high. NDCG is for graded relevance: a perfect match counts more than a partial one, with a logarithmic discount by position. That is the usual metric for a ranked results page."
4 · Where recall@k fits "Recall at k is for a first-stage retriever feeding a reranker or an LLM. There the question is whether the right documents made it into the candidate set; the order is fixed later."
5 · The deciding question "The trap across all of them is incomplete labels: unjudged documents count as irrelevant, so a new system that finds new good results looks worse."
Close "One answer: MRR. Graded page: NDCG. Candidate stage: recall at k. And always check the labels first."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
RR        = 1 / rank of the first relevant result            MRR = mean over queries
AP        = mean of precision@i at each relevant position    MAP = mean over queries
DCG@k     = Σᵢ (2^relᵢ − 1) / log₂(i + 1)                    NDCG@k = DCG@k / ideal DCG@k
recall@k  = relevant results in the top k / all relevant results
Metric Relevance labels Sensitive to order Blind to
MRR binary only up to the first hit all later results
MAP binary yes degrees of relevance
NDCG@k graded yes, log-discounted anything below k
recall@k binary no order inside the top k

stages.name: Where MRR fits
stages.html:
Prove it — one ranked list, graded 0–3, scored four ways:

import math
rel = [0, 3, 0, 1, 2]                        # graded relevance of the top 5, in ranked order
hits = [i for i, r in enumerate(rel, 1) if r > 0]
rr = 1 / hits[0]
ap = sum((n + 1) / i for n, i in enumerate(hits)) / len(hits)
dcg = lambda rs: sum((2 ** r - 1) / math.log2(i + 1) for i, r in enumerate(rs, 1))
ndcg = dcg(rel) / dcg(sorted(rel, reverse=True))
print("RR", round(rr, 3), "| AP", round(ap, 3), "| NDCG@5", round(ndcg, 3), "| recall@5 = 3 of however many exist")
# → RR 0.5 | AP 0.533 | NDCG@5 0.64 | recall@5 = 3 of however many exist
Use Why MRR
navigational queries, "go to the pricing page" the user wants one thing
extractive QA, autocomplete only the first correct item is used

The trap: a system that puts one relevant result first and nine irrelevant ones after it scores a perfect 1.0.

stages.name: Where MAP and NDCG fit
stages.html:
MAP NDCG@k
Labels relevant or not graded (0–3 or similar)
Rewards every relevant result placed high the most relevant results placed highest
Typical use literature or legal search with binary judgments product and web search pages
The trap treats a perfect and a marginal match as equal the "ideal" order is built from judged documents only

In the snippet the best document (grade 3) sits at rank 2, so NDCG@5 is 0.64, not 1.

stages.name: Where recall@k fits
stages.html:
Two-stage stack:queryretriever, top 100rerankertop 10user or LLM
Stage Metric Because
retriever recall@100 a document that isn't retrieved can never be reranked
reranker NDCG@10 or MRR@10 now the order matters
RAG context recall@k for small k, plus answer quality the LLM reads only a few passages

The trap: recall@100 of 0.95 says nothing about whether the right passage is at rank 1 or rank 97.

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html:
Label problem Effect Mitigation
Unjudged counted as irrelevant a new retriever that finds new relevant documents is penalised judge the top results of every system being compared (pooling)
Labels from clicks position bias: top results get clicked because they are on top debias, or sample human judgments
Few queries differences are noise report an interval, test significance

Why this matters: I'd spend the first hour of an evaluation on the label set, not on the metric choice.

followUps.question: Why the log discount in NDCG?
followUps.html:
To model attention falling with position, steeply at first and slowly later.

position   1      2      3      10
discount   1.00   0.63   0.50   0.29        ← 1 / log₂(position + 1)

It is a convention, not a law; the shape is what matters.

followUps.question: "Precision@10 went up, so search improved."
followUps.html:
Only if the user needed ten results and order didn't matter.

Hidden by precision@10 Seen by
the best result moved from rank 1 to rank 9 MRR, NDCG
a query with 2 relevant documents can never exceed 0.2 recall, NDCG

followUps.question: 🧪 Relevant results at ranks 1 and 4 of 2 relevant. Average precision?
followUps.html:
0.75.

precision@1 = 1/1 = 1.0
precision@4 = 2/4 = 0.5
AP = (1.0 + 0.5) / 2 = 0.75

followUps.question: How do offline metrics relate to online ones?
followUps.html:
Offline metrics decide what is worth testing; online metrics decide what ships.

offline NDCG on judged queriesinterleaving or A/B testclick-through, reformulation rate, zero-result rate

A rise offline with no movement online usually means the judged queries don't look like live traffic.

followUps.question: How many judged queries do you need?
followUps.html:
Enough that the difference you care about is larger than its confidence interval.

  • Start with a few hundred queries sampled from logs, stratified by head, torso and tail.
  • Bootstrap over queries to get an interval on the metric difference.
  • Refresh the set on a schedule, because query mix drifts.

dontSay: "NDCG is the best metric" — not for a single-answer task or a candidate stage.
"Recall@k is high, retrieval is solved" — it ignores order.
Any metric quoted without saying how the relevance labels were produced.

nlp-classical-q19.testing: whether you can say what the loss is computed over in each family, and place LTR between retrieval and the final page.
nlp-classical-q19.trap: describing three model architectures. The difference is the loss, not the model.
nlp-classical-q19.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "Learning to rank trains a model to order candidates for a query from many signals at once. The three families differ only in what one training example is: a document, a pair, or a whole list."
2 · How the three differ "Pointwise predicts a relevance score per document, like regression. Pairwise learns which of two documents should be higher. Listwise optimises a loss over the full ranked list, so it can follow a metric like NDCG directly."
3 · Prove it "The reason the top matters: swapping ranks one and two changes the position discount by about zero point three seven; swapping nine and ten by about zero point zero one. LambdaMART weights each pair by that change."
4 · What it costs or breaks "The weak point is labels. Click data is biased by position, and features computed differently offline and online skew the model."
5 · So what for the system "In the stack it sits in the middle: retrieval returns about a thousand candidates, a gradient-boosted LTR model cuts that to a hundred using text, behaviour and business features, and a neural reranker handles the last few."
Close "Same model, three losses; and LTR is where text scores meet everything else you know about the item."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
"A text score alone can't rank a product page. LTR combines it with everything else."

Feature group Examples
Query–document text BM25 per field, dense similarity, exact-match flags
Document freshness, popularity, rating, stock
Behaviour historical click-through for this query–item pair
Context locale, device, user segment

stages.name: How the three differ
stages.html:
Pointwise Pairwise Listwise
Training example one (query, document, label) two documents of the same query all documents of a query
Loss regression or classification is A above B: logistic on the score difference a function of the whole ordering
Known methods any regressor RankNet, RankSVM ListNet, LambdaMART (pairs weighted by a list metric)
Weakness optimises scores, not order treats all pairs alike unless weighted costlier, needs full lists
Pick when few labels, simple baseline click pairs are the data graded labels and a metric to optimise 
pairwise (RankNet)   P(A above B) = σ(s_A − s_B)
LambdaMART           gradient for the pair  ×  |ΔNDCG if A and B were swapped|

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: a swap at the top is worth thirty times more
stages.html:
Prove it — change in position discount for one swap, and pairs per query:

import math
gain = lambda pos: 1 / math.log2(pos + 1)
print(round(gain(1) - gain(2), 3), round(gain(9) - gain(10), 3))   # what one swap is worth, top vs bottom
n = 100; print(n, "docs →", n * (n - 1) // 2, "pairs per query")
# → 0.369 0.012
# → 100 docs → 4950 pairs per query
Swap Change in discount So the loss should
ranks 1 and 2 0.369 care a lot
ranks 9 and 10 0.012 care little

Plain pairwise loss counts both swaps equally. Weighting pairs by the metric change is what makes it focus on the top of the list.

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.html:
Failure Symptom Control
Position bias the model learns "whatever was on top is relevant" inverse-propensity weighting, randomised slots, or human judgments
Train–serve skew offline NDCG up, online flat one feature pipeline for both; log features at serving time
Leaky features a feature that includes the label (post-click data) time-correct joins
Feedback loop popular items get more clicks, then rank higher exploration traffic

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html:
The funnel:corpusretrieval (BM25 + dense), ~1,000LTR (gradient-boosted trees), ~100neural reranker, ~10business rulespage
Stage Optimised for Typical model
Retrieval recall, milliseconds over millions inverted index, ANN
LTR combining many cheap features LambdaMART
Neural rerank deep text relevance on few items cross-encoder

Candidate counts are illustrative. The LTR stage is where non-text signals enter, which is why it survives next to neural rerankers.

followUps.question: Is LambdaMART pairwise or listwise?
followUps.html:
Pairwise in form, listwise in effect.

Aspect Answer
Gradients computed over pairs
Each pair weighted by the change in a list metric (NDCG) if swapped

Either label is defensible if you explain this.

followUps.question: "Pointwise is fine: predict relevance well and the order follows."
followUps.html:
A small score error can flip an order that matters, and the loss doesn't know.

  • Pointwise spends capacity on getting absolute scores right, including for documents at rank 500.
  • Queries with many documents dominate the loss.
  • It is still a reasonable baseline when labels are few.

followUps.question: 🧪 A query has 100 candidates. How many training pairs?
followUps.html:
Up to 4,950, fewer in practice.

100 × 99 / 2 = 4,950 pairs
pairs with equal labels are dropped, so the usable count is lower

followUps.question: How do you turn clicks into labels?
followUps.html:
As preferences between results, corrected for position.

shown listclicked result preferred over skipped ones above itweight by inverse propensity of the positionpairwise examples

followUps.question: With cross-encoders and LLM rerankers, why keep the LTR stage?
followUps.html:
Because relevance is not only text, and the neural stage is too slow for a hundred-plus items.

Need Met by
freshness, stock, margin, personalisation LTR features
latency over hundreds of candidates trees: microseconds per item
explainability to merchandisers feature importances

dontSay: "Pointwise, pairwise and listwise are three kinds of model" — they are three kinds of loss.
"We train on clicks" with no mention of position bias.
"The reranker replaces LTR" — they solve different parts of the problem.

nlp-classical-q20.testing: whether you know each metric is similarity to a reference, and can show a case where a wrong output scores well.
nlp-classical-q20.trap: "BERTScore fixed BLEU's problems, so use that."
nlp-classical-q20.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "All three compare an output with a reference text. None of them checks whether the output is true. They differ in what counts as a match: exact n-grams, or embeddings."
2 · What BLEU measures "BLEU is n-gram precision: what share of the output's n-grams appear in the reference, with a penalty for being too short. It was built for translation and is meaningful at corpus level."
3 · What ROUGE measures "ROUGE is the recall side: what share of the reference's n-grams the output covers. It was built for summarization."
4 · What BERTScore measures "BERTScore matches tokens by contextual-embedding similarity instead of exact string, so a paraphrase scores well."
5 · Why none gates alone "Here is the problem. Take a reference that says the payment was not refunded and an output that says it was refunded. Unigram precision is one point zero, and an embedding metric scores it high too. The meaning is reversed. So I use these as regression alarms, and gate releases on task checks: faithfulness, human review of a sample, and slices."
Close "They measure resemblance to a reference, and a release needs correctness."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: all three are similarity to a reference
stages.html:
BLEU ROUGE BERTScore
Match unit exact n-grams (1–4) exact n-grams, or longest common subsequence token embeddings
Direction precision recall (F-score variants exist) precision, recall, F1
Built for machine translation summarization any generation
Blind to paraphrase, meaning paraphrase, meaning negation, facts, numbers

stages.name: What BLEU measures
stages.claim: n-gram precision with a length penalty
stages.html:
BLEU = BP × exp( Σₙ wₙ · ln pₙ )            ← geometric mean of modified n-gram precisions, n = 1..4
pₙ   = clipped matching n-grams / n-grams in the output
BP   = 1 if output is longer than the reference, else exp(1 − ref_len / out_len)
       out 4 words, ref 5 words  →  exp(1 − 5/4) = exp(−0.25) ≈ 0.78
  • Clipping stops "the the the the" from scoring full unigram precision.
  • Sentence-level BLEU is unstable: one missing 4-gram makes the product zero without smoothing.

stages.name: What ROUGE measures
stages.claim: how much of the reference is covered
stages.html:
Prove it — reference "the payment was not refunded", output "the payment was refunded":

from collections import Counter
ref = "the payment was not refunded".split()
hyp = "the payment was refunded".split()
def overlap(n):
    grams = lambda t: Counter(zip(*[t[i:] for i in range(n)]))
    h, r = grams(hyp), grams(ref); m = sum((h & r).values())
    return round(m / sum(h.values()), 2), round(m / sum(r.values()), 2)
print("unigram precision, recall:", overlap(1))
print("bigram  precision, recall:", overlap(2))
# → unigram precision, recall: (1.0, 0.8)
# → bigram  precision, recall: (0.67, 0.5)
Variant Measures
ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 unigram and bigram recall
ROUGE-L longest common subsequence: rewards keeping the order

Reading the output: precision 1.0 and recall 0.8 on unigrams, for a sentence that says the opposite.

stages.name: What BERTScore measures
stages.html:
How it scores:embed tokens of both textscosine between every paireach token takes its best matchaverage into precision, recall, F1
Gain over n-gram metrics Remaining problem
"car" matches "automobile" "refunded" and "not refunded" are close in embedding space
correlates better with human judgments on many tasks (Zhang et al., 2020) scores depend on the model and layer; raw values bunch in a narrow range

stages.name: Why none gates alone
stages.html:
Failure the metrics miss What catches it
dropped negation, wrong number, swapped entity entailment or faithfulness check against the source
fluent but unhelpful output human rubric, or an LLM judge calibrated against humans
regression on one user group sliced evaluation
only one reference among many valid answers multiple references, or reference-free checks

How I use them: overlap metrics run on every build as cheap alarms; a release is gated on the task-level checks above.

followUps.question: Why is BLEU reported at corpus level?
followUps.html:
Because n-gram counts are pooled over the whole test set before the precision is computed.

  • Sentence level: short outputs often have zero 4-gram matches, which zeroes the score.
  • Corpus level: counts are large enough to be stable.
  • Comparisons need the same tokenisation; use a standard implementation such as sacreBLEU.

followUps.question: "BERTScore understands meaning, so it can replace human evaluation."
followUps.html:
It measures embedding similarity, and antonyms and negations sit close together there.

Pair Embedding similarity Meaning
"was refunded" / "was not refunded" high opposite
"approved" / "rejected" fairly high: same contexts opposite

followUps.question: 🧪 Output has 4 words, reference has 5, all 4 match. Unigram BLEU-1?
followUps.html:
About 0.78: perfect precision, cut by the brevity penalty.

p₁ = 4 / 4 = 1.0
BP = exp(1 − 5/4) ≈ 0.78
BLEU-1 = 0.78 × 1.0 = 0.78

followUps.question: What do you use for LLM outputs with no single reference?
followUps.html:
Reference-free checks tied to the task.

  • Faithfulness: is each claim supported by the provided context.
  • Rubric scoring: an LLM judge with a written rubric, validated against human labels.
  • Programmatic checks: schema validity, required fields, forbidden content.

followUps.question: A release improves ROUGE by one point. Do you ship?
followUps.html:
Not on that alone.

Question If the answer is no
is the gain outside the bootstrap interval? it is noise
did faithfulness and the human sample hold or improve? block
did every slice hold? investigate the slice that dropped

dontSay: "BLEU measures translation quality" — it measures n-gram overlap with a reference.
"High ROUGE means a good summary" — a summary can copy the lead and be wrong on the facts.
"BERTScore is semantic, so it is enough."

nlp-classical-q21.testing: whether you distrust an aggregate, and have a repeatable routine for turning complaints into slices and slices into fixes.
nlp-classical-q21.trap: defending the metric ("F1 is up, users are wrong") or retraining with more data before looking at a single failing example.
nlp-classical-q21.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name it "An aggregate that rises while users complain means the average is hiding a regression on some slice, or the test set no longer looks like production."
2 · Rule out the fakes "First, is the gain even real? A three-point gain on a hundred examples has a bootstrap interval that includes zero. I'd also check for leakage and for a test set that has gone stale."
3 · Confirm with evidence "Then I read the complaints. I sample fifty, label each with a failure category, and turn the biggest categories into slices with their own metric. Typically the head improved and one tail slice fell."
4 · Fix by experiment "I fix the largest slice first: targeted data for it, or a rule or a routing change, one change at a time."
5 · Validate "I validate per slice, with a rule that no slice may drop by more than an agreed margin, even if the aggregate rises."
6 · Productionise "Then the slices become a permanent regression suite and a dashboard, and complaints feed the next round of labels."
Close "Fixed means the complaint category shrinks in production, not that the average moved."

stages.name: Name it
stages.claim: the average is hiding a slice
stages.html:
examples   before   after
head queries        900      90%      94%      ← improved
tail slice          100      80%      60%      ← collapsed
aggregate          1000      89.0%    90.6%    ← (810+80)/1000 → (846+60)/1000: looks like progress

Users in the tail slice are the ones writing in.

stages.name: Rule out the fakes
stages.claim: is the gain real at all
stages.html:
Prove it — paired bootstrap on 100 test examples, 82% against 85% correct:

import random
random.seed(7)
a = [1] * 82 + [0] * 18; b = [1] * 85 + [0] * 15       # per-example correctness, old vs new model
random.shuffle(a); random.shuffle(b)
diffs = []
for _ in range(2000):
    idx = [random.randrange(100) for _ in range(100)]
    diffs.append(sum(b[i] - a[i] for i in idx) / 100)
diffs.sort()
print("95% interval for the gain:", round(diffs[50], 2), "to", round(diffs[1949], 2))
# → 95% interval for the gain: -0.09 to 0.14
Fake Check
Noise interval from −0.09 to +0.14 contains zero: not a demonstrated gain
Leakage near-duplicates of test items in the new training data
Stale test set compare its label and length distribution with last month's traffic
Metric mismatch F1 on labels, while users care about one costly error type

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.html:
The routine:sample complaintslabel a failure category eachcountbuild a slice per top categorymetric per slice, old model against new
Observation Likely cause Next action
one category holds most complaints a slice regressed measure that slice on both models
complaints spread evenly expectations or UX changed, not the model check product changes shipped at the same time
errors on inputs absent from the test set distribution shift add them to the test set first
the model is right, the label is wrong label noise relabel the slice, re-measure

stages.name: Fix by experiment
stages.html:
Experiment 1

Targeted data

I'd add labelled examples for the failing slice and retrain.

Why? The slice was under-represented, so the model traded it away for the head.

Best suited when the slice is learnable and labels are obtainable.

Experiment 2

Route the slice

I'd detect the slice at inference and send it to a rule, the previous model, or an LLM.

Why? It restores behaviour for those users today, while the data fix is prepared.

Best suited when the slice is easy to detect, such as a language, a length or a product line.

stages.name: Validate
stages.html:
Gate Rule
Aggregate not worse, with an interval
Each named slice may not drop by more than the agreed margin
Costly error type reported separately, with its own threshold
Shadow or canary complaint rate compared between old and new on live traffic

stages.name: Productionise
stages.html:
The loop:production logs and complaintssampled and labelled weeklyslices updatedregression suite runs on every candidaterelease decision
  • A dashboard shows metrics per slice, never only the aggregate.
  • Every incident adds at least one example to the suite.

followUps.question: How do you find slices you didn't think of?
followUps.html:
Let the errors propose them.

  • Cluster the misclassified examples by embedding and read each cluster.
  • Group by metadata: language, length, source, customer tier.
  • Train a small model to predict "was wrong" and inspect its top features.

followUps.question: "The gain is three points, that is clearly significant."
followUps.html:
Not on a hundred examples.

100 examples, 82% → 85%:  95% interval for the gain ≈ −0.09 to +0.14      ← contains 0

The same three points on ten thousand examples would be convincing.

followUps.question: F1 is up on every slice you can find, and complaints still rise.
followUps.html:
Then the metric and the user's cost have diverged.

Possibility Check
one error type is far more costly weight errors by cost
latency or UX regressed with the new model compare response times and UI changes
traffic grew complaints per thousand requests, not raw count

followUps.question: Macro or micro F1?
followUps.html:
Macro when small classes matter, micro when every example counts the same.

Averages over Dominated by
Micro examples large classes
Macro classes nothing: each class counts once

A rise in micro-F1 with a fall in macro-F1 is this exact incident in miniature.

followUps.question: How do you make the team stop shipping on the aggregate?
followUps.html:
Put the slice gates in the release checklist and the dashboard.

  • A written margin per slice, agreed with product.
  • The release report template has the slice table above the aggregate.
  • An owner for the evaluation set, with a refresh schedule.

dontSay: "The metric improved, so the model is better" — better on average, worse for someone.
"Let's add more training data" before reading the failures.
"It's statistically significant" without an interval.

nlp-classical-q22.testing: whether you protect a clean test set before doing anything clever, and know how each label-multiplying technique goes wrong.
nlp-classical-q22.trap: augmenting all 400 examples and then splitting, so paraphrases of test items sit in the training set.
nlp-classical-q22.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "First I'd ask how many classes, how much unlabelled text exists, and what an error costs. And before anything else I'd set aside about a hundred of the four hundred as a test set that is never augmented."
2 · Baseline first "Then a baseline in an hour: a few-shot LLM prompt, and a small model fine-tuned on the three hundred. If one of those already meets the bar, I stop."
3 · Augment the labels "Augmentation makes new examples from labelled ones: back-translation, or LLM paraphrases. It teaches the model that wording varies while the label stays."
4 · Weak supervision "Weak supervision labels the unlabelled pool with noisy sources: keyword rules, existing metadata, an LLM as labeller. A label model combines the votes, and I train on the result."
5 · Failure modes "Each fails in a known way. Augmentation can flip the label, for example by dropping a negation. Weak labels carry correlated errors. And any copy of a test item in training inflates the score."
6 · What I'd ship "With a deadline I'd have an LLM label the unlabelled pool, spot-check a sample against my own labels, train a small model on it, and spend remaining labelling effort on the examples it is least sure about."
Close "Guard the test set, multiply labels cheaply, and measure the noise you added."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.claim: and lock the test set first
stages.html:
Order of operations:400 labelshold out ~100 as test, untouched300 to work withaugment and weak-label only on this side
Ask Why it changes the plan
how many classes, how imbalanced? 400 over 2 classes is workable; over 40 it is 10 per class
is there unlabelled in-domain text? it is the raw material for weak supervision
what does a false positive or negative cost? sets the metric and the threshold

stages.name: Baseline first
stages.html:
Baseline Needs Tells you
few-shot LLM prompt a dozen examples the ceiling without training
TF-IDF + logistic regression on 300 minutes the floor
small encoder fine-tuned on 300, or a few-shot method such as SetFit under an hour what the labels alone buy

All three are scored on the same 100 held-out examples: measure.

stages.name: Augment the labels
stages.html:
Technique How Risk
Back-translation translate to another language and back meaning drift on short or idiomatic text
LLM paraphrase "rewrite, keep the intent" all outputs share one style
Token edits (synonym swap, deletion) random small edits deleting "not" flips the label
LLM-generated new examples "write 20 complaints about billing" cleaner and more typical than real data
Safe use:augment training rows onlycheck a sample by handkeep the original-to-synthetic ratio modest

stages.name: Weak supervision
stages.html:
Prove it — three labelling functions, majority vote (1 = complaint):

texts = ["refund not received", "love the app", "app crashes, want refund", "ok"]
lfs = [lambda t: 1 if "refund" in t else None,     # 1 = complaint
       lambda t: 0 if "love" in t else None,
       lambda t: 1 if "crash" in t else None]
for t in texts:
    votes = [v for v in (lf(t) for lf in lfs) if v is not None]
    print(t, "→", votes, "abstain" if not votes else round(sum(votes) / len(votes)))
# → refund not received → [1] 1
# → love the app → [0] 0
# → app crashes, want refund → [1, 1] 1
# → ok → [] abstain
The flow:unlabelled poollabelling functions vote or abstainlabel model weighs themprobabilistic labelstrain the end model
Source of weak labels Example
keyword or pattern rules "refund" → complaint
existing metadata the queue the ticket was filed in
another model or an LLM zero-shot label with a confidence

The last row abstains: coverage is a property to measure, next to accuracy.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Failure Symptom Control
Leakage through augmentation test score far above production split before augmenting; deduplicate across splits
Label-flipping augmentation model gets worse on negation review a sample; forbid edits to negation words
Correlated labelling functions the label model is over-confident check agreement patterns; drop redundant functions
Synthetic text is too clean good on synthetic, poor on real typos and slang always evaluate on real held-out data
Class prior drift weak labels over-produce one class compare predicted class shares with the true shares

stages.name: What I'd ship
stages.claim: LLM-labelled pool, small model, active learning
stages.html:
Plan:LLM labels the unlabelled poolcompare with my 300 labels where they overlaptrain a small modellabel the least-confident examples by handretrain
Step Evaluation hook
LLM labelling agreement with human labels on a sample
Small model macro-F1 on the untouched 100
Each active-learning round does the held-out score still rise

The small model serves traffic; the LLM stays in the labelling loop.

followUps.question: How does a label model beat majority vote?
followUps.html:
It estimates how accurate each labelling function is from their agreements, with no ground truth.

Majority vote Label model
Weights every function equal higher for functions that agree with the consensus
Output hard label a probability, usable as a soft label

followUps.question: "Augment first, then do the train-test split."
followUps.html:
That puts paraphrases of test items into training.

Wrong:augment all 400splittraininflated score
Right:splitaugment the training side onlytrainhonest score

followUps.question: One class has only 12 examples. Does augmentation help?
followUps.html:
A little; it can't invent variety it hasn't seen.

  • Paraphrases of 12 examples are still 12 ideas.
  • Better: search the unlabelled pool for more real examples of that class with rules or nearest neighbours.
  • Report that class separately; macro-F1 will be driven by it.

followUps.question: How do you pick which examples to label next?
followUps.html:
Uncertainty sampling, with a random share to stay honest.

model scores the pooltake examples nearest the decision boundaryadd a random samplelabelretrain

The random share keeps the labelled set representative, which pure uncertainty sampling does not.

followUps.question: Is 100 test examples enough to make a ship decision?
followUps.html:
Enough for a coarse call, not for small differences.

accuracy 85% on 100 examples → 95% interval roughly 78% to 92%     ← ± 2·√(0.85·0.15/100) ≈ ± 7 points

I'd state the interval with the number, and grow the test set as labels arrive.

dontSay: "I'd augment the whole dataset" — the test set stays untouched.
"Synthetic data solves low-resource" — it copies the generator's idea of the task.
"Weak labels are free" — they cost a measurement of their noise.

nlp-classical-q23.testing: whether you can locate the failure stage by stage, and triage with cheap fixes first instead of asking for a new model.
nlp-classical-q23.trap: "translate everything to English first" as the whole answer.
nlp-classical-q23.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name it "This is distribution shift at the input: romanised Hindi mixed with English inside one sentence, spelled without a standard, plus emoji that carry the sentiment."
2 · What breaks where "It breaks at every stage. Language detection returns one label for a two-language sentence. The tokenizer splits romanised Hindi into meaningless pieces. English lexicons and stopword lists don't apply. And cleaning steps that strip emoji delete the clearest signal."
3 · Confirm with evidence "I'd confirm by slicing the evaluation set by language mix and measuring each slice, and by reading the tokenizer output on twenty tickets."
4 · Fix by experiment "Triage runs cheapest first. Unicode normalisation and keeping emoji cost nothing. Next, swap to a multilingual encoder that has seen transliterated text and fine-tune on a few hundred in-domain labels. The hard tail goes to an LLM."
5 · Validate "Each step is judged on the code-mixed slice and on the English slice, so a fix for one doesn't cost the other."
6 · Productionise "In production I tag each ticket with its language mix, monitor the share and the metric per tag, and keep collecting labels from that slice."
Close "Find the stage that fails, fix inputs before models, and keep the slice visible."

stages.name: Name it
stages.claim: input shift, not a model bug
stages.html:
"mera order abhi tak nahi aaya 😡 refund chahiye asap"

Property Why an English pipeline isn't ready
two languages in one sentence no single language label is right
romanised Hindi not in English vocabularies, not in Devanagari ones either
no standard spelling nahi, nahin, nhi, nai are one word
emoji and abbreviations carry intent, and are often stripped

stages.name: What breaks where
stages.html:
Stage What breaks Symptom
Cleaning emoji and non-ASCII stripped the angry face and Devanagari text vanish
Language ID one label per document routed to the English model, or to "unknown"
Tokenisation romanised words split into rare pieces weak embeddings, more tokens per ticket
Lexicons, stopwords, stemmer English-only sentiment and keyword features are empty
NER and intent trained on English word order entities missed, intent wrong

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.claim: the same text is not the same bytes
stages.html:
Prove it — three ways text that looks identical breaks exact matching:

import unicodedata
a, b = "caf\u00e9", "cafe\u0301"                      # same word on screen
print(a == b, len(a), len(b), unicodedata.normalize("NFC", b) == a)
wide = "\uff46\uff52\uff45\uff45"                    # full-width "free"
print(wide.lower() == "free", unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", wide) == "free")
thumb = "\U0001F44D\U0001F3FD"                        # thumbs-up + skin tone: one glyph
print(len(thumb), len(thumb.encode()))
# → False 4 5 True
# → False True
# → 2 8
Line What it shows
1 two encodings of "café" are unequal until normalised to NFC
2 full-width "free" only equals "free" after NFKC
3 one visible emoji is 2 code points and 8 bytes
Observation Likely cause Next action
code-mixed slice far below English slice tokenizer and model never saw this text multilingual encoder plus in-domain labels
errors vanish when emoji are kept cleaning step stop stripping them
duplicate-looking strings don't match Unicode forms normalise at ingestion

stages.name: Fix by experiment
stages.html:
Experiment 1

Fix the input

I'd normalise Unicode, keep emoji (or map them to words for a classical model) and remove the English-only cleaning steps.

Why? It is free and removes self-inflicted damage.

Best suited as step zero, always.

Experiment 2

Multilingual encoder, fine-tuned

I'd switch to an encoder pre-trained on Indian languages including transliterated text, such as MuRIL (Khanuja et al., 2021), and fine-tune on a few hundred labelled code-mixed tickets.

Why? The model has to have seen romanised Hindi for its subwords to mean anything.

Best suited when this slice is a large, steady share of traffic.

Experiment 3

LLM for the tail

I'd send low-confidence tickets to an LLM.

Why? Large models usually handle code-mixing well zero-shot, at a cost that only the tail can justify.

Best suited for rare mixes and new slang.

stages.name: Validate
stages.html:
Slice Baseline After each experiment
code-mixed measure measure
English only measure measure: must not drop
emoji-heavy measure measure

stages.name: Productionise
stages.html:
Per ticket:normaliseword-level language tagsmix label (en, hi-Latn, mixed)modellog label and confidence
  • A rising share of "mixed" is an early warning before quality drops.
  • A fixed number of tickets from this slice is labelled every week.

followUps.question: Why not translate everything to English first?
followUps.html:
It adds a lossy, slow stage in front of every ticket.

Issue Detail
errors compound a wrong translation becomes a wrong label
signal is lost tone, emphasis and emoji don't survive
cost and latency an extra model call per ticket

It can work as a fallback for a rare language, not as the default path.

followUps.question: How does word-level language identification work?
followUps.html:
As sequence labelling: one language tag per token, using character n-grams and context.

tokenscharacter n-gram featurestagger (CRF or small transformer)hi-Latn hi-Latn en hi-Latn …

followUps.question: How do you handle the spelling variants of romanised words?
followUps.html:
Either normalise them or use a representation that tolerates them.

  • Normalise: a variant dictionary or a transliteration model to one canonical form.
  • Tolerate: character n-gram features, or a subword model trained on such text.
  • Avoid: an English spell-checker, which "corrects" Hindi words into English ones.

followUps.question: A ticket is written in Devanagari and Latin script together.
followUps.html:
The same word can now appear in two scripts.

Option Trade-off
transliterate to one script before the model adds a component; unifies the vocabulary
use a model trained on both forms simpler pipeline; depends on the model's coverage

followUps.question: When is this slice worth a dedicated model?
followUps.html:
When its volume and its error cost together exceed the upkeep of a second model.

  • Share of traffic and how fast it is growing.
  • Cost of a wrong route for those customers.
  • Upkeep: a second evaluation set, labelling stream and release gate.

Below that line, one multilingual model plus LLM escalation is easier to run.

dontSay: "We'll detect the language and route" — the sentence has two.
"Strip emoji and special characters" — that deletes the signal.
"Translate to English" as the complete plan.

nlp-classical-q24.testing: whether you can avoid the all-pairs comparison with a named algorithm and its probability curve, and treat PII removal as a recall problem with layers.
nlp-classical-q24.trap: "embed every document and cluster", or "use an LLM to remove PII", at a billion documents.
nlp-classical-q24.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "First I'd separate three kinds of duplicate: byte-identical, near-duplicate with small edits, and same meaning in different words. And I'd ask which PII types matter and whether masking must be reversible."
2 · Constraints and numbers "A billion documents is about five times ten to the seventeen pairs, so anything pairwise is out. Every step has to be a single pass or a hash lookup."
3 · Baseline design "So the pipeline is tiered. Normalise the text, hash it to drop exact duplicates, then MinHash with locality-sensitive hashing for near-duplicates. PII goes through patterns with checksums for structured types, and an NER model for names and addresses."
4 · Deep-dive the hard part "The core is MinHash. Each document becomes a set of word shingles and then a short signature, and the share of matching signature positions estimates Jaccard similarity. LSH splits the signature into bands, and documents sharing any band become candidates. That gives an S-shaped curve: with twenty bands of five rows, similarity zero point eight is almost always caught and zero point three almost never."
5 · Failure modes "The failures are boilerplate making different pages look alike, very short documents, and PII recall: one missed number is a leak."
6 · Evolve "Later I'd make it incremental and add an embedding pass for paraphrased duplicates on what survives."
Close "Hash for exact, MinHash-LSH for near, layers for PII, and a measured miss rate on each."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.claim: three duplicate kinds, two PII kinds
stages.html:
Kind Example Algorithm
Exact the same file crawled twice hash of the normalised text
Near-duplicate same article, different footer or date MinHash + LSH, or SimHash
Semantic a rewritten press release embeddings + ANN (costly: only on survivors)
PII type Detect with
structured: emails, phone numbers, card and ID numbers patterns plus checksums
unstructured: names, addresses, organisations NER model

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
pairs            10⁹ × (10⁹ − 1) / 2 ≈ 5 × 10¹⁷               ← no pairwise method survives this
signature size   128 hashes × 4 bytes = 512 bytes per document
signature store  512 bytes × 10⁹ = 512 GB                     ← fits a distributed job, not one machine's RAM

So every stage must be O(n): a map over documents plus grouping by key.

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html: Deduplicating first means PII detection, the expensive stage, runs on fewer documents.

stages.name: Deep-dive the hard part
stages.html:
Per document:textword 3-shinglesset64–128 min-hashessplit into bandsbucket per band

Prove it — the signature estimates Jaccard similarity:

import hashlib
def shingles(t, k=3): w = t.split(); return {" ".join(w[i:i + k]) for i in range(len(w) - k + 1)}
def sig(s, n=64): return [min(int(hashlib.md5(f"{i}:{x}".encode()).hexdigest(), 16) for x in s) for i in range(n)]
a = shingles("the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog near the river bank today")
b = shingles("the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog near the river bank yesterday")
c = shingles("quarterly revenue grew while costs fell across every region this year again")
jac = lambda x, y: round(len(x & y) / len(x | y), 2)
est = lambda x, y: round(sum(p == q for p, q in zip(sig(x), sig(y))) / 64, 2)
print("near-dup: true", jac(a, b), "estimate", est(a, b), "| unrelated: true", jac(a, c), "estimate", est(a, c))
# → near-dup: true 0.85 estimate 0.81 | unrelated: true 0.0 estimate 0.0

P(two documents become candidates) = 1 − (1 − sʳ)ᵇ        s: Jaccard, b bands of r rows
threshold ≈ (1/b)^(1/r) = (1/20)^(1/5) ≈ 0.55

Candidates are then verified with the real Jaccard, and connected components give the duplicate clusters.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Failure Symptom Control
Shared boilerplate unrelated pages from one site merge strip navigation and footers before shingling
Very short documents few shingles: unstable similarity exact hash only below a length cutoff
Over-merging chains of "similar to similar" form giant clusters verify against the cluster's canonical document
Missed PII a leak layered detectors; sample audits for recall
Over-masking product codes masked as phone numbers checksums (Luhn for cards), context words
PII in logs and error messages the pipeline itself leaks log hashes and offsets, never the matched text

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
Next step How
Incremental ingestion keep the LSH buckets as an index; a new document is one lookup
Semantic duplicates embed the survivors, ANN search, verify with a cross-encoder
Reversible masking replace PII with typed tokens plus a vault mapping, when policy allows
Deletion requests the audit log maps a person's identifiers to affected documents

Evaluation hook: precision and recall of both stages on a hand-labelled sample, reported per document source.

followUps.question: MinHash or SimHash?
followUps.html:
MinHash estimates Jaccard over sets; SimHash gives a fingerprint whose Hamming distance tracks cosine.

MinHash + LSH SimHash
Signature tens to hundreds of integers one 64-bit value
Best at tunable similarity threshold very small edits, tiny storage

followUps.question: "Just embed everything and cluster."
followUps.html:
It is the most expensive tool applied to the cheapest part of the problem.

  • Exact and near duplicates are most of the volume and need no model.
  • Embedding a billion documents is a large GPU job; run it only on what the cheap tiers leave.
  • Embeddings merge paraphrases, which may not be what "duplicate" means for this corpus.

followUps.question: 🧪 With b = 20 and r = 5, what is the chance a pair at 0.5 similarity is compared?
followUps.html:
About 47%.

1 − (1 − 0.5⁵)²⁰ = 1 − (1 − 0.03125)²⁰ ≈ 0.47

To catch 0.5 reliably, use fewer rows per band, and accept more candidates.

followUps.question: How do you measure PII recall with no labels?
followUps.html:
Sample, label by hand, and plant known values.

  • Audit sample: annotators mark PII in a random sample of output.
  • Canaries: insert synthetic emails and numbers and check they are removed.
  • Per-type recall, because a 99% average can hide a weak detector for one type.

followUps.question: Who signs off that the corpus is clean?
followUps.html:
Privacy or legal, against a stated residual risk, not engineering alone.

They need From the pipeline
what was detected and how detector versions and rules
how much is missed audited recall per PII type
how to remove later the audit log and a deletion path

dontSay: "Compare every pair" — it is 5 × 10¹⁷ comparisons.
"The LLM will strip PII" at this volume, with no recall measurement.
"Dedup is solved by hashing" — only for exact copies.

nlp-classical-q25.testing: whether you treat the label set, the labelling budget and the feedback loop as the design, with the model as the easy part.
nlp-classical-q25.trap: starting with "I'd fine-tune BERT" when there are no labels and no agreed taxonomy.
nlp-classical-q25.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "I'd start with the taxonomy: how many classes, can a text have several, is there an 'other', and who owns the definitions. Then volume, latency and what a wrong label costs."
2 · Constraints and numbers "Labels are the scarce resource. Two thousand labels at thirty seconds each is about seventeen hours of annotator time, so I plan where each label goes."
3 · Baseline design "For the cold start, a zero-shot LLM and a few rules label a sample. People verify those labels, which also sharpens the guidelines. Then I train a small model on the verified set and serve it with a reject option."
4 · Deep-dive the hard part "The budget splits two ways. A random, stratified part becomes the test set and is never touched by the model. The rest is spent with active learning: label what the current model is least sure about."
5 · Failure modes "What goes wrong is rarely the model: classes that overlap, annotators anchored by model suggestions, and new topics the taxonomy doesn't have."
6 · Evolve "In production, low-confidence and sampled predictions go back to labelling. I monitor class shares and confidence for drift, retrain on a schedule or a trigger, and promote a new model only if it beats the current one on a fresh test set."
Close "Agree the labels, spend them deliberately, and keep the loop running after launch."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.claim: the taxonomy is the first design decision
stages.html:
Ask Why
single-label or multi-label? changes the output layer, the metric and the guidelines
is there an "other" or "unknown"? without it every new topic is forced into a wrong class
who owns class definitions? disagreements need a decider
volume and latency? decides small model against LLM for serving
cost of each error type? sets thresholds and the reject band

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
2,000 labels × 30 s = 60,000 s ≈ 16.7 annotator-hours        (illustrative)
split:  500 random, stratified  → test set, frozen
        300 random              → first training set and guideline pilot
        1,200                   → active-learning rounds
double-label 10% of everything  → agreement measurement
Budget per request (illustrative) Target
latency tens of milliseconds, in process or one hop
model small encoder on CPU, or distilled
LLM share only the rejected band

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.claim: from zero labels to a served model
stages.html: Verifying a suggested label is several times faster than labelling from scratch, which is what makes the cold start affordable.

stages.name: Deep-dive the hard part
stages.html:
Prove it — uncertainty sampling picks the examples nearest 0.5:

probs = {"t1": 0.97, "t2": 0.52, "t3": 0.08, "t4": 0.61, "t5": 0.45}    # P(positive) from the first model
print(sorted(probs, key=lambda k: abs(probs[k] - 0.5))[:3])
# → ['t2', 't5', 't4']
Label pool Chosen how Used for
Test set random, stratified by source and time honest evaluation: never chosen by a model
Seed training set random first model and guideline pilot
Active-learning rounds least confident, plus a random share fastest gain per label
Double-labelled sample random 10% inter-annotator agreement

Why this matters: a test set picked by the model's own uncertainty over-represents hard cases and can't estimate production accuracy.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Failure Symptom Control
Overlapping classes low annotator agreement on two classes merge them, or add a decision rule to the guidelines
Anchoring on suggestions annotators accept wrong LLM labels hide the suggestion on a sample; compare
Imbalance rare class never predicted macro-F1; search the pool for more rare examples
New topic confident wrong predictions "other" class, reject band, drift monitor
Guideline change old labels mean something else version the guidelines with the labels

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
The loop:servelog inputs, predictions, confidencesample and labeldetect driftretraincompare on a fresh test setpromote or keep
Monitor Signal of drift
predicted class shares a class grows or shrinks against its baseline
confidence distribution more predictions in the reject band
weekly labelled sample accuracy on fresh data falls
Retrain trigger Promote when
on a schedule, or when a monitor crosses its threshold the challenger beats the champion on fresh labels, on every key slice

followUps.question: Why a reject option?
followUps.html:
Because a wrong automatic label often costs more than a deferred one.

Confidence Action
above the threshold label automatically
below it send to a person or an LLM; the result becomes a training label

The threshold is set from the calibration curve and the review capacity.

followUps.question: "Skip the small model, the zero-shot LLM is accurate enough."
followUps.html:
Perhaps for accuracy; check volume, latency and stability too.

  • Per-request cost and latency scale with traffic.
  • Behaviour can shift when the provider updates the model.
  • A distilled small model trained on LLM labels often keeps most of the quality.

followUps.question: A new class has to be added after launch.
followUps.html:
It is a taxonomy migration, not just a retrain.

update guidelinesrelabel affected old examplesadd examples of the new classretrainrebuild the test setrelease

Old examples that now belong to the new class are the step most often skipped.

followUps.question: How do you know the labels are good enough to train on?
followUps.html:
Inter-annotator agreement, measured before training.

  • Cohen's kappa on the double-labelled sample, per class.
  • Low agreement on a class means the definition is unclear; fix the guideline first.
  • The model can't beat the consistency of its labels.

followUps.question: What does this system cost to run each quarter?
followUps.html:
Mostly people, not compute.

Line Driver
labelling weekly sample size × time per label
LLM calls reject-band share × traffic
serving small model on CPU
ownership someone maintaining guidelines, test set and release gate

dontSay: "I'd fine-tune a transformer" as the first sentence — on which labels, for which classes?
"The test set comes from active learning" — it has to be random.
"Once deployed, it's done" — text drifts.

nlp-classical-q26.testing: whether you design two different systems, per-keystroke suggestions and full search, each inside a stated latency budget.
nlp-classical-q26.trap: one pipeline for both, or a neural model on the keystroke path.
nlp-classical-q26.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "These are two systems with different budgets. Autocomplete answers on every keystroke and must feel instant. Search runs once per query and can afford several ranking stages. I'd also ask catalog size, update rate and languages."
2 · Constraints and numbers "I'd budget roughly a hundred milliseconds end to end for a suggestion and three hundred for a results page, and assign each stage a share."
3 · Baseline design "Indexing builds an inverted index with per-field analyzers, a vector index, and a suggestion index. A search query is normalised and spell-corrected, retrieved by BM25 and vectors together, fused, ranked by a learning-to-rank model, and the top few are reranked."
4 · Deep-dive the hard part "Autocomplete is the hard part. The top completions for every prefix are precomputed from query logs, so serving is a single lookup. Ranking mixes popularity, freshness and whether the suggestion returns results."
5 · Failure modes "Failures are zero-result queries, stale stock, offensive suggestions, and popularity feeding itself."
6 · Evolve "Then I'd add query understanding, such as detecting category and attributes, and personalisation, each gated by an online test."
Close "Precompute for the keystroke, cascade for the query, and give every stage a number of milliseconds."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html:
Autocomplete Search
Triggered every keystroke once per submitted query
Input a prefix, often 2–5 characters a full query
Returns 5–10 query or product suggestions a ranked page with facets
Budget tens of milliseconds server-side hundreds
Method precomputed lookup multi-stage ranking

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
Autocomplete (illustrative, ~100 ms felt) Share
client debounce and network most of it
server lookup under 20 ms

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
Index path:catalog changeanalyzers per fieldinverted index + vector index + suggestion indexnear-real-time refresh
Query path:querynormalise, spell-correctBM25 + dense retrievalfuseLTRrerank top 20business rulespage
Layer Candidates (illustrative) Uses
Retrieval ~1,000 title, brand and attribute fields with different weights; vectors for paraphrase
LTR ~100 text scores, popularity, rating, stock, margin
Rerank ~20 cross-encoder on query and title
Rules page pinned items, diversity, out-of-stock demotion

stages.name: Deep-dive the hard part
stages.html:
Prove it — top completions per prefix, built at index time:

from collections import defaultdict
queries = {"iphone 15": 900, "iphone case": 700, "ipad": 400, "ip camera": 120, "jeans": 800}
top = defaultdict(list)                        # prefix → completions, built at index time
for q, n in queries.items():
    for i in range(1, len(q) + 1): top[q[:i]].append((n, q))
top = {p: [q for _, q in sorted(v, reverse=True)[:3]] for p, v in top.items()}
print(top["ip"]); print(top["iph"]); print(len(top), "prefixes stored")
# → ['iphone 15', 'iphone case', 'ipad']
# → ['iphone 15', 'iphone case']
# → 27 prefixes stored
Serving:prefixnormaliselookup in the prefix mapfilter blocked termsreturn top k
Design choice Options Trade-off
Structure prefix map, trie, or finite-state transducer memory against flexibility
Source query logs, product titles logs reflect demand; titles cover the cold start
Score frequency, recency, conversion, has-results popularity alone goes stale
Typos fuzzy match within edit distance 1 more candidates per keystroke

Five queries already produce 27 stored prefixes, so real systems cap prefix length and keep only the top k per prefix.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Failure Symptom Control
Zero results user leaves spell correction, relax filters, fall back to dense retrieval
Stale stock or price clicks on unavailable items near-real-time updates for those fields; filter at query time
Offensive or legally risky suggestions reputational harm block list and review before a suggestion can be shown
Popularity loop suggested queries get more traffic, then rank higher decay by time; explore new suggestions
Identifier queries SKU not found by the dense arm keyword field and exact-match route

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
Step What it adds Gate
Query understanding "red nike shoes size 9" → category, brand, colour, size filters precision of the extracted attributes
Personalisation re-order by user history online test, with a non-personalised holdout
Semantic suggestions complete by meaning, not only prefix latency budget on the keystroke path

Evaluation hook: offline NDCG on judged queries; online click-through, zero-result rate and reformulation rate.

followUps.question: Why not run the neural reranker on all 1,000 candidates?
followUps.html:
It is one forward pass per candidate.

20 candidates × ~5 ms  = 100 ms        (illustrative)
1,000 candidates × ~5 ms = 5 s         ← far outside the budget

The cascade exists so each stage's cost per item can rise as the item count falls.

followUps.question: "Use an LLM to generate autocomplete suggestions."
followUps.html:
Not on the keystroke path.

Path Fit
per keystroke a lookup: the budget is milliseconds
offline an LLM can propose or clean suggestions that are then precomputed

followUps.question: A new product launches with no query history.
followUps.html:
Seed suggestions from the catalog until logs catch up.

  • Product titles and brands enter the suggestion index at ingestion.
  • A freshness boost gives new items a chance to earn clicks.
  • Marketing terms can be pinned for the launch window.

followUps.question: How does spell correction fit the query path?
followUps.html:
As a noisy-channel step before retrieval, with a guard.

querycandidates within edit distancescore by query-log frequencycorrect only if the original has few results

Brand names and SKUs look like typos, so "search instead for" keeps the original reachable.

followUps.question: Which metric do you take to the business review?
followUps.html:
One user-outcome metric with its guardrails.

Kind Metric
outcome conversion from search sessions
quality guardrail zero-result rate, reformulation rate
system guardrail p95 latency per path

dontSay: "Autocomplete is search with a shorter query" — it is a precomputed lookup.
"We'll rerank everything with a cross-encoder" — the budget forbids it.
A design with no latency number on any stage.

nlp-classical-q27.testing: whether you expose thresholds as policy dials owned by the business, and size the human-review queue they create.
nlp-classical-q27.trap: "maximise F1" as the objective, with one threshold for every harm category.
nlp-classical-q27.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "I'd ask which harm categories are in scope, what each kind of mistake costs, and how many people can review. A missed threat and a wrongly removed joke are different costs, and they differ by category."
2 · Constraints and numbers "Review capacity is the hard constraint. If a million posts a day arrive and three percent fall in the uncertain band, that is thirty thousand reviews a day."
3 · Baseline design "The pipeline is a cascade. Cheap filters first: hash lists and rules. Then a classifier gives a score per category. Two thresholds split the score: above the high one, remove automatically with an appeal; below the low one, publish; in between, a person decides."
4 · Deep-dive the hard part "The thresholds are the business decision. Moving the high threshold down removes more harm and more innocent posts. I'd show the trade as a table per category and let policy owners pick the operating point, with the review load each choice creates."
5 · Failure modes "Failures are adversarial spelling, context such as quotes and reclaimed words, drift in slang, and uneven error rates across dialects."
6 · Evolve "Reviewer decisions and appeals become training labels. An LLM can take the grey band for policies that need reasoning, with people sampling its decisions."
Close "The model produces a score; the business sets the thresholds; capacity decides the band between them."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.claim: the cost of each error, per category
stages.html:
Category (examples) A miss costs A wrong removal costs So favour
illegal content, credible threats severe harm, legal exposure an appeal recall
harassment, hate user harm silencing legitimate speech balance, with review
spam annoyance a lost legitimate post precision

One global threshold can't serve all three rows.

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
posts per day                 1,000,000            (illustrative)
share in the uncertain band   3%          →  30,000 reviews per day
reviews per reviewer per day  500         →  60 reviewers
widen the band to 5%                      →  50,000 reviews, 100 reviewers
Budget Target (illustrative)
decision latency before publish under 200 ms for the automatic path
review turnaround minutes for severe categories, hours for the rest

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html: Text is normalised first (Unicode NFKC, look-alike characters, repeated letters) so that obfuscated spellings reach the classifier in a standard form.

stages.name: Deep-dive the hard part
stages.claim: the threshold is a policy dial
stages.html:
Prove it — ten scored posts, four truly harmful, three thresholds:

scores = [(.95, 1), (.9, 1), (.8, 0), (.7, 1), (.6, 0), (.4, 1), (.3, 0), (.2, 0), (.1, 0), (.05, 0)]   # (score, harmful?)
for t in (0.85, 0.5, 0.25):
    tp = sum(s >= t and y for s, y in scores); fp = sum(s >= t and not y for s, y in scores)
    fn = sum(s < t and y for s, y in scores)
    print(t, "| precision", round(tp / (tp + fp), 2), "| recall", round(tp / (tp + fn), 2), "| wrongly removed", fp, "| missed", fn)
# → 0.85 | precision 1.0 | recall 0.5 | wrongly removed 0 | missed 2
# → 0.5 | precision 0.6 | recall 0.75 | wrongly removed 2 | missed 1
# → 0.25 | precision 0.57 | recall 1.0 | wrongly removed 3 | missed 0
Threshold Precision Recall Wrongly removed Missed Reads as
0.85 1.0 0.5 0 2 safe for speech, weak on harm
0.5 0.6 0.75 2 1 middle
0.25 0.57 1.0 3 0 catches everything, removes three innocent posts
Who decides:policy owner picks the operating point per categoryengineering reports the review load it impliesboth sign the threshold as config

The scores must be calibrated, or "0.85" means something different after every retrain.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Failure Symptom Control
Obfuscation "h@te", spaced letters, look-alike characters normalisation, character n-gram features
Context quoting abuse to report it, reclaimed terms thread context as input; grey band to people
Drift new slang and coded terms weekly labelled sample; fast rule updates
Uneven errors one dialect flagged more often error rates per group in every evaluation
Reviewer load fatigue, inconsistent decisions rotation, double review on a sample, wellbeing limits

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
The loop:review decisions and appeal outcomeslabelled setretrain and recalibratere-derive the threshold tablepolicy sign-off
Addition Role
LLM on the grey band applies a written policy to hard cases; a sample is audited by people
Policy as config thresholds and category definitions versioned outside the code
Transparency log what was removed, by which rule or model version, and the appeal result

Model output triggers an action here, so the automatic-removal path is the trust boundary: it gets the strictest threshold and an appeal.

followUps.question: Why two thresholds instead of one?
followUps.html:
To spend human attention only where the model is unsure.

Scores Decision Cost
very high or very low automatic none
the band between human reviewer time

The band's width is set by capacity; the positions by the error costs.

followUps.question: "Pick the threshold that maximises F1."
followUps.html:
F1 assumes a miss and a false alarm cost the same.

expected cost = missed × cost_of_miss + wrongly_removed × cost_of_wrong_removal

For a severe category the first term dominates, and the right threshold is far from the F1 optimum.

followUps.question: Harmful content is 0.1% of posts. What changes?
followUps.html:
Precision collapses even with a good classifier, and accuracy is meaningless.

1,000,000 posts, 1,000 harmful; classifier: 95% recall, 1% false-positive rate
flagged = 950 true + 9,990 false   →   precision ≈ 8.7%

Hence the review band, and evaluation by precision and recall, never accuracy.

followUps.question: How do you measure recall when you only review flagged posts?
followUps.html:
By also reviewing a random sample of what was published.

  • Random audit of unflagged posts estimates the miss rate.
  • User reports are a second, biased signal.
  • Without the random sample, recall is unknown.

followUps.question: A regulator asks why a post was removed.
followUps.html:
The system must be able to answer from its logs.

  • Stored per decision: category, score, threshold in force, model and policy version, reviewer if any.
  • Appeal path with outcome recorded.
  • Periodic report of volumes and error estimates per category.

dontSay: "We tune for the best F1" — the costs are unequal and belong to the business.
"The model decides what is removed" — the thresholds decide, and people own them.
"Accuracy is 99.9%" on a problem where 99.9% of posts are fine.

nlp-classical-q28.testing: whether you have an ordered set of questions that ends in a decision, and know the answer is usually a cascade.
nlp-classical-q28.trap: a philosophy ("it depends on the use case") with no questions, no numbers and no default.
nlp-classical-q28.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "I run three questions in order. Is the output closed and the task definition stable? Is the volume high or the latency budget tight? And can I get labels, including from an LLM?"
2 · Where classical wins "A small model or a rule wins when the output is a fixed set of labels or spans, traffic is high, latency is tens of milliseconds, and the decision has to be explained. Per-item cost is close to zero and behaviour doesn't change unless I change it."
3 · Where the LLM wins "The LLM wins when the output is open-ended, the task keeps changing, there are no labels, or volume is low enough that engineering time costs more than tokens."
4 · The deciding question "The deciding number is the measured quality gap on my evaluation set against the cost and latency of closing it. If the small model is within a point or two, volume decides."
5 · What I'd pick here "In practice the answer is a cascade. The LLM labels data and handles the low-confidence tail; the small model serves the bulk. That starts fast and gets cheaper as the small model improves."
Close "LLM to start and for the tail, classical for the volume, and an eval set to say when to move work between them."

stages.name: Frame the axis
Where classical wins
stages.html:
Dimension Small model or rules
Cost per item near zero after training
Latency microseconds to milliseconds, in process
Determinism same input, same output, until I retrain
Explainability feature weights, matched rule
Data residency runs inside my network
Needs labels, an owner, a retraining loop

Typical tasks: routing and intent, spam and moderation first pass, NER on a fixed schema, language ID, keyword retrieval, deduplication.

stages.name: Where the LLM wins
stages.claim: open tasks, no labels, changing definitions
stages.html:
Dimension LLM API
Time to first version hours: a prompt and a few examples
Output open-ended text, reasoning over context, many languages
When the task changes edit the prompt, no relabelling
Cost per item per token, grows linearly with traffic
Latency a network round trip plus generation time
Risks provider model changes, rate limits, output that needs validation

Typical tasks: summarisation, extraction with a schema that changes often, drafting, low-volume classification, the hard tail of any classifier.

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: the measured gap against its cost
stages.html:
volume                10,000,000 items per day, ~300 tokens each       (illustrative)
through an LLM        3,000,000,000 input tokens per day, plus a network call per item
through a CPU model   ~1 ms per item → 10,000 CPU-seconds ≈ 2.8 CPU-hours per day
cascade, 5% escalated 500,000 LLM calls per day: one twentieth of the LLM-only volume
Evidence I'd collect Decision it drives
quality of each option on the same eval set is there a gap worth paying for
p95 latency against the budget whether the LLM can sit on the request path at all
traffic forecast where per-item cost overtakes fixed cost
cost of an error how much quality gap is tolerable

stages.name: What I'd pick here
stages.claim: a cascade that shifts over time
stages.html:
Day one:all trafficLLMoutputs logged as labels
Steady state:all trafficsmall modelconfidentdone
The tail:low confidenceLLManswer, plus a new training label
Phase Share to the LLM Trigger to move on
prototype 100% task definition has stopped changing
distilled model live the reject band small model within the agreed gap on the eval set
mature shrinking each retrain narrows the band

Fix layer: this is an orchestration decision; neither model changes.

followUps.question: Where does a fine-tuned small language model fit?
followUps.html:
Between the two: generative output at self-hosted cost.

Option Fits when
classical or small encoder closed labels or spans
fine-tuned small generative model structured generation at volume, data must stay in-house
frontier API model open tasks, low volume, fastest start

followUps.question: "Token costs keep falling, so just use the LLM for everything."
followUps.html:
Cost is one of four axes.

  • Latency: a network call can't meet a 20 ms budget.
  • Stability: a provider update can shift behaviour under a fixed prompt.
  • Residency and audit: some text can't leave the network.
  • Explainability: some decisions must be justified per feature.

followUps.question: The LLM is 6 points better and traffic is 500 items a day.
followUps.html:
Use the LLM and stop.

Factor Value
volume too low for per-item cost to matter
engineering time a labelled set and a retraining loop would cost more than the calls

The framework has to be allowed to answer "LLM only".

followUps.question: How do you keep the cascade honest?
followUps.html:
Sample the confident path too.

  • A random share of small-model decisions goes to the LLM or a person for comparison.
  • Agreement rate is tracked per class.
  • A drop triggers retraining or a wider reject band.

followUps.question: How do you present this to a leadership team?
followUps.html:
As a table with three options and one recommendation.

Option Quality Latency Run cost at forecast volume Time to ship
LLM only measure measure measure shortest
small model only measure measure measure longest
cascade measure measure measure in between

The recommendation names the trigger for revisiting it: a volume level or a quality gap.

dontSay: "It depends on the use case" without the questions that decide it.
"LLMs are too expensive" or "classical is obsolete" as a blanket claim.
A recommendation with no eval set behind it.

nlp-classical-q29.testing: whether you treat an embedding model as a schema that every stored vector depends on, and can run a model change without downtime.
nlp-classical-q29.trap: "swap in the better embedding model": vectors from two models are not comparable.
nlp-classical-q29.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "I'd ask how many vectors, how often documents change, the query latency target, and whether the embedding model is self-hosted or an API I don't control."
2 · Constraints and numbers "A hundred million vectors at seven hundred sixty-eight dimensions in float32 is about three hundred gigabytes before the index. That decides between an in-memory graph and a compressed index."
3 · Baseline design "The design has three parts: an embedding service that stamps every vector with a model version, an approximate-nearest-neighbour index, and a golden query set that measures recall against exact search."
4 · Deep-dive the hard part "The hard part is changing the model. Vectors from two versions live in different spaces, so I never mix them. I build a second index, backfill it, write new documents to both, compare on shadow traffic, then switch an alias and keep the old index for rollback."
5 · Failure modes "Failures are mixed versions, stale vectors after a document edit, deletes that linger in the graph, and a provider silently updating the model."
6 · Evolve "Then monitoring for drift: similarity-score distributions, recall on the golden set, and the share of queries with a weak top match."
Close "Version the vectors, measure ANN recall, and migrate with two indexes, never in place."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html:
Ask Why
how many vectors, what dimension? memory and index type
how often do documents change or get deleted? freshness path and delete handling
query latency and throughput? index parameters, replicas
self-hosted model or API? who controls when the model changes
filters with the search? filtered ANN behaves differently from plain ANN

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
raw vectors        100,000,000 × 768 × 4 bytes = 307.2 GB
product-quantised  100,000,000 × 64 bytes      = 6.4 GB        ← 48× smaller, some recall lost
re-embedding       100,000,000 documents through the model     ← a batch job, plan it like a migration
Index Memory Strength Pick when
HNSW (graph) vectors plus links, in RAM high recall at low latency the set fits in memory
IVF + PQ compressed codes very large sets, disk-friendly memory is the constraint
exact (flat) vectors perfect recall small sets, and as the ground truth

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
Write path:document changechunkembedding servicevector + model_version + doc_versionindex upsert
Read path:querysame model versionANN search with filterstop kreranker
Component Rule
Embedding service one place owns model, tokenizer, pooling, normalisation and truncation
Metadata on every vector model version, source document version, created time
Golden set a few hundred queries with exact-search results, rerun on every index or parameter change

stages.name: Deep-dive the hard part
stages.html:
Migration:build index v2backfill all documentsdual-write new changesshadow queries on bothswitch aliaskeep v1 for rollbackdrop v1
Step Check before moving on
backfill vector count in v2 equals document count
shadow retrieval quality on the golden set and on sampled live queries: v2 not worse
switch alias change is atomic; the query encoder switches in the same release
rollback window v1 kept and still dual-written until confidence is established

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Failure Symptom Control
Mixed model versions in one index results look random for part of the corpus version in metadata; reject mismatched writes
Query and document encoders differ recall drops with no error one service, one version, for both
Stale vectors search finds text that was edited away re-embed on document change, keyed by document version
Deletes linger removed documents still returned tombstones filtered at query time; periodic rebuild
Provider updates the model score distribution shifts overnight pin the model version; alert on distribution change
Truncation long chunks lose their tail enforce chunk size in tokens of this tokenizer

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
Monitor What it catches
ANN recall on the golden set index or parameter regressions
top-1 similarity distribution queries drifting away from the corpus
share of queries below a similarity floor content gaps: users ask what the corpus lacks
embedding latency and error rate service health
index size against document count missed writes or deletes

Evaluation hook: retrieval quality (recall@k, NDCG) on labelled queries is the release gate for any model, index or chunking change.

followUps.question: How do HNSW parameters trade off?
followUps.html:
Two build-time settings fix the graph; one query-time setting moves along the recall–latency curve.

Parameter Higher value gives
M (links per node) better recall, more memory
ef_construction better graph, slower build
ef_search better recall, slower queries

followUps.question: "The new model has the same dimension, so we can reuse the index."
followUps.html:
Same shape, different space.

v1("refund") and v2("refund")unrelated coordinatescosine between them is meaningless

Every vector must be re-embedded, and query and documents must switch together.

followUps.question: 🧪 How much memory for 10 million 1,024-dimensional float32 vectors?
followUps.html:
About 41 GB, before index overhead.

10,000,000 × 1,024 × 4 bytes = 40.96 GB

followUps.question: What goes wrong with filtered vector search?
followUps.html:
A selective filter can leave the ANN search with too few valid neighbours.

Strategy Problem
filter after search top k may contain no matching items
filter before search graph traversal is cut; may fall back to brute force

Check how the store implements filtering, and test recall with realistic filters.

followUps.question: Build on a managed vector database or run your own?
followUps.html:
Managed until scale, residency or cost shape forces otherwise.

Factor Points to
small team, moderate scale managed
data must stay in a given network self-hosted or a private deployment
very large, steady workload self-hosted may be cheaper to run

Either way the version stamps, golden set and two-index migration are mine to build.

dontSay: "We'll upgrade the embedding model in place."
"ANN search returns the nearest neighbours" — approximately; the recall has to be measured.
"Embeddings don't need monitoring" — they fail without errors.
