nlp-classical-q30.testing: whether you see RAG as retriever-plus-reader with the reader swapped for a generator, and can carry the old failure modes forward.
nlp-classical-q30.trap: presenting RAG as a 2023 invention with no ancestry.
nlp-classical-q30.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The three families "There are two independent choices. Is the passage given, or must the system find it? And is the answer a span copied from the passage, or newly written text? SQuAD-era systems were given the passage and extracted a span."
2 · How extractive works "An extractive reader scores every token as a possible start and a possible end of the answer, and returns the best valid span. It can't invent anything, and it can't answer what isn't written word for word."
3 · The open-domain step "Open-domain QA added a retriever in front. DrQA paired TF-IDF retrieval with a neural reader in 2017; dense passage retrieval replaced the sparse retriever with learned embeddings in 2020."
4 · What RAG kept "RAG kept that pipeline and swapped the span reader for a generator. So the answer can combine several passages and be phrased naturally. It also inherited the rule that the reader can only be as good as what was retrieved."
5 · Where it still breaks "And it brought back the abstractive risk: a fluent answer the passages don't support. So the old controls still apply: measure retrieval recall separately, allow 'not in the documents', and cite spans."
Close "RAG is open-domain QA with a generative reader, and it fails in the places its ancestors did."

stages.name: The three families
stages.html:
Answer is a copied span Answer is generated
Passage given extractive reading comprehension (SQuAD, 2016) abstractive QA over a document
Passage must be found open-domain extractive (DrQA, 2017; DPR, 2020) retrieval-augmented generation (2020 onward)

stages.name: How extractive works
stages.claim: pick a start and an end
stages.html:
Prove it — best span from start and end scores (toy logits), question "When was BM25 published?":

toks = ["BM25", "was", "published", "in", "1994", "by", "Robertson"]
start = [0.1, 0, 0, 0.1, 2.3, 0.2, 1.1]; end = [0, 0, 0, 0, 2.0, 0, 1.4]      # span-head logits (toy)
spans = ((i, j) for i in range(7) for j in range(i, min(i + 3, 7)))
i, j = max(spans, key=lambda ij: start[ij[0]] + end[ij[1]])
print((i, j), toks[i: j + 1], round(start[i] + end[j], 1))
# → (4, 4) ['1994'] 4.3
The reader:question + passageencoderstart score and end score per tokenbest pair with start ≤ endspan
Property Consequence
output is a quote no fabricated facts; easy to highlight in the source
one contiguous span can't answer yes/no, counts, or anything needing two sentences
SQuAD 2.0 added unanswerable questions the model must be able to return "no answer"

stages.name: The open-domain step
stages.html:
Retriever–reader:questionretriever over the corpustop k passagesreaderanswer
Year System Retriever Reader
2017 DrQA (Chen et al.) TF-IDF over Wikipedia neural span extractor
2020 DPR (Karpukhin et al.) dense bi-encoder span extractor
2020 RAG (Lewis et al.) dense sequence-to-sequence generator
now LLM-based RAG hybrid plus reranker large language model

stages.name: What RAG kept
stages.claim: the same pipeline, a different reader
stages.html:
Inherited from classical QA Form in a RAG system
retrieve, then read the same two stages, evaluated separately
reader bounded by retrieval answer quality can't exceed recall of the retrieved context
unanswerable questions abstention: "the documents don't say"
exact match and token F1 still used for short factual answers, joined by faithfulness checks
answer span citations pointing at the supporting passage

What changed: the generator can merge several passages and write a full sentence, which the span reader never could.

stages.name: Where it still breaks
stages.html:
Failure Came from Control, and its layer
the right passage was never retrieved open-domain QA hybrid retrieval, recall@k on a labelled set (retrieval)
answer not supported by the passages abstractive generation faithfulness check, required citations (orchestration)
question has no answer in the corpus SQuAD 2.0 abstain instruction plus a relevance threshold (prompt, retrieval)
needs two documents combined multi-hop QA query decomposition or iterative retrieval (orchestration)

followUps.question: Exact match and F1 in QA: what is the difference?
followUps.html:
Exact match is all-or-nothing; F1 gives credit for token overlap.

Gold: "in 1994" Exact match Token F1
prediction "1994" 0 0.67
prediction "in 1994" 1 1.0

Both are computed after normalising case, punctuation and articles.

followUps.question: "RAG is a new idea from the LLM era."
followUps.html:
The retrieve-then-read design is from 2017, and the name RAG from 2020.

DrQA (2017)DPR (2020)RAG paper (2020)LLM-based RAG

What is new is the strength of the reader, not the architecture.

followUps.question: The corpus doesn't contain the answer. What should each system do?
followUps.html:
Say so, and each needs a mechanism for it.

System Mechanism
extractive reader a "no answer" score compared with the best span
RAG a retrieval-score floor, plus an instruction to abstain when context is insufficient

Without one, both return their most plausible wrong answer.

followUps.question: Why did dense retrieval beat TF-IDF here?
followUps.html:
Questions and answer passages often share meaning but few words.

  • "Who wrote Hamlet?" against a passage saying "Shakespeare's tragedy …".
  • Dense retrievers are trained on question–passage pairs to bridge that gap.
  • Out of domain the advantage shrinks, which is why hybrid retrieval is the default.

followUps.question: When would you still ship an extractive reader?
followUps.html:
When the answer must be verbatim and auditable.

Requirement Why extractive
compliance or policy lookup the answer is a highlighted quote, nothing is rephrased
very high volume, short factual answers a small encoder is cheap and fast
zero tolerance for fabricated text faithful by construction

dontSay: "RAG replaced question answering" — it is question answering.
"The LLM answers from the documents" without separating retrieval quality from generation quality.
"Extractive QA is obsolete" — it is the auditable option.

nlp-classical-q31.testing: whether you can name the specific techniques that started in translation and now sit inside every LLM system.
nlp-classical-q31.trap: a history lecture with no "and that is why we do X today".
nlp-classical-q31.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The SMT recipe "Statistical translation was a pipeline of separately trained parts: a word-alignment model, a phrase table, a language model for fluency, and a decoder that searched for the best combination."
2 · What NMT changed "Neural translation replaced all of that with one encoder-decoder network trained end to end on sentence pairs. Attention removed the fixed-vector bottleneck and learned alignment as a by-product."
3 · Prove it "Decoding is one inheritance. Greedy search picks 'the' first and ends at probability zero point one five; a beam of two keeps 'a' alive and finds a sequence at zero point three six."
4 · Lessons that generalised "Five things generalised: end-to-end training beats pipelines of hand-built parts; attention; subword tokenization, introduced to handle rare words in translation; back-translation, which is synthetic data from a reverse model; and automatic metrics like BLEU, which sped the field up and then misled it."
5 · Where it still breaks "And the same weaknesses carried over: fluent output that is wrong, weak performance out of domain, and inconsistent terminology across a document."
Close "The transformer itself was a translation paper. Most of the modern toolkit was built to translate."

stages.name: The SMT recipe
stages.html:
noisy channel:  best English e for foreign f  =  argmax over e   P(f | e) × P(e)
                                                   └ translation model ┘ └ language model ┘
The pipeline:parallel textword alignment (IBM models)phrase tabledecoder with an n-gram language modelweights tuned on BLEU
Part Trained on Weakness
alignment and phrase table parallel sentences no generalisation across similar phrases
language model monolingual text short n-gram context
the whole each part separately errors compound; reordering across long distances is hard

stages.name: What NMT changed
stages.html:
Statistical MT Neural MT
Components several, tuned separately one encoder-decoder
Alignment an explicit model attention weights, learned jointly
Units words and phrases subwords
Generalisation exact phrase matches similar words share representations
Fluency from the n-gram model from the decoder itself
The steps:encoder-decoder (2014)attention (2015)subwords and back-translation (2016)transformer (2017)

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: greedy against beam on two steps
stages.html:
Prove it — the locally best first word leads to a worse sentence:

step1 = {"the": 0.5, "a": 0.4}
step2 = {"the": {"cat": 0.3, "dog": 0.3}, "a": {"cat": 0.9, "dog": 0.05}}
g1 = max(step1, key=step1.get); g2 = max(step2[g1], key=step2[g1].get)
print("greedy:", g1, g2, round(step1[g1] * step2[g1][g2], 2))
p, a, b = max((step1[a] * p, a, b) for a in step1 for b, p in step2[a].items())
print("beam 2:", a, b, round(p, 2))
# → greedy: the cat 0.15
# → beam 2: a cat 0.36
Decoder First word Sequence probability
greedy the (0.5) 0.15
beam of 2 a (0.4) 0.36

Beam search came from MT decoders and is still the default for translation and speech, while sampling is preferred for open-ended generation.

stages.name: Lessons that generalised
stages.html:
Lesson from MT Where it shows up now
End-to-end beats hand-built pipelines task pipelines collapsed into one pre-trained model
Attention the transformer, which was itself an MT paper (Vaswani et al., 2017)
Subword units (BPE for NMT, Sennrich et al., 2016) every LLM tokenizer
Back-translation (Sennrich et al., 2016) synthetic training data and LLM-generated augmentation
An automatic metric drives progress, then distorts it (BLEU, 2002) benchmark saturation; the move to task-level and human evaluation

stages.name: Where it still breaks
stages.html:
Failure In MT Same failure in LLM systems
Hallucination fluent output unrelated to the source under domain shift unsupported answers
Low-resource poor quality for language pairs with little data weak long-tail languages and domains
Terminology the same term translated three ways in one document inconsistent naming across a long output
Sentence-level context pronouns and formality lost across sentences lost references across chunks

Fix layer in MT today: glossaries and constrained decoding for terminology; document-level context; human post-editing for high-stakes text.

followUps.question: What exactly is back-translation?
followUps.html:
Making synthetic source sentences for real target sentences.

monolingual target textreverse model translates it to the source language(synthetic source, real target) pairstrain the forward model

The target side is real, so the model learns to produce fluent output even from noisy input.

followUps.question: "A wider beam always gives better translations."
followUps.html:
No. Past a small width, quality often falls.

  • Very wide beams find high-probability outputs that are too short or empty.
  • Length normalisation is needed to counter the bias toward short sequences.
  • Typical widths are small, around 4 to 10.

followUps.question: Is a general LLM now better than a dedicated MT model?
followUps.html:
Often for high-resource pairs and context-heavy text; not uniformly.

Situation Tendency
major language pairs, needs document context or style control LLM
high volume, low latency, fixed domain dedicated NMT model
low-resource pair measure both; neither is safe to assume

followUps.question: Why did subwords matter so much for translation?
followUps.html:
Because names, compounds and inflected forms are endless, and a word vocabulary isn't.

Without subwords With subwords
rare word → UNK → untranslatable rare word → known pieces → translated or copied piece by piece

followUps.question: How do you evaluate a translation system for a product?
followUps.html:
An automatic metric for regression, people for the release decision.

Layer Tool
every build BLEU or chrF, and a learned metric such as COMET
release human rating of adequacy and fluency on a sample, per domain
high-stakes content post-editing effort as the business metric

dontSay: "SMT was rule-based" — it was statistical; rule-based MT came before it.
"Attention came from the transformer."
"BLEU measures whether the translation is right."

nlp-classical-q32.testing: whether you can name, for each generation, the one limitation that forced the next.
nlp-classical-q32.trap: listing architectures in order with no cause linking them.
nlp-classical-q32.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Count tables "N-gram models count. They were killed by sparsity: a trigram table over fifty thousand words has over ten to the fourteen cells, and they can't share anything between similar words."
2 · Fixed-window networks "Bengio's 2003 model fixed sharing: words became embeddings, so 'cat' and 'dog' behave alike. It was killed by its window: it still saw only the last few words."
3 · Recurrent networks "RNNs removed the window by carrying a hidden state forward, so context is unbounded in principle. They were killed by vanishing gradients: multiply by zero point nine fifty times and half a percent of the signal is left."
4 · LSTMs "LSTMs added a cell state with gates, an additive path that lets gradients survive hundreds of steps. They were killed by being sequential: step fifty waits for step forty-nine, so training can't use parallel hardware, and distant words are still many steps apart."
5 · Attention "Attention connects any two positions directly, and the transformer dropped recurrence entirely. Its own cost is that compute grows with the square of the sequence length."
Close "Each stage was killed by the next bottleneck: sparsity, window, gradient, then sequential compute."

stages.name: Count tables
stages.html:
trigram table over V = 50,000 words:  50,000³ = 1.25 × 10¹⁴ possible entries      ← almost all unseen
"the cat sat" tells the model nothing about "the dog sat"                         ← no sharing
Lineage at a glance Fixed Killed by
n-gram counts — sparsity, no similarity between words
fixed-window neural LM (Bengio et al., 2003) sharing through embeddings a fixed, short context
RNN LM (Mikolov et al., 2010) unbounded context vanishing gradients
LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) long-range gradients sequential compute, long paths
attention, then the transformer (2015, 2017) direct links, parallel training quadratic cost in length

stages.name: Fixed-window networks
stages.html:
The model:previous n−1 wordslook up embeddingsconcatenatehidden layersoftmax over the vocabulary
Gain Limit
similar words get similar vectors, so unseen n-grams get sensible probabilities context is still n−1 words; widening it multiplies the input size
the embedding table became the reusable artefact (later Word2Vec) a full softmax over the vocabulary is slow

stages.name: Recurrent networks
stages.html:
hₜ = tanh(W·hₜ₋₁ + U·xₜ)                     ← one state carries all history
gradient across k steps ∝ (factor)ᵏ
0.9⁵⁰ ≈ 0.0052      1.1⁵⁰ ≈ 117.4            ← vanishes or explodes

Exploding gradients are handled by clipping. Vanishing ones need a different architecture.

stages.name: LSTMs
stages.html:
cₜ = fₜ ⊙ cₜ₋₁ + iₜ ⊙ c̃ₜ        ← additive cell path: the gradient flows through fₜ, which can stay near 1
hₜ = oₜ ⊙ tanh(cₜ)
What the gates bought What still hurt
dependencies over hundreds of steps step t needs step t−1: no parallelism over time
the workhorse of 2014–2017 NLP two distant words are still k steps apart
ELMo: contextual embeddings from a bidirectional LSTM LM training on very large corpora was slow

stages.name: Attention
stages.html:
Property RNN / LSTM Transformer
Path between two tokens as many steps as the distance one attention hop
Training over a sequence sequential parallel across positions
Cost in sequence length n linear quadratic in attention
Order information built into the recurrence added with positional encodings

So what for a system today: context length is the expensive resource, which is why chunking, retrieval and KV caching exist.

followUps.question: Why does the LSTM cell state help gradients?
followUps.html:
Because the cell is updated by addition, not by repeated squashing.

RNN:gradienttimes weight and tanh slope, every stepshrinks
LSTM:gradienttimes forget gate, near 1 when memory is keptsurvives

followUps.question: "Transformers have no limitations compared with RNNs."
followUps.html:
They traded a gradient problem for a cost problem.

  • Quadratic attention in sequence length.
  • No built-in order, so positions must be encoded.
  • Constant memory streaming is easier with recurrent models, which is one reason state-space and recurrent variants are still researched.

followUps.question: 🧪 A gradient is scaled by 0.9 per step. How much is left after 20 steps?
followUps.html:
About 12%.

0.9²⁰ ≈ 0.122

followUps.question: Where does ELMo sit in this lineage?
followUps.html:
At the end of the LSTM era: the first widely used contextual embeddings.

static vectors (Word2Vec)ELMo: bidirectional LSTM language model, a vector per token in contextBERT and GPT on transformers

It showed that pre-training a language model and reusing its representations transfers across tasks.

followUps.question: Why does this history matter to someone building on LLM APIs?
followUps.html:
It tells you which costs are structural.

Structural fact Design consequence
attention cost grows with context retrieve and trim instead of sending everything
the model is a next-token predictor fluency is not evidence of correctness
representations come from pre-training domain gaps need retrieval or fine-tuning, not longer prompts alone

dontSay: "RNNs can't model long sequences" — they can represent them; they can't learn them, because of the gradient.
"LSTMs solved long-range dependencies" — they extended the range, at sequential cost.
"Attention replaced LSTMs in 2015" — attention was added to them first; the transformer removed them in 2017.

nlp-classical-q33.testing: whether you know the two representations, and can answer honestly that most downstream uses moved into end-to-end models, while naming what is left.
nlp-classical-q33.trap: claiming parsing is a required preprocessing step, or claiming nobody uses it.
nlp-classical-q33.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "Both describe sentence structure. Constituency parsing groups words into nested phrases: noun phrase, verb phrase. Dependency parsing links each word to its head with a labelled relation: subject, object."
2 · Where constituency fits "Constituency trees fit when phrase boundaries matter: grammar checking, linguistic study, extracting whole noun phrases."
3 · Where dependency fits "Dependency trees fit information extraction. Who did what to whom is one hop from the verb, they handle free word order, and Universal Dependencies gives one scheme across more than a hundred languages."
4 · Who uses parses now "In 2026 most pipelines that used to parse first go straight from text to output with a pre-trained model. Parses survive where output must be explainable and precise: rule-based extraction in clinical and legal text, negation scope, grammar tools, and low-resource languages."
5 · What I'd pick in 2026 "If I need structure today I take a dependency parse from spaCy or Stanza as a feature or a rule anchor. I wouldn't put a parser in front of a transformer by default."
Close "Constituency for phrases, dependency for relations, and neither as mandatory preprocessing."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
Constituency Dependency
Unit nested phrases (NP, VP, PP) word-to-head arcs with labels
Tree nodes words plus phrase nodes words only
Good for phrase boundaries, fixed word order relations, free word order
Standard resource Penn Treebank Universal Dependencies
Classic algorithm CKY chart parsing, cubic in sentence length transition-based (linear) or graph-based 
constituency:  [S [NP Acme] [VP acquired [NP Beta] [PP in [NP 2024]]]]
dependency:    acquired → Acme (nsubj), Beta (obj), in (prep) → 2024 (pobj)

stages.name: Where constituency fits
stages.claim: when the phrase is the unit
stages.html:
Use Why phrases
Grammar and style checking errors are defined on phrase structure
Noun-phrase extraction the answer is a whole constituent, such as "the outstanding loan amount"
Linguistic research, treebank study phrase structure is the object of study

stages.name: Where dependency fits
stages.html:
Prove it — a subject–verb–object triple read straight off the arcs:

sent = ["Acme", "acquired", "Beta", "in", "2024"]
heads = [1, -1, 1, 1, 3]; deps = ["nsubj", "root", "obj", "prep", "pobj"]     # one head per word
root = heads.index(-1)
pick = lambda label: [sent[i] for i, (h, d) in enumerate(zip(heads, deps)) if h == root and d == label]
print((pick("nsubj")[0], sent[root], pick("obj")[0]))
# → ('Acme', 'acquired', 'Beta')

The same two-line rule works for "Beta was acquired by Acme" once the passive labels are mapped, which a word-order pattern can't do.

stages.name: Who uses parses now
stages.html:
Consumer in 2026 What the parse gives them
Rule-based extraction in clinical or legal text auditable patterns: "no evidence of X" negates X by scope
Grammar and writing tools structural error detection
Low-resource languages Universal Dependencies resources where large models are weak
Linguistically aware chunking and query analysis head nouns, clause boundaries
Model analysis probing whether representations encode syntax
No longer needs an explicit parse Replaced by
sentiment, classification, translation, QA end-to-end pre-trained models
most relation extraction fine-tuned encoders or LLMs with a schema

stages.name: What I'd pick in 2026
stages.claim: a dependency parse, only when needed
stages.html:
Decision:does a rule or an audit need structure?dependency parse as a feature
Otherwise:raw textpre-trained model
Point What it means
Tools spaCy for speed in production, Stanza for coverage of many languages.
Cost a parser adds latency and its own error rate to everything after it.
Evaluation hook parser quality is labelled attachment score; what matters is the downstream task with and without the parse.

followUps.question: Transition-based or graph-based dependency parsing?
followUps.html:
Speed against global optimality.

Transition-based Graph-based
How shift and arc actions, left to right score all arcs, find the best tree
Complexity linear quadratic or more
Error profile early mistakes propagate better on long-distance arcs

followUps.question: "Transformers don't know syntax, so we should feed them parses."
followUps.html:
Probing studies found much syntactic structure recoverable from their representations (Hewitt & Manning, 2019).

  • Adding parse features to a strong encoder rarely helps and adds a failure point.
  • Parses help when the consumer is a rule or a person, not the encoder.

followUps.question: "I saw the man with the telescope." What does a parser do?
followUps.html:
It has to choose one attachment, and the sentence is truly ambiguous.

Attachment Meaning
"with the telescope" → saw I used the telescope
"with the telescope" → man the man has the telescope

Prepositional-phrase attachment is the classic source of parser errors; only context resolves it.

followUps.question: How is a parser evaluated?
followUps.html:
By attachment scores for dependencies and bracket F1 for constituents.

  • UAS: share of words with the correct head.
  • LAS: correct head and correct label.
  • Bracket F1: overlap of predicted and gold phrase spans.

followUps.question: When would you defend adding a parser to a production pipeline?
followUps.html:
When a decision must be explainable by a rule a domain expert can read.

Situation Parser earns its place
clinical negation and scope "denies chest pain" must not extract chest pain
contract obligations who owes what to whom, with the clause cited
no labelled data and no LLM allowed patterns over arcs are a workable baseline

dontSay: "You must parse before any NLP task" — that was the 2010 pipeline.
"Parsing is dead" — it moved to explainable, high-precision niches.
"Dependency and constituency are the same thing drawn differently" — they answer different questions.

nlp-classical-q34.testing: whether you can separate "the task disappeared as a pipeline stage" from "the problem disappeared", and name where coreference still bites.
nlp-classical-q34.trap: "LLMs solved all of this", with no mention of long documents or chunking.
nlp-classical-q34.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Three tasks defined "Word-sense disambiguation picks the meaning of a word in context: which 'bank'. Semantic role labelling finds who did what to whom around a verb. Coreference links every mention of the same entity: 'it', 'she', 'the company'."
2 · What LLMs absorbed "Word senses were absorbed first: a contextual embedding of 'bank' already differs by context, so nobody runs a separate sense tagger. Role labelling as an input feature went the same way; models read the roles implicitly."
3 · What still stands "Coreference is the one still standing as an engineering problem. It is long-range and document-level. And explicit roles are still useful when the output must be structured: events for a knowledge base."
4 · Where it breaks "It bites in retrieval. Split a document into chunks and a chunk that says 'it was terminated in March' has lost what 'it' refers to. The embedding and the reader both suffer."
5 · What I'd build "So I'd resolve references at ingestion: rewrite or annotate chunks so each one names its entities, and use an LLM or a coreference model for that. For structured extraction I'd ask for roles as a schema."
Close "The tasks left the pipeline; the problems moved to chunk boundaries and structured outputs."

stages.name: Three tasks defined
stages.html:
"The bank approved her loan after it reviewed the documents."

Task Question Answer here
Word-sense disambiguation which sense of bank? financial institution, not river side
Semantic role labelling for approved: who, what, when? agent: the bank · theme: her loan · time: after it reviewed the documents
Coreference what does it refer to? the bank

stages.name: What LLMs absorbed
stages.html:
Task Classical approach Status now
WSD Lesk overlap with dictionary glosses; supervised classifiers over WordNet senses implicit: contextual vectors for bank separate by context
SRL as a feature parser, then a role classifier over PropBank frames implicit: end-to-end models don't need it as input
Short-range coreference mention-pair classifiers, then end-to-end span models (Lee et al., 2017) handled within one context window, mostly

Why senses went first: static embeddings had one vector per word; contextual ones have one per occurrence, which is disambiguation by construction.

stages.name: What still stands
stages.html:
Still a real problem Why
Document-level coreference chains span pages; entities are renamed ("Acme", "the Seller", "it")
Cross-document entity resolution the same company in a thousand filings
Roles as output an event record needs fields: agent, object, date, amount
Rare and domain senses "discharge" in a hospital against a court against a battery

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.html:
Trace — a contract split into two chunks:

Chunk Text Problem
1 "The Agreement between Acme and Beta began in 2021." fine
2 "It was terminated in March after they missed two payments." It and they have no antecedent inside the chunk
The effect:query "when was the Acme–Beta agreement terminated"chunk 2 has no "Acme", "Beta" or "Agreement"weak match in both BM25 and dense retrievalanswer missed

stages.name: What I'd build
stages.claim: resolve at ingestion, structure at output
stages.html:
Ingestion:documentresolve references per sectionchunkprepend a context line or rewrite pronounsembed
Need Approach Layer
self-contained chunks add the document title and section, or an LLM-written context sentence, to each chunk retrieval
entity-centric search link mentions to IDs and index them as metadata retrieval
event extraction LLM with a schema: {agent, action, object, date}, validated orchestration
high-volume, fixed schema fine-tuned span model model

Evaluation hook: retrieval recall on questions whose answer sits in a pronoun-heavy chunk, before and after.

followUps.question: How did classical WSD work?
followUps.html:
By comparing the context with each sense's description, or by supervised classification.

Method Idea
Lesk pick the sense whose dictionary gloss shares the most words with the context
Supervised a classifier per ambiguous word, trained on sense-tagged text
Most-frequent-sense baseline surprisingly strong, and the bar to beat

followUps.question: "LLMs resolve pronouns perfectly, so coreference is solved."
followUps.html:
Within a short context, usually; across a long document or across chunks, no.

  • The reference may be outside the text the model was given.
  • Long chains with renamed entities still produce errors.
  • A retrieval miss happens before the model reads anything.

followUps.question: "The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big." What is "it"?
followUps.html:
The trophy; swap "big" for "small" and it becomes the suitcase.

Sentence ending Referent
"…because it was too big" the trophy
"…because it was too small" the suitcase

This is a Winograd schema: syntax is identical, so only world knowledge decides.

followUps.question: When is explicit SRL still worth running?
followUps.html:
When roles are the product, not an intermediate feature.

  • Event databases: who acquired whom, when, for what.
  • Compliance checks: which party carries which obligation.
  • Explainable extraction: a role frame is easier to audit than free text.

followUps.question: What does chunk-level context cost, and is it worth it?
followUps.html:
An ingestion-time cost per chunk, paid once, against a recall gain on every query.

Option Cost Gain
prepend title and section none modest, free
LLM-written context per chunk one call per chunk at ingestion larger, measure it
full coreference rewrite a model pass plus review of errors it introduces largest on pronoun-heavy text

I'd start with the free option and measure before paying for the others.

dontSay: "These tasks are obsolete" — they left the pipeline, not the problem space.
"Embeddings capture everything" — a chunk with only pronouns embeds poorly.
"SRL and dependency parsing are the same" — one gives semantic roles, the other syntactic arcs.

nlp-classical-q35.testing: whether you treat labels as a measured product, and know why raw percent agreement misleads.
nlp-classical-q35.trap: "hire annotators and collect ten thousand labels", with no pilot and no agreement number.
nlp-classical-q35.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify the task "I'd first pin down what one label means: the unit, the label set, whether labels can overlap, and what the model's output will be used for. A vague task can't be labelled consistently."
2 · Draft the guidelines "Then I write guidelines: a definition per label, positive and negative examples, and explicit rules for the borderline cases. I label fifty items myself first; that is where the unclear cases surface."
3 · Pilot and measure "Next a pilot: two or three annotators label the same couple of hundred items independently, and I measure agreement corrected for chance, Cohen's kappa or Krippendorff's alpha. Raw agreement isn't enough: with skewed classes two people can agree ninety-two percent of the time and have a kappa of zero point three."
4 · Scale with checks "I revise the guidelines until agreement is acceptable, then scale: hidden gold items, a double-labelled sample, and an adjudicator for disagreements."
5 · Failure modes "What goes wrong: guideline drift, annotators anchored by model suggestions, and tasks that are subjective by nature."
6 · Keep it alive "Finally the guidelines are versioned with the labels, because a changed definition silently invalidates old data."
Close "Labels are usable when independent people, following the written guideline, agree beyond chance."

stages.name: Clarify the task
stages.html:
Decide Options Why it matters
unit document, sentence, span, pair changes the tool and the agreement metric
label set closed list, with "other" and "unsure" forced choices create noise
overlap single-label, multi-label, nested spans changes guidelines and model head
who labels domain experts, trained annotators, crowd cost against consistency

stages.name: Draft the guidelines
stages.html:
A guideline entry has Example for the label "complaint"
a one-sentence definition the customer reports that something went wrong
positive examples "the parcel arrived broken"
near-miss negatives "how do I return an item?" is a question, not a complaint
a tie-break rule complaint plus question → label complaint
Order:label 50 items yourselfwrite down every hesitationturn each into a ruleonly then brief annotators

stages.name: Pilot and measure
stages.html:
κ = (p_observed − p_chance) / (1 − p_chance)       ← Cohen's kappa, two annotators

Prove it — (raw agreement, chance agreement, kappa) for balanced and for skewed labels:

def kappa(a, b):
    n = len(a); po = sum(x == y for x, y in zip(a, b)) / n
    pe = sum((a.count(l) / n) * (b.count(l) / n) for l in set(a) | set(b))
    return round(po, 2), round(pe, 3), round((po - pe) / (1 - pe), 2)
a = ["pos"] * 45 + ["neg"] * 40 + ["pos"] * 5 + ["neg"] * 10       # balanced labels, 85% raw agreement
b = ["pos"] * 45 + ["neg"] * 40 + ["neg"] * 5 + ["pos"] * 10
print(kappa(a, b))
a = ["neg"] * 90 + ["pos"] * 2 + ["neg"] * 4 + ["pos"] * 4         # 94% "neg", 92% raw agreement
b = ["neg"] * 90 + ["pos"] * 2 + ["pos"] * 4 + ["neg"] * 4
print(kappa(a, b))
# → (0.85, 0.5, 0.7)
# → (0.92, 0.887, 0.29)
Dataset Raw agreement Kappa Reading
balanced classes 0.85 0.70 substantial
94% in one class 0.92 0.29 higher raw agreement, far weaker real agreement
Metric Use when
Cohen's kappa two annotators, categorical labels
Fleiss' kappa, Krippendorff's alpha more than two annotators, missing labels, ordinal scales
pairwise span F1 span tasks such as NER, where "chance" is ill-defined

stages.name: Scale with checks
stages.html:
Control at scale Catches
hidden gold items in every batch an annotator who has drifted or is rushing
10% double-labelled agreement over time, per label
adjudication of disagreements by a senior annotator the final label, and new guideline rules
per-annotator confusion matrix one person systematically confusing two labels

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Failure Symptom Control
Guideline drift agreement falls in later batches recalibration sessions, refreshed gold
Anchoring on pre-labels annotators accept wrong model suggestions blind-label a sample and compare
Subjective task agreement plateaus low (toxicity, sarcasm) keep the label distribution per item, not one "truth"
Unrepresentative sample the model fails on live traffic sample from production, stratified by source and time
Speed incentives short, careless labels pay for quality checks, not only volume

stages.name: Keep it alive
stages.html:
Practice Why
version guidelines and store the version with every label a redefinition makes old labels a different task
keep the disagreements they are the hardest and most informative items
report human agreement next to model scores it is the practical ceiling for the model

Evaluation hook: a model scoring above inter-annotator agreement is fitting annotator habits, not the task.

followUps.question: What kappa is "good enough"?
followUps.html:
It depends on the task; the common bands are conventions, not laws.

Kappa Usual reading (Landis & Koch, 1977)
0.41–0.60 moderate
0.61–0.80 substantial
above 0.80 almost perfect

For a subjective task 0.5 may be the ceiling; for a factual one 0.7 should worry you.

followUps.question: "Annotators agree 95% of the time, so the labels are reliable."
followUps.html:
Not if 95% of items belong to one class.

both annotators say "negative" 95% of the time, independently
chance agreement ≈ 0.95 × 0.95 + 0.05 × 0.05 = 0.905
observed 0.95  →  κ = (0.95 − 0.905) / (1 − 0.905) ≈ 0.47

followUps.question: Agreement stays low after three guideline revisions.
followUps.html:
Then the task as defined may not have a single right answer.

Option When
merge the confused labels the distinction isn't needed downstream
keep soft labels (the distribution of votes) the disagreement is real signal
split the task into simpler yes/no questions one question was hiding several

followUps.question: Can an LLM be one of the annotators?
followUps.html:
Yes, measured exactly like a human annotator.

  • Compute its agreement with human labels on the pilot set.
  • Use it for pre-labels or a first pass; people adjudicate disagreements.
  • Watch for anchoring, and for systematic bias a human group wouldn't share.

followUps.question: How do you budget an annotation project?
followUps.html:
From the test-set size the decision needs, then outward.

budget ≈ (items × labels per item × seconds per label) + pilot + adjudication + gold upkeep
overlap of 10–20% is the price of knowing the label quality

Cutting the overlap saves money and removes the only evidence that the labels are usable.

dontSay: "We'll collect labels and clean them later" — the guideline is fixed before scale.
"Agreement is 92%" without a chance-corrected number.
"Majority vote gives the truth" on a subjective task.

nlp-classical-q36.testing: whether you pick by job (teach, process, model) and know that production systems usually combine them.
nlp-classical-q36.trap: ranking them as old, newer, newest and picking the newest.
nlp-classical-q36.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "They solve different jobs. NLTK is a toolkit of classical algorithms for learning and experiments. spaCy is a fast, opinionated processing pipeline. Hugging Face is a model hub with the libraries to load, fine-tune and tokenize for transformers."
2 · Where NLTK fits "I use NLTK for teaching, prototypes, and the odd utility: a stemmer, WordNet, a corpus reader. I don't put it on a hot path."
3 · Where spaCy fits "spaCy is my choice for production text processing: tokenization, sentence splitting, tagging, NER and rule matching, with batching and one consistent document object."
4 · Where Hugging Face fits "Hugging Face is where the pre-trained models are: embeddings, classifiers, generation, plus fast tokenizers and training utilities."
5 · What I'd pick here "A real system combines them: spaCy for segmentation and rules, a Hugging Face model for the learned step, exported and served behind my own inference layer, with every version pinned."
Close "Pick by job: learn with NLTK, process with spaCy, model with Hugging Face."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
NLTK spaCy Hugging Face
Core job classical algorithms and corpora industrial text-processing pipeline pre-trained transformer models
Style many options per task, strings in and out one tuned default per task, Doc objects model hub plus transformers, tokenizers, datasets
Speed slow, pure Python fast, Cython, batch API depends on model and hardware
Strength breadth, teaching, WordNet tokenization, tagging, parsing, NER, rule matchers state-of-the-art accuracy, fine-tuning
Pick when learning or a one-off utility deterministic preprocessing at volume the task needs a learned model

stages.name: Where NLTK fits
stages.html:
Good use Poor use
teaching tokenization, n-grams, HMM tagging per-request processing in a service
quick experiments with stemmers, WordNet, VADER large batch jobs
reading classic corpora anything needing consistent multi-step pipelines

stages.name: Where spaCy fits
stages.html:
A spaCy pipeline:texttokenizertaggerparserNERcustom componentsDoc
Property Why it matters in production
non-destructive tokenization every token keeps its character offsets, so spans map back to the source
nlp.pipe batching, component disabling throughput: run only the components you need
rule matchers next to statistical components patterns for IDs, dates and domain terms alongside the model
packaged, versioned pipelines reproducible deployments

stages.name: Where Hugging Face fits
stages.html:
Piece Role
Hub pre-trained and fine-tuned checkpoints, with model cards and licences
transformers load, fine-tune, run
tokenizers fast subword tokenization, the exact one the model expects
datasets, evaluation tools data loading and metrics for training

What it doesn't give you: a serving stack. That is a separate decision: an inference server, an ONNX or quantised export, or a hosted endpoint.

stages.name: What I'd pick here
stages.html:
Trace — a support-ticket pipeline, stage by stage:

Stage Library Why
sentence splitting, language-specific tokenization spaCy fast, offsets preserved
order IDs, dates, phone numbers spaCy rule matcher exact patterns, auditable
intent classification, embeddings Hugging Face model, exported for serving learned accuracy
TF-IDF baseline, metrics scikit-learn the baseline every model is compared with
topic exploration Gensim or an embedding-clustering library offline analysis
stemming for the keyword index the search engine's analyzer must match at index and query time

Operational rules: pin library and model versions together; check each model's licence; load models once per process, never per request.

followUps.question: Why is spaCy faster than NLTK?
followUps.html:
Compiled code and a design that processes a document once.

  • Cython internals with hashed strings instead of Python string operations.
  • One pass builds a shared Doc; components add annotations to it.
  • Batching with nlp.pipe, and the option to disable unused components.

followUps.question: "Hugging Face replaces spaCy."
followUps.html:
They sit at different layers, and spaCy can host transformer models as components.

Need Tool
sentence boundaries, offsets, rules spaCy
a fine-tuned transformer Hugging Face, alone or wrapped in a spaCy pipeline

followUps.question: The product must support 60 languages.
followUps.html:
Check coverage per language before choosing; the answer may differ by layer.

Layer Option with broad coverage
tokenization, tagging, parsing Stanza (Universal Dependencies models for many languages)
embeddings, classification multilingual transformer checkpoints
tokenization for scripts without spaces subword tokenizers or language-specific segmenters

followUps.question: Where does scikit-learn fit?
followUps.html:
As the classical modelling layer and the baseline.

textTfidfVectorizerlinear model, inside one Pipelinecross-validation

It is the fastest way to learn whether a task needs a transformer at all.

followUps.question: What are the operational risks of these dependencies?
followUps.html:
Version drift, licences and cold-start cost.

Risk Control
a tokenizer or model update changes outputs pin versions; golden-output tests
model licence forbids commercial use read the model card; keep a registry of approved models
large models load slowly warm instances; load once; smaller distilled models

dontSay: "NLTK is outdated, spaCy is outdated, use Hugging Face" — they do different jobs.
"We'll call the Hugging Face pipeline API in production" — with no serving, batching or version plan.
A library choice with no mention of the baseline it was compared against.

links.label: Library Landscape (NLTK vs spaCy vs HF)

nlp-classical-q37.testing: whether you can argue for a simple representation on its merits, with conditions, instead of apologising for it.
nlp-classical-q37.trap: "only when you can't afford a transformer": that frames it as a budget compromise.
nlp-classical-q37.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "A bag of words keeps which terms occur and drops their order. So the question is whether the label depends on word choice or on word arrangement."
2 · Where bag-of-words wins "It is the right call when specific words carry the label: topic routing of long documents, spam, language identification with character n-grams. It is also right when I need microsecond latency, a weight per term I can show an auditor, or daily retraining against an adversary."
3 · Where it loses "It loses when meaning lives in order or paraphrase: negation, short texts, questions phrased ten different ways."
4 · The deciding question "So I ask: could a person label this from a shuffled list of the words? If yes, sparse features are probably enough."
5 · What I'd pick here "I'd start with TF-IDF over word and character n-grams and a linear model, measure the gap to a transformer on my data, and keep the simple model whenever that gap doesn't pay for the latency and upkeep."
Close "When the words are the signal, counting them is the right model, not the cheap one."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
Representation Keeps Drops
unigram bag of words which words, how often all order
word n-grams (2–3) short local order ("not good", "credit card") long-range structure
character n-grams sub-word patterns, robust to typos word identity
contextual embeddings meaning in context per-term transparency

stages.name: Where bag-of-words wins
stages.claim: when the words are the signal
stages.html:
Condition Why sparse features are right Example
topical labels on long text many label-bearing words per document routing reports to departments
microsecond budget, huge volume a sparse dot product, no GPU first-pass spam filter
explanation required one weight per term regulated decisions, appeals
fast adversarial drift retrains in seconds on today's data spam, abuse keywords
exact terms matter codes and citations are features, not noise legal or log classification
typos and unknown words character n-grams overlap anyway language ID, noisy user text

Prove it — character-trigram overlap survives a typo and an inflection:

def grams(w, n=3): w = f"<{w}>"; return {w[i:i + n] for i in range(len(w) - n + 1)}
def jac(a, b): return round(len(grams(a) & grams(b)) / len(grams(a) | grams(b)), 2)
print(jac("refund", "refnud"), jac("refund", "refunds"), jac("refund", "invoice"))
# → 0.2 0.62 0.0

A word-level feature gives refnud zero overlap with refund. Character trigrams still give 0.2, and 0.62 for the plural.

stages.name: Where it loses
stages.html:
Case Why counts fail
"not good" against "good, not bad" similar words, opposite meaning; bigrams help only locally
"my card was charged twice" against "duplicate payment" no shared words
five-word queries too few features to separate classes
cross-lingual transfer a new language is a new vocabulary

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: could you label it from shuffled words
stages.html:
Shuffled-words test Suggests
label still obvious ("invoice overdue payment reminder") sparse features
label lost ("not was it what I expected great") a model that reads order
unsure run both and compare on a held-out set

stages.name: What I'd pick here
stages.claim: baseline first, keep it if the gap is small
stages.html:
Baseline:textTF-IDF on word 1–2-grams and character 3–5-gramslogistic regression or linear SVMcalibrated scores
Compare Sparse + linear Fine-tuned transformer
quality on my eval set measure measure
p95 latency measure measure
retrain time seconds to minutes minutes to hours
explanation top weighted terms needs attribution tooling

Bigram naive Bayes and linear SVM baselines were shown long ago to be strong on topic and sentiment tasks (Wang & Manning, 2012), so the gap is something to measure, not assume.

followUps.question: What is the hashing trick and when do you need it?
followUps.html:
Mapping features to a fixed number of columns with a hash, so no vocabulary is stored.

Vocabulary dictionary Feature hashing
Memory grows with the data fixed
New words at serving time dropped hashed like any other
Cost — collisions; features can't be named back

followUps.question: "Sparse models can't compete with transformers on accuracy."
followUps.html:
On keyword-driven tasks the gap is often small, and sometimes zero.

  • Where it is large: short, paraphrased or order-dependent text.
  • Where it is small: long topical documents, spam, language ID.
  • The honest answer is a number from your own evaluation set.

followUps.question: The vocabulary keeps growing in production.
followUps.html:
Bound it, or it becomes a memory and drift problem.

  • Minimum document frequency drops one-off tokens.
  • Feature hashing fixes the size.
  • Scheduled refits bring in new terms deliberately.

followUps.question: Naive Bayes or logistic regression on these features?
followUps.html:
Naive Bayes with very little data, logistic regression once there is more.

Naive Bayes Logistic regression
Assumes features independent given the class nothing about feature independence
Small data strong can overfit without regularisation
Probabilities over-confident better calibrated

followUps.question: How do you defend this choice in a design review full of LLM enthusiasts?
followUps.html:
With the comparison table, and the cost of running each option for a year.

Argument Evidence
quality is equal or close both models on the same held-out set
it is faster and cheaper measured latency, hardware needed
it is easier to own retrain time, explanation per decision

And I'd name the condition under which I would switch: a measured gap above an agreed threshold.

dontSay: "Bag-of-words is what you use when you have no GPU."
"It ignores context, so it is useless" — many labels don't need context.
"The transformer is better" with no number from the task at hand.

nlp-classical-q38.testing: whether you can write the two-factor formula, say what each factor is estimated from, and recognise the same decomposition in speech and translation.
nlp-classical-q38.trap: "find the closest dictionary word by edit distance": that is only the candidate step.
nlp-classical-q38.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "The noisy-channel model treats a typo as an intended word that passed through a channel which corrupted it. Correction is asking: which word most probably produced what I see?"
2 · How it works "By Bayes, that is the word maximising two factors: the prior, how likely the word is in the language, times the channel, how likely this particular error is given that word. Candidates come from words within one or two edits."
3 · Prove it "For the typo 'teh', the candidate 'the' wins with ninety-nine percent of the mass: it is a very common word, and swapping two adjacent letters is a very common error."
4 · What it costs or breaks "A word-level prior can't fix real-word errors like 'their' for 'there'; that needs context, so the prior becomes a language model over the sentence. And it over-corrects names and product codes."
5 · So what for the system "In search I use query logs as the prior, correct only when the original returns few results, and always keep the original reachable. The same decomposition is classical speech recognition and statistical translation: a model of how the signal was produced, times a language model."
Close "Prior times channel: what people mean, times how it gets garbled."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
The story:intended word wnoisy channel (fingers, keyboard, OCR)observed string xrecover w
Piece Question it answers
candidate generation which real words are near x?
channel model how likely is this specific error?
language model (prior) how likely is the word, here?

stages.name: How it works
stages.html:
ŵ = argmax over candidates w   P(w | x)
  = argmax  P(x | w) × P(w)             ← Bayes; P(x) is the same for every candidate
            └ channel ┘  └ prior ┘
Factor Estimated from
candidates dictionary words within Damerau–Levenshtein distance 1–2: insert, delete, substitute, transpose
channel P(x given w) confusion counts from real error logs: which letters get swapped, dropped or doubled
prior P(w) word frequency; better, an n-gram or neural language model with context 
strings one edit away from a word of length n (26 letters):
n deletes + (n − 1) transposes + 25n substitutions + 26(n + 1) inserts = 53n + 25
n = 3  →  184 strings, of which only a few are real words

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
Prove it — posterior over candidates (illustrative probabilities):

prior = {"the": 0.05, "then": 0.004, "they": 0.006, "tea": 0.0003}       # P(word), illustrative
channel = {"the": 0.02, "then": 0.0005, "they": 0.001, "tea": 0.003}     # P("teh" | word), illustrative
score = {w: prior[w] * channel[w] for w in prior}
z = sum(score.values())
print({w: round(s / z, 3) for w, s in sorted(score.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1])})
# → {'the': 0.991, 'they': 0.006, 'then': 0.002, 'tea': 0.001}
Candidate Prior Channel Why it loses or wins
the very high high: adjacent transposition wins on both factors
they moderate low: needs an insertion and a transposition channel
tea low moderate: one substitution prior

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.html:
Failure Example Fix
Real-word error "I'll be their at six": every word is in the dictionary context-aware prior: score the whole sentence
Over-correction a brand or SKU "fixed" into a common word protect known entities; require a confidence margin
Unknown intended word new slang, a new product name update the vocabulary from logs
Cognitive errors "definately", phonetic spellings phonetic keys, or a learned channel

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html:
In search:querycandidatesscore with query-log prior × channelcorrect only if the original has few resultsshow "search instead for"
Task "Channel": P(observed given intended) "Prior": P(intended)
spelling correction typing-error model language model
classical speech recognition acoustic model language model
statistical machine translation translation model target-language model
OCR post-correction character-confusion model language model

The reusable idea: separate "how the signal gets distorted" from "what is plausible to say", and estimate each from its own data.

followUps.question: Where does the channel model's data come from?
followUps.html:
From observed corrections.

  • Query logs: a query quickly followed by a reformulation one edit away.
  • Edit histories and correction corpora.
  • Keyboard layout as a prior when data is thin: adjacent keys are confused more.

followUps.question: "Pick the dictionary word with the smallest edit distance."
followUps.html:
Ties are the normal case, and edit distance alone can't break them.

Typo acress Edit distance Decided by
actress, across, acres, access all 1 prior and channel, ideally with context

This is the classic example from Kernighan, Church and Gale (1990).

followUps.question: The misspelling is itself a valid word.
followUps.html:
Then every word is a candidate for correction, and context decides.

for each wordcandidates including itselfscore each sentence variant with a language modelchange only if the gain is large

A high bar for changing a real word keeps false corrections down.

followUps.question: Would you just let an LLM fix spelling?
followUps.html:
For documents, often yes; for per-keystroke or per-query correction, no.

Setting Fit
search queries, autocomplete a lookup-speed noisy channel
long-form text, offline a neural or LLM corrector, with a diff shown to the user

followUps.question: How do you know the corrector helps and doesn't harm?
followUps.html:
Measure both directions.

Metric Reads
correction precision of changes made, how many were right
harm rate correct queries that were wrongly changed
online zero-result rate, and clicks on "search instead for"

A rising click rate on "search instead for" is the alarm for over-correction.

dontSay: "Spelling correction is edit distance" — that is one third of it.
"Always auto-correct" — names, codes and new words get damaged.
"The noisy channel is only for typos" — it is the template for speech and translation decoding too.

nlp-classical-q39.testing: whether you use a public leaderboard only to shortlist, and decide on your own queries, corpus and constraints.
nlp-classical-q39.trap: "pick the top model on the leaderboard."
nlp-classical-q39.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "Intrinsic evaluation tests the vectors by themselves: do similar sentences score as similar. Extrinsic evaluation tests them inside the task: does my retrieval find the right documents."
2 · What intrinsic tells you "Intrinsic scores and public benchmarks tell me which models are generally competent. I use them to shortlist three or four candidates that fit my constraints."
3 · What extrinsic tells you "The decision comes from an extrinsic test: a few hundred real queries with labelled relevant documents from my corpus, chunked the way I'll chunk in production, scored by recall at k and NDCG, with BM25 as a row in the table."
4 · The traps "The traps are domain mismatch, benchmark data the model may have trained on, forgetting the query and document prefixes a model expects, silent truncation of long chunks, and comparing only quality while ignoring dimension, latency and cost."
5 · How I'd decide "So I decide from one table: quality on my data, with the hybrid variant, next to index size and latency. If two models are within noise, the smaller one wins."
Close "The leaderboard picks the candidates; my own queries pick the model."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: the vectors alone, or inside the task
stages.html:
Intrinsic Extrinsic
Tests properties of the embedding space the downstream task result
Examples similarity benchmarks, analogies, clustering quality retrieval recall@k, NDCG, answer quality in RAG
Cost cheap, no system needed needs labelled queries and the real corpus
Risk weak link to your task none: it is your task
Use it to shortlist decide

stages.name: What intrinsic tells you
stages.html:
Source Reads Caveat
semantic-similarity benchmarks do similarity scores track human ratings sentence pairs, not query–document retrieval
public retrieval benchmarks (MTEB, BEIR) broad competence across tasks and domains your domain may not be among them
word analogies linear structure of the space weak predictor of task quality
Shortlisting:filter by licence, languages, max tokens and dimensiontake the top few on retrieval tasksadd one small, cheap model as a control

stages.name: What extrinsic tells you
stages.html:
Protocol:sample real querieslabel relevant documentsindex the corpus with production chunkingrun each candidatefill one table
Candidate recall@10 NDCG@10 + BM25 hybrid Dimension Index size p95 encode latency
BM25 only measure measure — — measure —
model A measure measure measure measure measure measure
model B measure measure measure measure measure measure
small control model measure measure measure measure measure measure
  • A few hundred queries, stratified by type, with a bootstrap interval on each difference.
  • No query logs yet: generate questions from documents with an LLM, then have a person review a sample.

stages.name: The traps
stages.claim: why a good score doesn't transfer
stages.html:
Trap Symptom Guard
Domain mismatch strong on the leaderboard, weak on your legal or medical text evaluate on your corpus
Benchmark contamination the model was trained on the benchmark's data trust held-out, in-house queries
Missing prefixes or instructions quality drops with no error follow the model card: query and passage prefixes, pooling, normalisation
Truncation long chunks lose their tail chunk in this model's tokens, below its limit
Symmetric against asymmetric a similarity model used for short-query-to-long-passage search pick a model trained for retrieval
Thresholds carried over a cosine cut-off from the old model is reused recalibrate per model
Quality only the winner needs four times the memory include dimension, index size and latency in the table

stages.name: How I'd decide
stages.claim: smallest model within noise of the best
stages.html:
Situation Decision
one model clearly ahead on my data, beyond the interval take it, if it fits the budget
two models within noise take the smaller or cheaper one
hybrid closes the gap for a weaker model prefer hybrid with the cheaper model
every model is weak on one query type the fix is elsewhere: chunking, a keyword field, or fine-tuning

Why this matters: changing the embedding model later means re-embedding the corpus, so this choice is expensive to undo.

followUps.question: How do you build the labelled query set cheaply?
followUps.html:
Start from logs or generate, then review.

real or generated queriespool the top results of every candidatea person marks relevant onesfixed evaluation set

Pooling across candidates avoids penalising a model for finding relevant documents the others missed.

followUps.question: "This model tops the leaderboard, so it is the best for us."
followUps.html:
The leaderboard average is over tasks you don't have.

  • Ranks shuffle between domains.
  • Top entries are often large and slow.
  • Small differences at the top are within noise.

followUps.question: Queries are in Hindi and English, documents only in English.
followUps.html:
Then cross-lingual retrieval is the task, and it must be in the test.

Check Why
a slice of Hindi queries against English documents multilingual models differ widely here
BM25 on that slice it will be near zero, so the dense arm carries it

followUps.question: Does a higher dimension mean a better model?
followUps.html:
Not reliably, and it always costs memory.

100,000,000 vectors × 4 bytes:   384 dims → 153.6 GB     1,024 dims → 409.6 GB

Some models are trained so that a prefix of the vector still works (Matryoshka representation learning), which lets you trade size for quality after the fact.

followUps.question: When would you fine-tune instead of choosing another model?
followUps.html:
When every candidate fails on the same domain-specific queries and you have pairs to train on.

Signal Action
failures are jargon or in-house terms fine-tune with mined hard negatives, or add a keyword arm first
failures are scattered the model isn't the bottleneck: look at chunking and query quality
no training pairs generate synthetic pairs, and budget for re-embedding

dontSay: "We chose the number one model on MTEB."
"Embedding quality is the cosine similarity" — it is task performance.
A model choice with no BM25 row and no cost column.

nlp-classical-q40.testing: whether you design a retrieve-then-verify funnel instead of comparing all pairs, and can tie the system to a business outcome.
nlp-classical-q40.trap: one cosine threshold on embeddings, with no verification stage and no hard negatives.
nlp-classical-q40.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "I'd ask what counts as 'the same' for this product: same wording, same meaning, or same intent that deserves the same answer. And what happens on a match: merge, suggest or block."
2 · Constraints and numbers "A million texts is half a trillion pairs, so I can't score pairs directly. I need a cheap stage that proposes a handful of candidates per item."
3 · Baseline design "So it is a funnel. A bi-encoder embeds every text once. An approximate-nearest-neighbour index returns the top ten neighbours of each. A cross-encoder scores only those candidate pairs. A calibrated threshold makes the decision."
4 · Deep-dive the hard part "The hard part is pairs that look alike and aren't: 'how do I open an account' against 'how do I close an account'. Embeddings put them close. The verifier has to be trained on such hard negatives, and the threshold set from labelled pairs."
5 · Failure modes "Failures are differences in a number, a name or a negation; and chains, where A matches B and B matches C but A and C are different."
6 · Evolve "It earns money where repeated meaning is repeated work: deflecting support tickets to an existing answer, merging duplicate listings or questions, and a semantic cache in front of an LLM."
Close "Cheap recall first, precise verification second, and a threshold owned by the action it triggers."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.claim: what "same" means, and what a match triggers
stages.html:
Definition of "same" Example Method
near-identical wording copy with a changed date shingles + MinHash
same meaning "card charged twice" / "duplicate payment" embeddings + verifier
same intent, same answer two differently worded password-reset requests embeddings + verifier, labelled per answer
Action on a match Tolerance for a false match
suggest ("similar questions") high
auto-answer or serve from cache low
merge or delete very low

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
items                 1,000,000
all pairs             1,000,000 × 999,999 / 2 = 499,999,500,000      ← about 5 × 10¹¹ cross-encoder calls
ANN, top 10 each      1,000,000 × 10          = 10,000,000 candidate pairs
reduction             about 50,000×

For an online check, a new item costs one encode, one ANN lookup and ten verifier calls.

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
The funnel:textbi-encoder vectorANN top 10cross-encoder score per paircalibrated thresholdaction
Stage Optimised for Model
candidate generation recall, speed bi-encoder + ANN index
verification precision cross-encoder, or an LLM for a small volume
decision the cost of a false match threshold per action
grouping consistent clusters each item compared with a cluster representative

stages.name: Deep-dive the hard part
stages.claim: close in space, different in meaning
stages.html:
Trace — candidate pairs for one support FAQ:

Pair Embedding similarity Truly the same?
"card charged twice" / "duplicate payment on my card" high yes
"how do I open an account" / "how do I close an account" high no: one word flips the intent
"refund within 5 days" / "refund within 15 days" very high no: the number differs
"reset my password" / "forgot login details" medium yes
Training the verifier:mine top-ranked non-duplicateslabeladd as hard negativesfine-tunerecalibrate the threshold
Threshold choice Set from
per action precision required for that action
on labelled pairs from this domain never carried over from another model or dataset

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Failure Symptom Control
Number, name or negation differs wrong answer served with confidence hard negatives; a rule that key entities and numbers must match
Transitive chaining one giant cluster of loosely related items compare against the cluster's representative, not any member
Template text everything with the same greeting matches strip boilerplate before embedding
Domain shift precision falls on a new product line weekly labelled sample of accepted matches
Stale cache answers an old response is reused after a policy change version and expire cached entries

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
Use Value Metric
Support deflection a known answer is suggested before a ticket is filed deflection rate, with a satisfaction guardrail
Duplicate listings or questions cleaner catalogue, consolidated answers merge precision, search quality
Semantic cache for LLM calls repeated questions skip generation hit rate, and wrong-hit rate from sampled audits
Plagiarism or reuse detection policy enforcement precision at the review queue

A cached or auto-sent answer is an action taken on model output, so that path gets the strictest threshold and a sampled audit.

followUps.question: Why not use the bi-encoder score alone?
followUps.html:
Because it compresses each text separately, so word-level contrasts are blurred.

Bi-encoder Cross-encoder
Sees both texts together no yes
Catches "open" against "close" often not usually
Cost one vector per text one pass per pair

followUps.question: "Cosine above 0.9 means duplicate."
followUps.html:
The number means something different for every model and domain.

  • Calibrate on labelled pairs from your own data.
  • Set it per action, from the precision that action needs.
  • Re-derive it whenever the model changes.

followUps.question: 🧪 100,000 items, top 20 neighbours each. Candidate pairs, against all pairs?
followUps.html:
2 million against about 5 billion.

candidates = 100,000 × 20 = 2,000,000
all pairs  = 100,000 × 99,999 / 2 ≈ 5 × 10⁹

followUps.question: How do you evaluate the whole funnel?
followUps.html:
Each stage on what it is for.

  • Candidate stage: recall of known duplicate pairs within the top k.
  • Verifier: precision and recall on labelled pairs, with a hard-negative slice.
  • End to end: precision of accepted matches from a sampled audit.

followUps.question: What is the risk of a semantic cache in front of an LLM?
followUps.html:
Serving the right answer to a different question, at scale.

Risk Control
near-match with a different constraint key the cache on normalised query plus extracted entities and numbers
user-specific answers shared never cache across users or tenants where content is personal
stale answers expiry, and invalidation when source documents change

dontSay: "Compute cosine for all pairs" — it is 5 × 10¹¹ at a million items.
"Embeddings understand paraphrase" — they also think "open" and "close" are paraphrases.
"We'll merge duplicates automatically" without a precision number for that action.
