nlp-classical-q41.testing: whether you can state the two independence assumptions exactly and explain what they prevent the model from using.
nlp-classical-q41.trap: saying discriminative models won "because they are more accurate" without naming the feature restriction.
nlp-classical-q41.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "A hidden Markov model tells a story of how a tagged sentence is generated: pick a tag given the previous tag, then emit a word given that tag, and repeat."
2 · How it works "That story rests on two assumptions. The Markov assumption: a tag depends only on the tag before it. Output independence: a word depends only on its own tag. So the joint probability is a product of transition and emission probabilities, both read from counts."
3 · Prove it "For 'fish swim fast', noun-verb-noun scores about zero point zero four, nearly forty times the all-noun reading. Viterbi finds that best sequence."
4 · What it costs or breaks "The cost is in the second assumption. The model can't use the word's suffix, its capitalisation or the neighbouring words without modelling how all of those are generated. And it spends effort modelling the words, which we already have."
5 · So what for the system "Discriminative models, logistic taggers and then CRFs, model the tags given the words directly, so any overlapping feature is allowed. Neural encoders then learned the features. HMMs remain where labels are scarce, because they can be trained without them."
Close "The HMM models how text is produced; its successors model only the decision, and can look at anything."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: a story of how tagged text is produced
stages.html: Tags are the hidden states and words are what we observe. Horizontal arrows are transitions; vertical arrows are emissions.

stages.name: How it works
stages.html:
P(words, tags) = Π over positions i   P(tagᵢ | tagᵢ₋₁) × P(wordᵢ | tagᵢ)
                                      └ transition ┘     └ emission ┘

Markov assumption        tagᵢ depends only on tagᵢ₋₁
output independence      wordᵢ depends only on tagᵢ
Parameter Estimated as
transition count(tag A followed by tag B) / count(tag A)
emission count(word with tag) / count(tag)
without labels Baum-Welch (expectation–maximisation)
Tagging:sentenceViterbi over the trellismost probable tag sequence

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: the joint probability of three taggings
stages.html:
start: N 0.6, V 0.4      transitions: N→V 0.7, N→N 0.3, V→N 0.8, V→V 0.2
emissions: fish|N 0.5, fish|V 0.3, swim|N 0.1, swim|V 0.6, fast|N 0.4

N V N:  0.6 × 0.5 × 0.7 × 0.6 × 0.8 × 0.4 = 0.04032        ← the winner
V V N:  0.4 × 0.3 × 0.2 × 0.6 × 0.8 × 0.4 = 0.00461
N N N:  0.6 × 0.5 × 0.3 × 0.1 × 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.00108
Reading Probability Ratio to the best
N V N 0.04032 1
V V N 0.00461 about 1/9
N N N 0.00108 about 1/37

Toy numbers; the same model is decoded step by step in the Viterbi answer.

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.html:
Useful evidence for a tag Why an HMM can't use it directly
suffix -ing, -ly, -tion the emission is over whole words
capitalisation, digits, hyphens the same
the next word, or the word two back each word depends only on its own tag
an unseen word emission probability is zero without smoothing
Weakness Consequence
models P(words) as well capacity spent on generating text we already observe
features must be independent overlapping features would be double-counted

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.claim: model the decision, not the text
stages.html:
Model Models Features Weak point
HMM joint P(words, tags) word identity only the two assumptions
MEMM each tag given previous tag and features arbitrary, overlapping label bias from per-step normalisation
CRF the whole tag sequence given the words arbitrary, overlapping slower training
neural encoder + softmax or CRF the same, with learned features learned from text needs data or pre-training

Where HMMs still earn a place: unsupervised or very low-label settings, speech alignment, biological sequence analysis. And the "emission plus transition" scoring lives on inside every CRF layer.

followUps.question: Generative against discriminative, in one line each?
followUps.html:
One models how the data arose; the other models only the boundary between labels.

Generative (HMM, naive Bayes) Discriminative (logistic regression, CRF)
Learns P(x, y) P(y given x)
Small data often better can overfit
Rich features awkward natural

followUps.question: "HMMs lost because they are less accurate."
followUps.html:
They lost because they can't use the evidence that makes taggers accurate.

  • The accuracy gap is the effect; the feature restriction is the cause.
  • With a suffix and capitalisation feature set, a discriminative tagger handles unknown words that an HMM guesses blindly.

followUps.question: A word never seen in training appears.
followUps.html:
Its emission probability is zero for every tag unless you smooth.

Fix Idea
smoothing reserve mass for unseen words per tag
unknown-word classes map rare words to shapes: "ends in -ing", "capitalised", "has digit"
discriminative model use those shapes as features directly

followUps.question: What is label bias in MEMMs?
followUps.html:
Normalising per step makes states with few outgoing options ignore the observation.

state with one successor: P(next | state, word) = 1 whatever the word says
→ paths through low-branching states get unearned probability
CRF fix: normalise once over whole sequences

followUps.question: When would you still reach for an HMM today?
followUps.html:
When there are no labels and the structure is truly sequential and simple.

  • Unsupervised segmentation or regime detection in logs or sensor streams.
  • Forced alignment of audio and transcript.
  • A transparent baseline whose parameters a domain expert can read.

dontSay: "An HMM assumes words are independent" — it assumes each word depends only on its tag.
"CRFs are HMMs with neural networks" — a CRF is discriminative and globally normalised; no network is required.
"Hidden means the model is a black box" — hidden refers to the unobserved tags.

nlp-classical-q42.testing: whether you can describe a text CNN as a learned n-gram detector, and state the structural reason it lost.
nlp-classical-q42.trap: "CNNs are for images" or "transformers are just better".
nlp-classical-q42.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · What they did well "Around 2014 a one-layer CNN over word embeddings matched or beat far heavier models on sentence classification. It was fast, parallel, and good at spotting key phrases wherever they occur."
2 · How it works "A filter of width three slides over the sentence and fires on a particular kind of three-word pattern: a learned, soft n-gram detector. Max-over-time pooling then keeps each filter's strongest activation, whatever its position."
3 · Why transformers won "They lost for two structural reasons. A filter sees only a fixed window, so relating two distant words needs many stacked layers. And max pooling throws away where things were and in what order. Self-attention connects any two positions in one layer, and it scaled with pre-training."
4 · What survived "What survived: convolutional front-ends in speech models, character-level convolutions for building word representations, and the general idea that local pattern detectors are cheap."
5 · Where I'd still use one "I'd still consider a small text CNN on a device or a microsecond budget, for keyword-driven classification, when a transformer doesn't fit."
Close "Text CNNs detect local patterns very cheaply; language needed long-range links, and attention gives those directly."

stages.name: What they did well
stages.html:
Strength Why
Key-phrase classification "not good", "highly recommend" decide the label wherever they sit
Parallel every window is computed at once, unlike an RNN
Small and fast one convolution layer plus pooling (Kim, 2014)
Position-invariant the same filter fires anywhere in the sentence

stages.name: How it works
stages.claim: slide a filter, keep the maximum
stages.html:
The model:word embeddingsfilters of width 3, 4, 5activation per windowmax-over-time poolingconcatenateclassifier

Prove it — one width-2 filter that learned "not good" (toy activations):

sent = ["the", "plot", "was", "not", "good", "at", "all"]
filt = {("not", "good"): 3.0, ("was", "not"): 0.5}      # a width-2 filter that learned "not good" (toy)
acts = [filt.get(pair, 0.0) for pair in zip(sent, sent[1:])]
print(acts, "→ max", max(acts), "at position", acts.index(max(acts)))
# → [0.0, 0.0, 0.5, 3.0, 0.0, 0.0] → max 3.0 at position 3
Step Result
filter slides over 6 windows fires weakly on "was not", strongly on "not good"
max-over-time pooling keeps 3.0, and forgets it came from position 3

One number per filter goes to the classifier: "was this pattern present anywhere?"

stages.name: Why transformers won
stages.html:
receptive field of L stacked layers, kernel k:   1 + L × (k − 1)
k = 3, L = 4            →  9 tokens
dilations 1, 2, 4, 8    →  1 + 2 × (1 + 2 + 4 + 8) = 31 tokens
self-attention, 1 layer →  the whole sequence
Limit of text CNNs Self-attention's answer
distant words meet only after many layers any two positions interact in one layer
max pooling discards position and order every position keeps its own representation
weights are fixed per offset weights depend on content: what to attend to changes per input
pre-training gains were modest masked and causal language-model pre-training scaled

stages.name: What survived
stages.html:
Survivor Where
Convolutional front-end speech models downsample audio features with convolutions before the transformer layers
Character-level convolutions building word vectors from characters, as in ELMo
Convolutional sequence models fully parallel translation before the transformer (Gehring et al., 2017)
The idea local n-gram detectors are cheap, and attention handles the rest

stages.name: Where I'd still use one
stages.html:
Constraint Fit for a small text CNN
on-device or microsecond latency good: tiny, no attention cost
label decided by short phrases good
long documents with cross-sentence reasoning poor
little labelled data poor against a pre-trained transformer
Decision:baseline with TF-IDF + linearsmall CNN if phrases matter and budget is tightdistilled transformer otherwise

Evaluation hook: the three are compared on the same held-out set with latency next to quality.

followUps.question: Why several filter widths?
followUps.html:
Each width detects patterns of a different length.

Width Detects
2–3 short phrases, negations
4–5 longer expressions, idioms

Their pooled outputs are concatenated, so the classifier sees all scales.

followUps.question: "CNNs can't handle sequences, they are for images."
followUps.html:
A 1-D convolution over tokens is the same operation along one axis.

  • Images: filters slide over height and width.
  • Text: filters slide over position; the embedding dimension is the channel axis.
  • They handled sequences well when the signal was local.

followUps.question: 🧪 Kernel 3, six stacked layers, no dilation. Receptive field?
followUps.html:
Thirteen tokens.

1 + 6 × (3 − 1) = 13

followUps.question: What does max-over-time pooling lose?
followUps.html:
Position, order and count.

Sentence Pooled feature for "good"
"good, good, good" same as one "good"
"good start, bad ending" and "bad start, good ending" identical features

followUps.question: Is there any reason to combine convolutions with transformers today?
followUps.html:
Yes: to cut sequence length cheaply before attention.

raw signal or charactersstrided convolutionsfewer, richer positionstransformer layers

Since attention cost grows with the square of length, halving the sequence quarters that cost.

dontSay: "CNNs never worked for text" — they were state of the art for sentence classification.
"Transformers won because they are bigger" — they won on path length between positions and on pre-training.
"Pooling keeps the important information" — it keeps presence and drops position.

nlp-classical-q43.testing: whether you hold a compact mental model of the field and can place any new task on it in a sentence.
nlp-classical-q43.trap: reciting a list of twenty task names with no organising idea.
nlp-classical-q43.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The levels "Language is analysed in layers: the form of words, their arrangement into sentences, the meaning of sentences, and meaning across sentences and in context. In the usual terms: morphology, syntax, semantics, discourse and pragmatics."
2 · One sentence through them "Take 'Can you pass the salt?'. Morphology and syntax say it is a yes-no question. Semantics says it asks about ability. Pragmatics says it is a request."
3 · The task families "Tasks group by the shape of their output: one label for a text, one label per token, a span, a new sequence, a ranking, or a structure such as a tree."
4 · Where ambiguity lives "Every level has its own ambiguity, and the higher the level, the more context is needed to resolve it."
5 · How I use the map "When a new problem arrives I ask two things: which level is the difficulty at, and what output shape do I need. That picks the model family and the metric."
Close "Levels tell me where the difficulty is; output shape tells me what to build."

stages.name: The levels
stages.claim: from word form to meaning in context
stages.html:
Level Studies Classical task Example difficulty
Phonology sounds speech recognition, text-to-speech "recognise speech" / "wreck a nice beach"
Morphology word structure stemming, lemmatization, subword tokenization "unhappiness" = un + happy + ness
Lexical word meaning word-sense disambiguation "bank"
Syntax sentence structure tagging, parsing "I saw the man with the telescope"
Semantics sentence meaning role labelling, entailment who did what to whom
Discourse meaning across sentences coreference, coherence what "it" refers to
Pragmatics meaning in context and intent intent detection, sarcasm "Can you pass the salt?"

stages.name: One sentence through them
stages.claim: the same words at each level
stages.html:
Trace — "Can you pass the salt?"

Level Analysis What a system would output
morphology can, you, pass, the, salt tokens, lemmas
syntax auxiliary + subject + verb + object: a yes/no question parse tree, question type
semantics asks whether the listener is able to pass the salt predicate pass(you, salt), modality: ability
pragmatics a polite request to pass the salt intent: request

A system that stops at semantics answers "Yes." A system that reaches pragmatics hands over the salt.

stages.name: The task families
stages.html:
Output shape Family Tasks Usual metric
one label per text classification sentiment, intent, topic, language ID accuracy, macro-F1
one label per token sequence labelling part-of-speech tagging, NER entity-level F1
a span in the input extraction extractive QA, keyphrases exact match, token F1
a new sequence generation translation, summarization, dialogue overlap metrics plus faithfulness and human review
a score per pair, or a ranking matching and retrieval search, paraphrase, entailment recall@k, NDCG, MRR
a structure structured prediction parsing, coreference chains, relation graphs attachment score, cluster metrics

stages.name: Where ambiguity lives
stages.html:
Level Ambiguity Resolved by
lexical "bank": river or money the surrounding words
syntactic who has the telescope the wider sentence, or world knowledge
referential "the trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big" world knowledge
pragmatic "great, another outage" tone, situation, speaker
The trend:formstructuremeaningintent, with more context needed at each step

stages.name: How I use the map
stages.claim: two questions for any new task
stages.html:
New request Level of difficulty Output shape So I'd reach for
"route tickets to teams" lexical, some pragmatics one label per text a classifier
"pull drug names and doses from notes" lexical and syntactic spans and relations NER plus relation extraction
"answer questions from our policies" semantics, discourse ranking, then a new sequence retrieval plus generation
"detect sarcastic reviews" pragmatics one label per text a large pre-trained model, and modest expectations

Why this matters: the higher the level, the more context the model needs, and the less a keyword method can do.

followUps.question: Where do LLMs sit on this map?
followUps.html:
They cover every level in one model, and every output shape through generation.

What changed What didn't
no separate component per level difficulty still rises with the level
any task can be phrased as text in, text out the output shape still decides the metric

followUps.question: "Modern NLP doesn't need linguistics."
followUps.html:
The models don't need it as input; the engineer needs it to diagnose them.

  • Naming the level of a failure tells you whether more context, a rule or a different model will fix it.
  • Evaluation sets are built by people who know what phenomena to cover.

followUps.question: Where does retrieval fit: it isn't a "level".
followUps.html:
It is an output shape, a ranking, that can draw on any level.

Retrieval method Level it works at
keyword (BM25) lexical
dense embeddings semantic
reranking with a cross-encoder semantic, some discourse

followUps.question: Give one task per output shape that people confuse.
followUps.html:
Extractive against generative QA, and classification against sequence labelling.

Pair Difference
extractive QA / generative QA a copied span / newly written text
sentiment / aspect sentiment one label per text / labels attached to spans

followUps.question: How does this map help in a design review?
followUps.html:
It turns "can AI do this?" into two answerable questions.

  • Which level is hard here, and so how much context and model capacity is needed.
  • Which output shape, and so which metric and how much labelling.
  • A mismatch (a keyword model on a pragmatic task) is visible before anything is built.

dontSay: A list of task names with no grouping.
"Semantics and pragmatics are the same" — literal meaning against intended meaning.
"LLMs made the levels irrelevant" — they made the pipeline irrelevant, not the difficulty.

nlp-classical-q44.testing: whether you see the eras as layers that are all still present in a production system, not as a sequence of replacements.
nlp-classical-q44.trap: "each era made the previous one obsolete."
nlp-classical-q44.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The rules era "The rules era encoded expert knowledge by hand: grammars, lexicons, patterns. It got precision and explainability right, and failed on coverage: language has too many exceptions to write down."
2 · The statistical era "The statistical era learned from data: n-gram models, HMMs, CRFs, with features designed by people. It got probabilistic modelling and honest evaluation on held-out data right, and was limited by feature engineering and sparsity."
3 · The neural era "The neural era learned the features too: embeddings, then sequence models, then pre-trained transformers. It got representation learning and transfer right, and gave up transparency and control."
4 · What each handed on "Each kept the best of the one before. Statistics kept linguistic structure as features. Neural kept the probabilistic objectives and the evaluation culture."
5 · What it means today "A production system uses all three: rules as guardrails and for exact patterns, statistical thinking for evaluation and calibration, neural models for understanding."
Close "Rules for control, statistics for measurement, neural for representation: three layers, not three replacements."

stages.name: The rules era
stages.html:
Rules (1950s–1980s)
Knowledge comes from linguists and domain experts
Artefacts grammars, lexicons, regular expressions, finite-state transducers
Got right precision, explainability, no training data needed
Hit the wall on coverage and upkeep: every exception is another rule

stages.name: The statistical era
stages.html:
Statistics (1990s–2000s)
Knowledge comes from annotated corpora, with features chosen by people
Artefacts n-gram language models, HMMs, CRFs, SVMs, phrase-based translation
Got right probability as the framework; shared benchmarks and held-out evaluation; graceful handling of noisy input
Hit the wall on feature engineering per task; sparsity; no sharing between similar words

stages.name: The neural era
stages.html:
Neural (2013 onward)
Knowledge comes from raw text at scale, then a little task data
Artefacts word embeddings, sequence-to-sequence with attention, pre-trained transformers, LLMs
Got right learned representations; transfer from pre-training; one architecture for most tasks
Hit the wall on transparency, control, cost, and confident wrong output
The arc:hand-written ruleslearned weights on hand-built featureslearned featurespre-trained general models

stages.name: What each handed on
stages.html:
Trace — "find the dates in this text", solved in each era:

Era Solution Still used for
rules a regular expression per date format exact, well-formed patterns; validation of model output
statistics a CRF tagger with features: digit shape, month lexicon, neighbours low-label, high-volume tagging
neural a fine-tuned encoder, or an LLM with a schema messy, varied phrasing ("the Friday after next")
Handed on From To
linguistic structure (tags, trees, lexicons) rules statistics, as features and label schemes
probabilistic objectives, likelihood, Bayes statistics neural training losses
benchmarks, held-out test sets, significance statistics all model evaluation since
decoding algorithms (Viterbi, beam search) statistics neural generation and tagging

stages.name: What it means today
stages.html:
Layer in a 2026 system Era it comes from Job
input validation, output schemas, block lists, constrained decoding rules control and guarantees
evaluation sets, calibration, thresholds, A/B tests, BM25 statistics measurement and cheap baselines
embeddings, rerankers, LLMs neural understanding and generation

Example: an LLM extracts an invoice total (neural); a rule checks it is a valid amount that matches the line items (rules); a sampled audit tracks the error rate with an interval (statistics).

Why this matters: when a neural component fails, the fix is often a rule around it or a measurement that was missing, not a larger model.

followUps.question: What actually triggered each shift?
followUps.html:
More data and compute, plus a method that could use them.

Shift Enabler
rules → statistics large machine-readable corpora and treebanks; success of statistical speech recognition
statistics → neural GPUs, word embeddings, then attention and pre-training

followUps.question: "Rule-based systems are dead."
followUps.html:
They moved to the edges of the system, where guarantees are needed.

  • Before the model: input validation, routing by pattern, PII patterns.
  • After the model: schema checks, business rules, block lists.
  • Inside decoding: grammars that constrain output to valid JSON or SQL.

followUps.question: Are LLMs a fourth era?
followUps.html:
Arguably: the method is neural, but the way of working changed.

Neural era, earlier Pre-trained LLMs
Per task train or fine-tune a model write a prompt, add context
Bottleneck labelled data evaluation and control

Whether it is a new era or a late phase is a naming question; the practical change is real.

followUps.question: What did the neural era lose that the statistical era had?
followUps.html:
Inspectable parameters and cheap retraining.

  • A CRF's feature weights can be read; a transformer's can't.
  • A linear model retrains in seconds, so drift is cheap to follow.
  • Calibration was often better in simpler models and has to be restored deliberately.

followUps.question: How does this history change how you staff or plan a project?
followUps.html:
Budget for all three layers, not only the model.

Layer Work that needs an owner
rules validators, schemas, policy lists
statistics evaluation sets, labelling, monitoring
neural model choice, prompts, fine-tuning

Projects that fund only the third row tend to stall at the demo.

dontSay: "Each era replaced the last" — each one moved to a different layer.
"The statistical era was just n-grams" — it gave the field its evaluation method.
"Neural models need no rules" — every production deployment wraps them in rules.

nlp-classical-q45.testing: whether you can argue a position with concrete mechanisms and your own evidence, without dismissing LLMs.
nlp-classical-q45.trap: nostalgia ("fundamentals matter") or defensiveness. The case has to be made in money, quality and risk.
nlp-classical-q45.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · State the claim "My claim is that an architect who knows classical NLP builds LLM systems that are cheaper, more accurate and easier to debug. It is leverage in three places."
2 · Leverage on cost "First, cost. Most text traffic is routing, filtering, deduplication and extraction of fixed fields. A small classifier or a rule does that in a millisecond. Knowing when that is enough lets me keep the LLM for the part that needs it."
3 · Leverage on retrieval "Second, retrieval. RAG quality is mostly retrieval quality, and retrieval is classical information retrieval: BM25, hybrid fusion, ranking metrics. The person who knows why an embedding misses a product code fixes it in an afternoon."
4 · Leverage on evaluation "Third, evaluation. Sliced metrics, agreement between annotators, significance, error analysis: that discipline comes from classical NLP, and it is what decides whether an LLM feature can ship."
5 · My evidence "I can point to this in my own work: <fill: one sentence, your strongest of the three anchor stories>."
Close "So I don't see classical and LLM as a choice. Classical fluency is how I decide where the LLM goes, and how I know it is working."

stages.name: State the claim
stages.html:
Without classical fluency With it
every text problem becomes an LLM call each problem goes to the cheapest tool that meets the bar
retrieval is "embed and hope" retrieval is measured, hybrid and tuned
quality is judged by demos quality is judged by sliced metrics with intervals
failures are "the model hallucinated" failures are located: tokenizer, retriever, chunking, labels

stages.name: Leverage on cost
stages.claim: the cheap tool for the bulk
stages.html:
The cascade:all trafficrules and a small modelconfidentdone
The remainder:uncertain or open-endedLLM
Workload Classical tool that often suffices
routing, intent, spam TF-IDF or small encoder classifier
fixed-format fields patterns, a tagger
deduplication at scale hashing, MinHash-LSH
language identification character n-grams 
cost per item = cost_small + escalation_rate × cost_LLM          ← the lever is the escalation rate

stages.name: Leverage on retrieval
stages.html:
RAG symptom Classical diagnosis Fix
misses exact codes and names lexical gap of dense vectors BM25 arm, keyword field
right document retrieved at rank 40 first stage fine, ranking weak reranker; measure NDCG, not only recall
chunks full of "it" and "they" coreference lost at chunk boundaries context added at ingestion
"it got worse after the model change" no golden set recall@k on labelled queries per release

Why this matters: each row is a retrieval-layer fix. None of them is solved by a larger generator.

stages.name: Leverage on evaluation
stages.html:
Classical practice What it prevents in an LLM project
held-out test set, frozen tuning prompts on the examples you report
sliced metrics an average that hides a failing user group
inter-annotator agreement trusting labels, or an LLM judge, that people don't agree with
bootstrap intervals shipping a difference that is noise
error analysis by category fixing symptoms instead of the largest failure bucket

stages.name: My evidence
stages.html:
Anchor story One-sentence shape Your version
Hybrid-retrieval save an exact-match failure fixed with a sparse arm, and the sliced eval that caught it <fill: system, the failing query type, what you added, the before and after number>
Cost-ladder call a classical component replaced, or deliberately not replaced, by an LLM call <fill: the component, the decision, the measured cost and quality outcome>
Data-quality fix deduplication, label noise or a guideline change that moved the metric more than a model change <fill: what was wrong with the data, what you changed, the effect>

Pick the strongest one for the spoken answer and keep the other two for follow-ups.

followUps.question: "Isn't this just nostalgia? LLMs do all of these tasks."
followUps.html:
They can do them; the question is at what cost, latency and risk.

Axis Why "can do" isn't the end of it
cost and latency per-token pricing and network calls at high volume
control exact matching and guarantees need rules and indexes
measurement an LLM feature still needs the classical evaluation method

followUps.question: Which classical topics would you make a new team member learn first?
followUps.html:
The ones that show up in every LLM system.

  • Tokenization: cost, limits and why IDs fragment.
  • BM25 and ranking metrics: the retrieval half of RAG.
  • Evaluation method: slices, agreement, intervals.
  • A linear baseline: so every model has something to beat.

followUps.question: Where is classical NLP truly legacy?
followUps.html:
As pipeline stages that end-to-end models absorbed.

Legacy as a pipeline step Still alive as
parsing before every task a tool for explainable rules
hand-built features per task a baseline and an interpretability aid
separate sense tagging implicit in contextual embeddings

Saying this in the interview makes the rest of the case credible.

followUps.question: How would this change your first 90 days here?
followUps.html:
I'd look for the three levers in your existing systems.

Audit:list text workloads by volumemark which are closed tasks on an LLMcheck retrieval has a BM25 row and a golden setcheck evals are sliced

Each finding comes with a measured before and after, not a rewrite proposal.

followUps.question: Give me a number from your own work.
followUps.html:
<fill: one metric from the anchor story you chose, with its unit and the comparison> Shape:

Part Content
baseline what the system did before, on which slice
change the one classical technique you applied
result the number after, and how it was measured

dontSay: "Fundamentals always matter" — say which fundamental, and what it saved.
"LLMs are overhyped" — the case is about placing them well, not against them.
Any claim of impact without an example of your own.
